Initially created: 2026-01-26T10:34:06.778+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Composed by Xiāo Jí, Duke of Kaiguo of Chéngyáng Commandery, Grand Master of the Palace with Honours, Upper Pillar of State.
All things in the world inherently possess their own substance and form.
The sage observed their categories and resemblances,
and thus established their names.
Therefore it is said: names are used to define the substance.
The nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth;
having names is the origin of the myriad things.
Because they involve function and utility,
appellations were established.
The Book of Rites says:
When a child is three months old,
it smiles and is then named.
Before it is born,
it fundamentally has no name.
The Five Phases are prior to the myriad things;
their forms and functions are endowed by the process of creation.
How could their names not be established first,
and only then their substance and function be clarified?
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo says:
'Mù' (Wood) means 'to touch'.
It touches the earth and grows.
Xǔ Shèn says:
'Mù' (Wood) means 'to cover'.
It means to break forth covering the earth.
The character is derived from '屮' (sprout),
with the lower part depicting its roots.
Its season is spring.
The Book of Rites says:
'Chūn' (Spring) is related to 'chǔn' (to stir).
It is what produces the myriad things.
Its position is in the east.
Shīzǐ says:
'Dōng' (East) means 'movement'.
The stirring *qì* of Zhèn (the trigram) causes movement.
The Báihǔ Tōng says:
'Huǒ' (Fire) is related to 'transformation'.
When the yang *qì* is in operation,
the myriad things transform and change.
Xǔ Shèn says:
'Huǒ' (Fire) means flaming upward.
The character for 'huǒ' flames upward,
it is pictographic.
Its season is summer.
The Shàngshū Dàzhuàn says:
Why is it called 'Xià' (Summer)?
'Xià' means 'to lend' (jiǎ).
'To lend' means to call forth the myriad things
and nurture them.
The Shìmíng says:
'Xià' (Summer) as 'jiǎ' (to lend)
means to generously accommodate the myriad things,
enabling them to grow.
Its position is the south.
The Shàngshū Dàzhuàn says:
'Nán' (South) means 'to bear responsibility' (rèn).
It is the direction where things bear their responsibility.
The Yuánmìng Bāo says:
'Tǔ' (Earth) is related to 'to spit forth' (tǔ).
It contains and emits essential *qì*,
thereby giving birth to things.
Xǔ Shèn says:
'Tǔ' (Earth) is what gives birth by spitting forth.
Wáng Sù says:
'Tǔ' (Earth) is another name for the ground,
considered as one of the Five Phases.
Xǔ Shèn says:
The character uses two strokes to represent what is below and within the earth.
With one vertical stroke
depicting a thing first emerging from the earth.
Its season is late summer.
'Jì' (Late) means 'old'.
By this time, the myriad things achieve completion.
'Old' and 'king' are associated with the last of the four seasons.
Therefore it is called 'old'.
Its position is the center, 'within'.
'Within' means 'to connect'.
The Lǐ Dǒu Wēiyí says:
It obtains the correct *qì* of the Supreme Ultimate,
contains the virtue of the central yellow,
and can encompass the myriad things.
Xǔ Shèn says:
'Jīn' (Metal) means 'to restrain'.
When the yin *qì* first arises,
the myriad things are restrained.
Metal is born from earth.
The character is derived from 'tǔ' (earth),
with marks on the left and right,
depicting metal within the earth.
Its season is autumn.
The Book of Rites says:
'Qiū' (Autumn) is related to 'sorrow' (chóu).
It is the time to inspect and uphold righteousness.
Shīzǐ says:
'Qiū' (Autumn) means 'stern' (sù).
The myriad things cannot but be stern, respectful, reverent, and solemn;
it is the master of ritual.
The Shuōwén says:
When the earth causes things to return, it is autumn.
Its position is the west.
The Shàngshū Dàzhuàn says:
'Xī' (West) means 'fresh' (xiān).
'Fresh' means 'message' (xùn).
'Message' refers to the appearance of things first entering.
The Shìmíng, Guǎngyǎ, and Báihǔ Tōng all say:
'Shuǐ' (Water) means 'level' (zhǔn).
It levels and standardizes the myriad things.
The Yuánmìng Bāo says:
'Shuǐ' (Water) is related to 'to extend' (yǎn).
Through yin transformation it becomes moist and sodden,
flowing, spreading, and moving hiddenly.
Therefore, in forming the character,
two people intersecting with one emerging in the center represents water.
'One' is the beginning of numbers.
The two people represent male and female.
Yin and yang interact to give rise to the One.
Water is where the Five Phases begin;
it is the coalesced fluid of the primordial *qì*.
Guǎnzǐ says:
Water is the blood and *qì* of the earth,
that which flows through its sinews and vessels.
Therefore it is called water.
Xǔ Shèn says:
The character resembles springs flowing together,
with the subtle yang *qì* within.
Its season is winter.
Shīzǐ says:
'Dōng' (Winter) means 'end'.
By winter, the myriad things reach their end and are stored away.
The Book of Rites says:
'Dōng' (Winter) is related to 'center' (zhōng).
'Center' means 'to store'.
Its position is the north.
Shīzǐ says:
'Běi' (North) means 'to lie hidden'.
By winter, all things lie hidden.
The noble and base become as one.
The seasons and directional positions of the Five Phases
have thus been separately explained.
As for the Celestial Stems and Earthly Branches,
they were established based on the Five Phases.
In ancient times, during the era of Xuānyuán (the Yellow Emperor),
they were created by Dà Náo.
Cài Yōng's Yuèlìng Zhāngjù says:
Dà Náo adopted the principles of the Five Phases
and observed the indications of the Dipper's mechanism.
He first created Jiǎ and Yǐ
to name the days,
calling them 'stems' (gān).
He created Zǐ and Chǒu
to name the months,
calling them 'branches' (zhī).
For matters pertaining to Heaven,
the days (stems) are used;
for matters pertaining to Earth,
the months (branches) are used.
This is the distinction between yin and yang,
hence the names 'stems' and 'branches'.
And each has both a general and a specific designation.
First, the general names will be discussed,
then the specific appellations.
The general name 'zhīgàn' (branches and stems):
The character 'gàn' (stem) actually has three different forms:
one is written as '幹',
the second as '簳',
and the third as '干'.
Now, explaining the character '簳':
These branches (zhī) and stems (gǎn),
being matched together to form a system,
are like the branches, twigs, stalks, and stems of a tree,
which together constitute the tree's body.
Therefore, it is called 'gǎn' (stem).
Also written as '幹':
'幹' carries the meaning of 'to accomplish' or 'to manage'.
Writing it as '支' (branch):
'支' carries the meaning of 'to support' or 'to bear responsibility'.
Using these days and hours,
to bear responsibility and manage all affairs.
Therefore, they are called 'zhīgàn' (branches and stems).
Also written with the character '干':
This also carries the meaning of 'stem' or 'pole'.
Like things placed on a pole,
able to stand upright and conspicuously.
Therefore, it is also called 'gān' (pole).
Common writings tend towards simplicity,
hence '干' is used most often.
Regarding the alternative designations:
The Shī Wěi Tuīduò Zāi states:
Jiǎ means to press down;
in spring it opens,
in winter it closes.
Zhèng Xuán, in his commentary on the Lǐjì Yuèlìng, says:
Jiǎ means to press down.
Yǐ means to squeeze through.
In spring, all things shed their shells,
squeezing through and emerging.
Bǐng means a handle.
As things grow,
each grasps its own handle.
Zhèng Xuán says:
Bǐng means to be bright.
In summer, all things are strong and large,
brightly manifest.
Dīng means to halt.
To halt is like to stop.
As things grow,
they are about to reach their stop.
Wù means to trade.
Growth having reached its limit,
at the limit they should then trade and change their former forms.
Jǐ means to order.
Things having just completed their formation,
there is orderly arrangement.
Zhèng Xuán says:
Wù means luxuriance.
Jǐ means to rise.
It means all things have luxuriant branches and leaves,
and those containing blossoms
bend and then rise up.
Gēng means to change.
Xīn means new.
It means things complete their cycle,
change and become new again.
Zhèng Xuán says:
It means all things solemnly change,
their blossoms and fruits newly formed.
Rén means to bear.
Guǐ means to measure.
The yīn bears the yang,
and sprouts are measured out among things.
Zhèng Xuán says:
At this time, it stores and conceals all things;
they bear within below,
and sprouts are measured out.
Zǐ means to multiply.
The yang qi having stirred,
all things multiply and sprout.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
When the yang qi arrives,
it multiplies and nurtures life.
Chǒu means to knot.
To knot means to tie.
Continuing the sprouts and tying them for growth.
Therefore it is said:
They multiply and sprout at zǐ,
and knot their buds at chǒu.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
It speaks of dwelling at the boundary of end and beginning.
Therefore it is named for knotting and tying.
Yín means to shift.
Also said to mean to draw out.
The buds of things slightly protrude,
are drawn and extended,
and shift out from the earth.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Yín is when worms stir and are born.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Yín means to draw out.
It is the meaning of extending and establishing.
Mǎo means to cover.
Things grow large,
covering over the earth.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Mǎo means luxuriant.
Luxuriant indeed.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Mǎo means luxuriant.
When the yang qi reaches here,
things grow and flourish densely.
Chén means to shake.
Shaking and vibrating rapidly,
they leave their old forms.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
At the time of this month,
things all shake and grow.
Sì means to end.
The old forms washed away,
hereupon they are completely finished.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Sì means to rise.
When things reach this time,
they all finish completely and rise up.
Wǔ means to oppose.
Also said to mean calyx.
In the mid-summer month,
all things are grand and large,
their branches and calyxes spread out at wǔ.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Wǔ means to be contrary.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Wǔ means long,
and great.
Clearly, things all grow large.
Wèi means obscure.
The yīn qi has already grown,
all things slightly decline,
their forms hidden and obscure.
Therefore it is said: hidden and obscure at wèi.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Wèi means flavor.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
At this time, things approach completion,
all having their qi and flavor.
Shēn means to extend.
To extend is like to draw out.
It is to grow long.
Aging and declining, they draw out long.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Shēn means to groan.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Shēn means body.
Things all have their bodies fully achieved.
Yǒu means old.
Also said to mean ripe.
All things grow extremely old and become ripe.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Yǒu means full.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Yǒu means to shrink,
the meaning of drawing in.
At this time, things all shrink small and are completed.
Xū means to extinguish.
To kill.
In the ninth month, killing is extreme,
and things are all extinguished.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
At this time, things decline and perish.
Hài means kernel.
To obstruct.
In the tenth month, it stores and conceals all things;
they all enter the kernel obstruction.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Hài means to punish.
It says the yīn qi punishes and kills all things.
The Erya's "Suì Cì" states,
"When the Grand Year is in Yín, it is named Shètígē."
The commentary to the Huáinánzǐ states,
"Gé means 'to arise.'"
"All things receive the yang and arise."
"Mǎo is named Chányān."
"Chán means 'to exhaust.'"
"Yān means 'to stop.'"
"It means the yang qi pushes all things to arise,"
"and the yin qi is exhausted and stops."
"Chén is named Zhíxú."
"Zhí means 'to lie dormant.'"
"Xú means 'to spread out.'"
"It means the things lying dormant in hiding,"
"all disperse and emerge."
"Sì is named Dàhuāngluò."
"Huāng means 'great.'"
"It means all things are blazing and great,"
"scattered and spread out."
"Wǔ is named Dūnzāng."
The Huáinánzǐ states,
"Chánqiāng,"
"Dūn means 'abundant,'"
"Zāng means 'strong.'"
"It means all things are abundant and strong."
"Wèi is named Xiéqià."
The Huáinánzǐ states,
"Xié means 'harmonious.'"
"Qià means 'to combine.'"
"It means the yin desires to transform,"
"and all things are harmoniously combined."
"Shēn is named Tūntān."
The Huáinánzǐ states,
"Tūntān means 'great cultivation.'"
"It means all things cultivate their essential qi."
"Yǒu is named Zuò'è."
The Huáinánzǐ states,
"Named Zuò'è."
"Zuò'è means 'to wither and fall.'"
"It means all things decline and fall."
"Xū is named Yānmào."
"Yān means 'to cover.'"
"Mào means 'to envelop.'"
"It means all things are covered and enveloped."
"Hài is named Dàyuānxiàn."
"Yuān means 'to store,'"
"Xiàn means 'to welcome.'"
"It means all things end in Hài,"
"the great and small deeply stored,"
"hiding in burrows to welcome the yang."
"Zǐ is named Kùndūn."
"Kùn means 'chaotic.'"
"Dūn means 'turbid.'"
"It means the yang qi is chaotic and turbid,"
"and all things sprout buds."
"Chǒu is named Chìfènruò."
"Fèn means 'to rise up.'"
"Ruò means 'to follow.'"
"It means the yang qi rises vigorously and all things arise,"
"none not following their nature."
"Chì is the color of yang."
The Chūnqiū Wěi states,
"These are the names of where the Great Yin resides."
"This differs from the Huáinánzǐ and the Erya."
"These are all alternative names for the branches and stems."
"The general meaning ultimately follows the explanation by qi."
"Therefore, it is fully explained here."
"The 'substance' is named based on form and material,"
"the 'nature' is defined based on function and effect."
"Using the substance and nature of the Five Agents,"
"to benefit all things."
"Therefore, they are combined and distinguished."
"Wood occupies the position of Lesser Yang,"
"with harmonious spring qi,"
"warm, gentle, and soft."
"Fire is latent within it."
"Therefore, wood takes gentleness and warmth as its substance,"
"and pliability and straightness as its nature."
"Fire occupies the position of Greater Yang,"
"blazing, scorching, and radiant."
"Therefore, fire takes brightness and heat as its substance,"
"and flaming upward as its nature."
"Earth is in the middle of the four seasons,"
"at the end of Late Summer,"
"when yang declines and yin grows."
"Occupying the central position,"
"it encompasses the four agents,"
"accumulating dust to form solidity."
"Accumulation creates spaces."
"Having spaces,"
"thus it contains and accommodates."
"Forming solidity,"
"thus it can hold."
"Therefore, earth takes containing dispersion and holding solidity as its substance,"
"and sowing and reaping as its nature."
"Metal occupies the position of Lesser Yin."
"It is the place in the west where things are completed,"
"and when things are completed, they become congealed and strong."
"Lesser Yin is clear and cold."
"Therefore, metal takes strength and coldness as its substance,"
"and compliance and change as its nature."
"Water takes coldness and emptiness as its substance,"
"and moistening and descending as its nature."
"The Hóng Fàn states,"
"'Wood is called pliable and straight,'"
"'Fire is called flaming upward,'"
"'Earth is called sowing and reaping,'"
"'Metal is called compliant and changing,'"
"'Water is called moistening and descending.'"
"These are their natures."
"The Huáinánzǐ states,"
"'The accumulated essence of Heaven and Earth becomes yin and yang,'"
"'the concentrated essence of yin and yang becomes the four seasons,'"
"'the dispersed essence of the four seasons becomes all things.'"
"'The accumulated cold qi of yin,'"
"'turning back, becomes water.'"
"'The accumulated hot qi of yang,'"
"'turning back, becomes fire.'"
"Water, although a yin thing,"
"has yang within it."
"Therefore, water's substance is internally bright."
"Fire, although a yang thing,"
"has yin within it."
"Therefore, fire's substance is internally dark."
"Wood is Lesser Yang."
"Its substance also contains yin qi."
"Therefore, it is internally empty,"
"externally has flowers and leaves,"
"blooming gloriously, pleasing to see."
"Metal is Lesser Yin."
"Its substance is hard and sharp,"
"with a killing nature outwardly,"
"but internally also bright and capable of illumination."
"Earth encompasses the four virtues."
"Therefore, its substance can combine emptiness and solidity."
"The commentary to the Hóng Fàn states,"
"'Wood being called pliable and straight refers to the east.'"
"The Yì states,"
"'Wood on the earth is for observation.'"
"It means the wood emerging from the earth in spring,"
"is all pliable and straight,"
"with flowers and leaves pleasing to see."
"Like a person's dignified demeanor and appearance."
"Xǔ Shèn states,"
"'Among things on earth that are pleasing to see,'"
"'none surpasses wood.'"
"Therefore, the character for 'appearance' (相) has the 'eye' radical beside 'wood.'"
"The ancient kings,"
"when mounting their carriages, had the rhythm of luán bells,"
"when descending from their carriages, had the measure of jade pendants,"
"in hunting, had the regulation of three drives,"
"in drinking farewell toasts, had the ritual of offering and reciprocating."
"They undertook no activity without inspection tours,"
"and did not rob the people of their farming seasons."
"Because it is the beginning of spring farming."
"They had no greedy desires or treacherous schemes,"
"in order to comply with wood qi."
"When wood qi is compliant,"
"then it follows its nature,"
"flourishing abundantly and bearing fruit,"
"to be used by the people."
"The straight ones meet the marking line,"
"the curved ones meet the compass."
"If the ruler loses his dignified demeanor,"
"indulges in excessive wine and licentiousness,"
"imposes heavy corvée and taxes,"
"hunts without restraint,"
"then wood loses its nature,"
"does not grow in spring,"
"and is not usable by the people."
"Bridges and beams do not follow their marking lines."
"Therefore, it is said, 'wood is not pliable and straight.'"
Fire is said to blaze upward.
Blazing upward corresponds to the south,
radiating brilliance,
occurring in the height of summer,
when its energy reaches its peak upward.
Hence it is called blazing upward.
The king faces the light to govern.
This is likely based on its symbolism.
In ancient times, enlightened kings faced south to hear governance,
gathering the outstanding talents from across the realm,
assembling them at court,
to aid in enlightenment.
They dismissed treacherous and flattering ministers,
casting them out into the wilderness,
to clear blockages.
When the right people were appointed,
then the world was greatly well-governed,
and the ruler could govern effortlessly with folded hands.
The Yìjīng uses Lí to represent fire and brightness.
Double Lí means double brightness,
indicating that both ruler and ministers are enlightened.
Enlightenment aligns with the fire energy.
When fire energy is harmonious,
it follows its nature.
Following its nature,
it enables maturation,
serving the needs of the people.
When used, it rises;
when abandoned, it ceases.
If the ruler is not enlightened,
keeping the virtuous at a distance while promoting slanderers and flatterers,
discarding laws and alienating close kin,
killing loyal advisors and pardoning criminals,
depositing the legitimate heir and establishing a concubine’s son,
treating a concubine as the principal wife,
then fire loses its nature,
and when not used, it rises,
slanting with the wind,
burning ancestral temples and palaces,
setting ablaze the dwellings of the people.
Hence it is said: fire does not blaze upward.
Earth is said to sow and reap.
Sowing and reaping means:
planting is called sowing,
gathering is called reaping.
Earth represents the way of the earth,
through which all things penetrate and grow.
Hence it is called sowing and reaping.
Earth occupies the center,
governing the four seasons,
completing the cycle of the year.
The center corresponds to internal affairs.
It symbolizes palaces, spouses, and relatives.
In ancient times, from the Son of Heaven down to the common scholar,
in their palaces and dwellings,
there were proper regulations for height and humility.
It is better to be frugal than excessive.
Yǔ made his palaces humble,
and Confucius praised him for it.
The queen, consorts, and concubines had distinctions,
the nine clans were ordered,
and kin were treated with affection.
Serving as models for the common people,
it was thus.
Aligning with the harmonious central energy,
then earth maintains its nature.
Maintaining its nature,
then the hundred grains are full,
and sowing and reaping succeed.
If the ruler indulges his desires,
expanding palaces, towers, and pavilions,
carving and adorning with five colors,
exhausting human labor,
making no distinction between close and distant,
having excessive numbers of wives and concubines,
then earth loses its nature.
When earth loses its nature,
the energy becomes chaotic,
and sowing and reaping fail.
Hence the five grains do not ripen,
and wind and fog cause harm.
Hence it is said: earth does not sow and reap.
Metal is said to follow and change.
Following and changing means:
change is transformation.
Following a mold and transforming,
the form changes to become a vessel.
In the west, things are already formed,
and the energy of killing is strong.
Hence autumn energy rises,
and eagles and falcons strike;
spring energy stirs,
and eagles and falcons transform.
These are two aspects of killing and life.
Thus white dew becomes frost.
Frost is a symbol of execution and warfare.
The king trains troops,
gathers military affairs,
to punish the unrighteous,
suppress violence and chaos,
to bring peace to the people.
Ancient rulers,
in peace did not forget danger,
to guard against the unexpected.
Hence it is said:
though the world is at peace,
those who forget war are in danger;
though the state is strong,
those who love war will perish.
Killing and warfare must correspond to righteousness.
Corresponding to righteousness, then metal energy is harmonious;
when metal energy is harmonious,
it follows its nature.
Following its nature,
craftsmen smelt and cast,
transforming forms to make vessels.
If the ruler delights in aggression,
loves to attack and wage war,
covets beauty and bribes,
treats the lives of the people lightly,
causing the people to be in turmoil,
then metal loses its nature,
smelting and casting do not transform,
congealing and stagnating, becoming hard and brittle,
and many things fail to form.
In autumn, all things ripen,
the hundred grains are already mature.
If metal energy is opposed,
then all things fail to mature.
Hence it is said: metal does not follow and change.
Water is said to moisten and descend.
Moistening and descending means:
water flows to dampness and seeks low, dirty places.
The north is the ultimate yīn,
symbolizing ancestral temple sacrifices.
Winter is where yang begins,
and yīn ends.
Endings and beginnings
are the guiding principles of time.
The deceased: the soul energy ascends to heaven as spirits,
the bodily energy descends as ghosts.
The essential energy disperses outward and does not return.
Therefore, ancestral temples are established,
to gather what is dispersed.
The Yìjīng says:
Huàn brings success.
The king approaches the temple;
this refers to that.
Now, what can surpass filial piety in the virtue of the sage?
Therefore, the Son of Heaven personally plows,
to provide the sacrificial grains;
the queen personally tends silkworms,
to provide the sacrificial robes.
This is the utmost reverence.
With the utmost reverence,
then ghosts and spirits repay it,
with great blessings.
This aligns with water energy.
When water energy is harmonious,
it follows its nature.
Following its nature,
then springs flow freely,
benefiting the people’s use.
If the ruler neglects sacrifices,
disrespects ghosts and spirits,
opposes the heavenly timing,
then water loses its nature,
water bursts forth violently,
flooding and drowning,
destroying cities and towns,
harming people.
Hence it is said: water does not moisten and descend.
In the beginning of all things,
none do not start from non-being and then come into being.
Therefore, the Yìjīng has the Tàijí,
which generates the two modes,
the two modes generate the four sequences,
and the four sequences generate what is generated.
With the proliferation of all things,
then all things are formed and grow.
All arise from the two energies of yīn and yáng,
stirred and molded,
mutually interacting.
Thus solitary yáng cannot generate alone,
solitary yīn cannot form alone;
they must combine,
as in a furnace for smelting.
Only then do all things transform and connect.
Thus heaven has its images,
essential energy flows downward,
the way of earth contains transformation,
to provide the beginning of forms.
Yīn and yáng wax and wane,
life and killing accomplish their functions.
Clarifying this principle is difficult to clarify;
without numbers, it cannot be fully investigated.
Therefore, numbers are used to distinguish it.
Numbers manifest principles,
just as traps and snares are used to catch fish and rabbits.
Yang initiates and leads,
while Yin assists and completes.
To exhaust the numbers of odd and even,
to fully grasp the way of mutual completion,
and to reach the source of transformation—
all these are detailed in the numbers of the yarrow stalks.
Seven and eight represent stillness,
while nine and six represent movement.
Yang moves forward,
changing from seven to nine.
This symbolizes the breath of life.
It illustrates the expansiveness of the Yang way,
symbolizing the virtue of a ruler.
Leading without cease,
unyielding and never lagging behind,
even when one step away from the extreme,
it still advances.
Thus, nine is movement.
Yin moves backward,
changing from eight to six.
This symbolizes the dissipation of breath.
It illustrates the way of a minister.
Yielding and following,
merely responding and harmonizing.
When matters are close to the ruler,
one quiets down to listen to commands,
and must retreat and yield to clarify one’s duty.
Thus, eight is stillness.
The Yì says:
“Divide into two to symbolize the two forces,
set aside one to symbolize the three powers,
count by fours
to symbolize the four seasons.”
When the remainder in hand is four sevens,
it is called seven.
When it is four eights,
it is called eight.
These are the numbers of the still lines.
The Xià and Yīn dynasties valued simplicity,
and thus used still lines for divination.
When the remainder is four nines,
it is called nine.
When it is four sixes,
it is called six.
These are the numbers of the moving lines.
The Zhōu dynasty combined simplicity and refinement,
and thus used both moving and still lines.
In general, the Great Expansion reaches the numbers of Heaven and Earth, fifty-five.
Jīng Fáng combined the ten celestial stems, twelve earthly branches, and twenty-eight constellations,
making a total of fifty.
The one not used
is the vital breath of Heaven,
intended to seek substance through emptiness.
Thus, forty-nine are used.
Mǎ Róng took the Great Ultimate of the Yì
to mean the North Star.
It gives birth to the two modes,
the two modes give birth to the sun and moon,
the sun and moon give birth to the four seasons,
the four seasons give birth to the five phases,
the five phases give birth to the twelve months,
and the twelve months give birth to the twenty-four solar terms.
The North Star remains fixed and unmoving,
while the other forty-nine
rotate and are put to use.
Zhèng Xuán said:
“The six lines of the hexagram,
originally number fifty.
Of those determined for use,
forty-nine are employed.
The numbers of Heaven and Earth
originally total fifty-five.
Heaven’s five combines with Earth’s ten,
Heaven’s one combines with Earth’s six.
When counting them,
the breaths may merge,
and when merged, they should be subtracted.
The Great Expansion subtracts five,
thus leaving fifty.
Of those used, one is subtracted,
thus leaving forty-nine.
Those not merged
cannot be subtracted.”
Now, to summarize the numbers:
Fifty
refers to Heaven’s one to Earth’s ten,
totaling fifty-five.
This combines the numbers of generation and completion.
If speaking only of the generating numbers,
there are only fifteen,
from one to five.
What the Yì symbolizes,
the lines exhaust with profundity.
Thus, from Heaven and Earth downward,
the numbers of the sun, moon, and so on
are all encompassed by the yarrow stalks and hexagrams.
Cycling and transforming,
endless for ten thousand generations,
and fifty-five.
Five is originally a merged number.
Merged numbers mean Heaven and Earth
each share one entity.
Each entity has one,
directly corresponding and opposing.
Now, exceeding five
means the breaths have merged in number,
and once merged, they are not used again.
This is their matching principle.
Matching means emptiness,
not corresponding to substance.
Not corresponding to substance,
thus affairs have no master,
which is why the merged stalks are not used.
Moreover, setting one aside as empty
symbolizes non-being,
but non-being cannot be symbolized.
Thus, when the use of being reaches its limit,
the function of non-being appears.
Therefore, it is said:
“Seek the great undertaking and obtain auspiciousness and inauspiciousness,
seek auspiciousness and inauspiciousness and obtain the eight trigrams,
seek the eight trigrams and obtain the four seasons,
seek the four seasons and reach the two modes,
seek the two modes and reach the Great Ultimate.
The Great Ultimate
is the great cessation and the ultimate,
the extremity of non-being.
Abandoning being to reach profundity,
reducing the many to approach the few—
this is what it means.”
Thus, it is said:
“The Great Ultimate has nothing further to symbolize,
clarifying its emptiness and stillness,
which cannot be expressed by words or symbols.”
Speaking of five
clarifies that although the myriad things are numerous,
their numbers do not exceed five.
Thus, in Heaven, they are the five stars,
and their spirits are the Five Emperors.
Confucius said:
“I once heard from Lǎo Dān
that Heaven has the five phases:
wood, metal, water, fire, and earth.
Their spirits are called the Five Emperors.”
On Earth, they are the five directions,
and their guardians are the Five Sacred Mountains.
The *Wùlǐ Lùn* says:
“They are guarded by the Five Sacred Mountains.”
In humans, they are the five organs,
and their correspondences are the five sense organs.
The *Huángdì Sùwèn* says:
“The five organs correspond to the five sense organs:
eyes, ears, mouth, nose, and tongue.”
The five phases successively support one another,
alternating between rest and dominance, mutually generating,
giving birth to the myriad things,
operating without cease.
Thus, they are called ‘phases.’
The *Chūnqiū Fánlù* says:
“The breaths of Heaven and Earth
are arranged as the five phases.
The five phases are phases because they move.”
The upper appendix of the Yì says:
The numbers of heaven are five.
Wáng says:
This refers to one, three, five, seven, and nine.
Hán says:
These are the five odd numbers.
The numbers of earth are five.
Wáng says:
This refers to two, four, six, eight, and ten.
Hán says:
These are the five even numbers.
The five positions correspond to each other.
Wáng says:
The five positions are metal, wood, water, fire, and earth.
And each has its pairing.
Wáng says:
This means water in heaven is one,
on earth it is six,
six and one pair in the north.
Fire in heaven is seven,
on earth it is two,
two and seven pair in the south.
Metal in heaven is nine,
on earth it is four,
four and nine pair in the west.
Wood in heaven is three,
on earth it is eight,
three and eight pair in the east.
Earth in heaven is five,
on earth it is ten,
five and ten pair in the center.
Therefore it is said:
The five positions correspond to each other,
and each has its pairing.
Xiè says:
Yīn and yáng correspond to each other,
odd and even numbers are matched,
each has its pairing.
Hán says:
The numbers of heaven and earth
each have five,
the five numbers are matched
to combine and form metal, wood, water, fire, and earth.
The "Hóng Fàn" chapter of the Shàng Shū says:
The five agents:
the first is called water,
the second is called fire,
the third is called wood,
the fourth is called metal,
the fifth is called earth.
These are all their generative numbers.
The "Yuè Lìng" chapter of the Lǐ Jì says:
The number of wood is eight,
the number of fire is seven,
the number of metal is nine,
the number of water is six,
the number of earth is five.
These are all their completion numbers.
Only earth speaks of its generative number.
Heaven generates water with one in the north,
the position of the noble man.
The yáng qi subtly stirs beneath the Yellow Springs.
At the beginning of movement, there is no duality;
the number of heaven and yáng combine to become one.
Although water is a yīn entity,
yáng is within it.
Following the beginning of yáng,
therefore the number of water is one.
At the extreme of yáng, yīn is generated;
yīn begins at wǔ.
At the beginning, there is also no duality.
The two qì of yīn and yáng
each have their own beginning.
It should correctly be said to be one,
but it is said to be two,
because yáng is revered.
Since the revered encompasses the beginning,
yīn, being humble, assists, harmonizes, and pairs.
Therefore it can generate, and the number of yáng
pairs with yīn within fire.
Although fire is a yáng entity,
in principle it follows yīn to pair and match the beginning of yīn.
Therefore, it establishes its meaning from the beginning.
Hence the number of fire is two.
Lǎo Zǐ says:
Heaven obtains one and thereby is clear;
earth obtains one and thereby is tranquil.
From this we know that both have the meaning of one,
initiating and responding share the same beginning.
Therefore it is said:
Wood matches yáng in movement,
and grows on the left in the east.
Growing leads to flourishing,
flourishing leads to an increase in number.
Therefore the number of wood is three.
Yīn assists yáng in diminishing,
the yīn path turns right and resides in the west.
Being after yáng,
in principle there is no equality.
Therefore the number of metal is four.
The numbers of yīn and yáng
begin with one cycle,
then yáng reaches the center,
encompassing all four agents.
Encompassing leads to greater abundance.
Therefore the number of earth is five.
These are all generative numbers.
All say that it is based on the beginning,
but the completed numbers are not yet clear.
Since the numbers are not yet completed,
they also cannot be put to use.
Yǐng Róng,
in the "Chūnqiū Shìlì," says:
The generative numbers of the Five Phases
cannot yet transform and each accomplish their tasks.
Water congeals and cannot yet flow;
fire has form but does not yet produce blazing light;
wood is brittle and its body rigid;
metal is strong and can be forged;
earth is saline and fragmented.
Thereupon,
Heaven uses the five to oversee the people,
and the ruler transforms them.
The commentary says:
They are matched to become five.
The reason for using five
is that it is the central number of Heaven.
Thus,
water obtains from five,
its number becomes six,
and it can then moisten and descend.
Fire obtains from five,
its number becomes seven,
and it can then blaze and ascend.
Wood obtains from five,
its number becomes eight,
and it can then bend and straighten.
Metal obtains from five,
its number becomes nine,
and it can then follow and change.
Earth obtains from five,
its number becomes ten,
and it can then sow and reap.
Zhèng Xuán says:
If the numbers stopped at five,
then yang would have no mate,
and yin would lack a matching principle.
Therefore, they are combined to form the completed numbers.
The odd numbers are yang initiating at the beginning,
establishing the regulations and measures.
The even numbers are the root of yin,
which achieve completion by obtaining yang.
Thus, Heaven begins with one,
generating water in the north;
Earth uses its six to complete it,
causing it to flow and moisten.
Earth begins with two, generating fire in the south;
Heaven uses seven to complete it,
causing it to shine brightly.
Heaven begins with three, generating wood in the east;
Earth uses its eight to complete it,
causing it to stretch, grow, and flourish.
Earth begins with four, generating metal in the west;
Heaven uses nine to complete it,
causing it to be hard, sharp, and patterned.
Heaven combines qi with five in the center to generate earth;
Earth uses ten to complete it,
in order to provide all things between Heaven and Earth.
Combining them, Earth's six becomes the mate of Heaven's one;
Heaven's seven becomes the mate of Earth's two;
Earth's eight becomes the mate of Heaven's three;
Heaven's nine becomes the mate of Earth's four;
Earth's ten becomes the mate of Heaven's five.
When yin and yang each have their match,
then,
their qi and natures harmonize,
and transformation and action proceed.
Therefore, the movement of the four seasons
is accomplished through the Five Phases.
Earth encompasses the four phases,
occupying the end of each season,
to bring them to completion.
Both the "Wǔxíng Zhuàn" and the "Báihǔ Tōng" say:
Wood cannot grow without earth—
roots and kernels flourish.
Fire cannot blaze without earth—
it gains form by attaching to earth.
Metal cannot be formed without earth—
it enters the mold and takes shape.
Water cannot be contained without earth—
dams and embankments restrain its fullness.
Earth supports the weak and aids the declining,
responding to complete its way.
Thus, the Five Phases mutually require earth.
Earth rules the four seasons
and resides in the center,
not using its name to define the seasons.
Thus, we know they arise simultaneously,
but rely on their principles to generate each other.
The commentary says:
The Five Phases arise together,
each distinguished by name.
Cháng Cóng's discussion of numbers says:
The north is Hài and Zǐ, which are water;
the generative number is one.
Chǒu is earth;
the generative number is five.
One and five combined make six;
therefore, the completed number of water is six.
The east is Yín and Mǎo, which are wood;
the generative number is three.
Chén is earth;
the generative number is five.
Three and five combined make eight;
therefore, the completed number of wood is eight.
The south is Sì and Wǔ, which are fire;
the generative number is two.
Wèi is earth;
the generative number is five.
Two and five combined make seven;
therefore, the completed number of fire is seven.
The west is Shēn and Yǒu, which are metal;
the generative number is four.
Xū is earth;
the generative number is five.
Four and five combined make nine;
therefore, the completed number of metal is nine.
The center is Wù and Jǐ, which are earth;
the generative number is five.
Moreover, earth's position is in the center;
its fundamental number is five.
Two fives combined make ten;
therefore, the completed number of earth is ten.
These two qi of yin and yang
each complete one cycle.
When they share one cycle, it is the generative number.
When each completes its own cycle, it is the completed number.
Yang, being light and clear, ascends to become Heaven;
yin, being heavy and turbid, descends to become Earth.
And yang, reaching the fifth,
enters the center because
its substance is active and swift.
Therefore, it shares one cycle and enters the center.
Yin reaches the tenth before entering the center because
its substance is slow and tardy.
Therefore, it completes its own cycle before entering.
However, all Five Phases must obtain the central qi before they are completed.
Earth resides in the center and rules the four seasons;
all require earth to complete them.
The "Hóng Fàn"
is a book of ancient creation and institution.
Therefore, it speaks of generative numbers.
The "Yuè Lìng" chapter of the "Lǐ Jì"
is a book of seasonal timeliness.
What it values is the accomplishment of affairs and tasks.
Therefore, it speaks of completion numbers.
Only earth speaks of generative numbers,
because earth is valued for its ability to generate,
and moreover, it completes the four phases,
which suffices to summarize it.
This is the meaning of its ability to generate
and to complete.
Zhèng Xuán said,
"By matching heaven and earth,
one takes the principles of yīn and yáng.
Constantly following,
one harmonizes the numbers of the heavenly stems and earthly branches,
taking the days and celestial stems for application."
Although the two explanations differ,
their general meaning is still the same,
ultimately converging with the meaning in the "Yì Jīng" from "heaven's one" to "earth's ten."
The "Xiào Jīng Yuán Shén Qì" states,
"With one, it is established;
with two, it is planned;
with three, it emerges;
with four, it multiplies;
with five, it combines;
with six, it delights;
with seven, it transforms;
with eight, it expands;
with nine, it intensifies;
with ten, it balances."
For the five phases, with one, water is established;
one is the generative number.
By matching five with one,
it becomes water's completion number.
Therefore, it is said, "With one established, six delights."
"Delights" means flourishing.
Two is fire's generative number;
seven is fire's completion number.
Therefore, it is said, "With two, it is planned."
Fire takes transformation as its ability,
therefore it is said, "With seven, it transforms."
"Planning" refers to it being the beginning of change.
Three is wood's generative number;
eight is wood's completion number.
The five phases begin in the east,
therefore it is said, "With three, it emerges."
With eight, it grows and matures,
therefore it is said, "With eight, it expands."
Four is metal's generative number;
nine is metal's completion number.
The west is where things are accomplished,
therefore it is said, "With four, it multiplies."
Categories and types are different,
therefore it is called "With nine, it intensifies."
Five is earth's generative number;
ten is earth's completion number.
With heaven's five
combined with earth's ten,
the meaning of the numbers is thus complete.
Therefore, five speaks of its combination,
and ten speaks of its balance.
"Balance" means being fully prepared and complete.
The "Chūn Qiū Yuán Mìng Bāo" says,
"The embryo interweaves and dances continuously,
to achieve uniformity.
Movement combines with two, hence yīn and yáng.
Completion is received from three, hence the sun, moon, and stars.
Order is displayed through four, hence the seasons.
Arising and standing come from five, hence the phases.
Movement is distributed through six, hence the pitch standards.
Leaping divides through seven, hence the lunar lodges.
Change sprouts through eight, hence the winds.
Distribution reaches its limit through nine, hence the regions.
Exhalation concludes through ten, hence tasks are accomplished and numbers cease."
These, both warp and weft,
together clarify that the generative and completion numbers of the five phases do not exceed ten.
As for the numbers of the stems and branches,
there are generally two kinds.
The first is general numbers,
the second is specific numbers.
Now, first distinguish the general numbers,
then discuss the specific numbers.
General numbers refer to
the ten heavenly stems and twelve earthly branches.
The stems are ten because
they correspond to the great numbers of heaven and earth.
The "Xì Cí" of the "Yì Jīng" says,
"The numbers of heaven are five,
the numbers of earth are five."
The numbers of heaven and earth
do not exceed ten.
Therefore, the stems culminate at ten.
Ten governs the day;
ten days make one xún (a ten-day period).
The branches are twelve because
the "Lǐ Jī Mìng Zhēng" says,
"Administrative measures are twelve,
with honor and lowliness in order."
The "Yuán Shén Qì" says,
"Three threes proceed in participation,
four fours support each other."
Heaven has the qì of the four seasons,
and three months complete one season.
Therefore, it is said, "Three threes proceed in participation,
four fours support each other."
Heaven, earth, and humanity are called the three powers.
This being three
is the constant number for the generation of things.
Accordingly, each generates three;
the root is three and the branches are nine,
hence twelve.
The "Yuán Mìng Bāo" says,
"Numbers are completed through three,
therefore they combine with three.
Three months.
Yáng culminates at nine,
therefore one season is ninety days."
The branches symbolize the moon;
twelve months make one year.
This distinguishes the general numbers.
Regarding the distinct numbers:
the Earthly Branch numbers are:
zǐ is nine,
chǒu eight,
yín seven,
mǎo six,
chén five,
sì four,
wǔ nine,
wèi eight,
shēn seven,
yǒu six,
xū five,
hài four.
The Tàixuán Jīng states that zǐ and wǔ are nine because:
yang arises from zǐ,
and ends at wǔ;
yin arises from wǔ,
and ends at zǐ.
Therefore, zǐ and wǔ are opposite and confronting,
and are where the two qi of yin and yang originate.
Yín is the beginning of yang,
shēn is the beginning of yin.
Counting leftward from the point of origin,
the number is determined upon reaching the beginning point.
Thus, counting from zǐ to shēn yields nine,
counting from wǔ to yín also yields nine,
hence zǐ and wǔ are nine.
Chǒu and wèi are opposite and confronting.
Counting from chǒu to shēn yields eight,
counting from wèi to yín also yields eight,
hence chǒu and wèi are eight.
Yín and shēn are opposite and confronting.
Counting from yín to shēn yields seven,
counting from shēn to yín also yields seven,
hence yín and shēn are seven.
Mǎo and yǒu are opposite and confronting,
counting from mǎo to shēn yields six,
counting from yǒu to yín also yields six,
hence mǎo and yǒu are six.
Chén and xū are opposite and confronting.
Counting from chén to shēn yields five,
counting from xū to yín also yields five,
hence chén and xū are five.
Sì and hài are opposite and confronting.
Counting from sì to shēn yields four,
counting from hài to yín also yields four,
hence sì and hài are four.
It further states:
the yang number culminates at nine,
zǐ and wǔ are the warp of heaven and earth,
therefore they take the ultimate yang number.
From chǒu, wèi, and sì downward,
each number decreases by one,
from eight down to four,
the principle is self-evident.
Regarding the Heavenly Stem numbers:
jiǎ is nine,
yǐ eight,
bǐng seven,
dīng six,
wù five,
jǐ nine,
gēng eight,
xīn seven,
rén six,
guǐ five.
The Tàixuán Jīng states that jiǎ and jǐ are nine because:
jiǎ originates from jiǎzǐ,
following zǐ, hence nine.
Jǐ is paired with jiǎ,
therefore it shares the number nine with jiǎ.
Yǐ originates from yǐchǒu,
following chǒu, hence eight.
Yǐ is paired with gēng,
and shares the number eight with gēng.
Bǐng originates from bǐngyín,
following yín, hence seven.
Xīn is paired with bǐng,
and shares the number seven with bǐng.
Dīng originates from dīngmǎo,
following mǎo, hence six.
Dīng is paired with rén,
and shares the number six with rén.
Wù originates from wùchén,
following chén, hence five.
Guǐ is paired with wù,
and shares the number five with wù.
The Earthly Branches number twelve,
and because opposite pairs share the same number,
they range from nine to four.
The Heavenly Stems number only ten,
and because paired stems share the same number,
they range from nine to five.
It further states:
the Branches follow earth,
therefore their numbers culminate in yin,
using the even number four.
The Stems follow heaven,
therefore their numbers culminate in yang,
using the odd number five.
Five corresponds to the limit of the five qi.
Four corresponds to the limit of the four seasons.
The upper limit does not exceed nine,
as it is the ultimate yang number.
Regarding the numbers of the Five Phases and the Stems and Branches:
in the "flourishing" phase, they are doubled;
in the "king" phase, they are multiplied by ten and then doubled;
in the "resting" phase, they remain as the base number;
in the "imprisoned" and "dead" phases, they are halved.
Through this, by multiplying by four,
the numbers become limitless.
This all follows the increase and decrease of qi.
When qi is abundant, the number is greater;
when qi is weak, the number is smaller.
The theory of Na Yin numbers refers to the musical note to which a person's birth year belongs.
The notes are gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ.
"Na" means to take this note to harmonize with the element associated with the surname.
The Music Weft states:
Confucius said, "I, Qiū, determined surnames by blowing pitch pipes."
One utterance obtaining earth is called gōng;
three utterances obtaining fire is called zhǐ;
five utterances obtaining water is called yǔ;
seven utterances obtaining metal is called shāng;
nine utterances obtaining wood is called jué.
These are all yang numbers.
Generally, the Five Elements have three types of numbers: the birth number, the prime number, and the old number.
Wood: birth number three,
prime number eight,
old number nine.
Fire: birth number two,
prime number seven,
old number three.
Earth: birth number five,
prime number ten,
old number one.
Metal: birth number four,
prime number nine,
old number seven.
Water: birth number one,
prime number six,
old number five.
Guǎn Lù said:
"The old number of earth being one is because earth is the master of all things;
everything returns to it, hence it is one."
The interaction of the Three Powers (heaven, earth, man) completes human principles.
The virtue of fire takes the meaning of the Three Powers,
hence its old number is three.
Water corresponds above to the five stars,
and below matches the five viscera,
hence water's old number is five.
Metal pairs with the seven luminaries,
hence metal's old number is seven.
Wood in heaven is the nine stars,
on earth is the nine provinces,
in humans is the nine orifices,
hence wood's old number is nine.
First comes the birth number,
then the prime number,
lastly the old number.
Na Yin discusses one's birth year,
therefore it uses the final (old) number to explain it.
This explanation is still incomplete.
All things receive the qi of the Five Constants,
combine and transform to generate beings.
After birth, they must reach maturity.
After maturity, there must be decline and old age.
Hence there are three meanings.
The way of humans,
from maturity to old age,
none is not based on ritual and righteousness to establish oneself.
However, those who preserve ritual and righteousness:
all have a beginning,
but few can maintain it to the end.
Now, discussing the Na Yin to which a person belongs:
without humans, none can practice its ritual and righteousness.
Therefore, using the number of final old age,
ritual and righteousness are made clear.
One utterance obtaining earth:
earth, with its encompassing virtue, thickness, and high position, is the ruler.
The ruler is the master of the people;
the master has no second,
it initiates speech,
hence its number is one.
Three utterances obtaining fire:
fire governs ritual,
filial piety and respect come first,
not daring to abandon the virtue of one's birth,
hence its number is three,
following wood's number.
Water resides in the yin position,
the way of a minister.
Earth can control water,
like a ruler controlling a minister.
Release it and it flows;
block it and it stops.
Water does not act on its own authority,
hence it follows earth's number, five.
Metal governs righteousness,
righteousness is the way of husband and wife.
A wife has no independent authority;
there is the principle of following the husband.
Fire is the husband of metal,
hence it uses fire's number, seven.
Wood governs benevolence and filial piety.
Metal can overcome wood,
symbolizing the ancestral temple.
The Shì Jīng says:
"Metal is the skeleton,
wood is the inner and outer coffins."
This clarifies that metal and wood pertain to matters of ghosts and spirits,
to be served with reverence.
Hence wood follows metal's number,
therefore its number is nine.
One demonstrates the ruler's virtue;
two obeys parents;
three expresses the minister's integrity;
four respects and follows the husband;
five serves ghosts and spirits.
Thus ritual and righteousness are complete,
and human affairs are fulfilled.
Therefore, Na Yin uses these numbers.
Regarding Na Yin:
Zǐ and Wǔ belong to Gēng,
the days governed by the Zhèn trigram.
Chǒu and Wèi belong to Xīn,
the days governed by the Xùn trigram.
Yín and Shēn belong to Wù,
the days governed by the Kǎn trigram.
Mǎo and Yǒu belong to Jǐ,
the days governed by the Lí trigram.
Chén and Xū belong to Bǐng,
the days governed by the Gèn trigram.
Sì and Hài belong to Dīng,
the days governed by the Duì trigram.
One utterance obtaining earth:
birth year Gēngzǐ.
Zǐ belongs to Gēng;
counting one utterance,
thus it is obtained.
Three utterances obtaining fire:
birth year Bǐngyín.
Yín belongs to Wù.
Counting from Bǐng to Wù,
makes three in total.
Five utterances obtaining water:
birth year Rénxū.
Xū belongs to Bǐng.
Counting from Rén to Bǐng,
makes five in total.
Seven utterances obtaining metal:
birth year Rénshēn.
Shēn belongs to Wù.
Counting from Rén to Wù,
makes seven in total.
Nine utterances obtaining wood:
birth year Jǐsì.
Sì belongs to Dīng.
Counting from Jǐ to Dīng,
makes nine in total.
The sixty Jia-Zi combinations
all follow this pattern.
The branches belong to the eight trigrams.
For determining Na Yin,
all are taken in sequence based on opposition,
such as Zǐ and Wǔ belonging to Gēng:
Zǐ and Wǔ are directly opposite.
The remaining examples are all like this.
Now, yang bestows and yin transforms;
therefore, when receiving qi and determining form,
all rely on yin and yang
to nurture and complete them.
Thus, what humans belong to
is all spoken of in terms of yang numbers.
The reason why zǐ and wǔ belong to Gēng, for example,
is that Qián is the father,
Kūn is the mother,
and together they have six children.
Hence it is said:
Qián leads the three sons—
Zhèn, Kǎn, and Gèn;
Kūn leads the three daughters—
Xùn, Lí, and Duì.
Yin and yang generate each other,
so from Qián one seeks daughters,
and from Kūn one seeks sons.
Thus, Qián’s first seeking yields Xùn, called the eldest daughter;
the second seeking yields Lí,
called the middle daughter;
the third seeking yields Duì,
called the youngest daughter.
Kūn’s first seeking yields Zhèn,
called the eldest son;
the second seeking yields Kǎn,
called the middle son;
the third seeking yields Gèn,
called the youngest son.
Jiǎ is the beginning of the yang heavenly stems,
taken from the lower three lines of Qián.
Rén is the end of the yang heavenly stems,
taken from the upper three lines of Qián.
Yǐ is the beginning of the yin heavenly stems,
taken from the lower three lines of Kūn.
Guǐ is the end of the yin heavenly stems,
taken from the upper three lines of Kūn.
The remaining six stems
are assigned to the sons for yang,
and to the daughters for yin.
After Jiǎ and Yǐ,
come Bǐng and Dīng.
Thus, Bǐng is assigned to the youngest son Gèn,
and Dīng to the youngest daughter Duì.
After Bǐng and Dīng,
come Wù and Jǐ.
Thus, Wù is assigned to the middle son Kǎn,
and Jǐ to the middle daughter Lí.
After Wù and Jǐ,
come Gēng and Xīn.
Thus, Gēng is assigned to the eldest son Zhèn,
and Xīn to the eldest daughter Xùn.
This is because it proceeds from the youngest to the oldest,
from the small to the large,
and from the subtle to the manifest.
Once the assignment of stems is completed,
next the earthly branches are assigned.
Zhèn is the eldest son.
Thus, the first nine of its hexagram obtains Qián’s zǐ,
and the fourth nine obtains Qián’s wǔ.
Zhèn’s stem is Gēng,
so zǐ and wǔ belong to Gēng.
Xùn is the eldest daughter.
After zǐ comes chǒu,
so the first six of its hexagram obtains Kūn’s chǒu.
After wǔ comes wèi,
and the fourth six obtains Kūn’s wèi.
Xùn’s stem is Xīn,
so chǒu and wèi belong to Xīn.
Kǎn is the middle son.
After chǒu comes yín,
so the first six of its hexagram obtains Qián’s yín.
After wèi comes shēn,
and the fourth six obtains Qián’s shēn.
Kǎn’s stem is Wù,
so yín and shēn belong to Wù.
Lí is the middle daughter.
After yín comes mǎo,
so the first nine of its hexagram obtains Kūn’s mǎo.
After shēn comes yǒu,
and the fourth nine obtains Kūn’s yǒu.
Lí’s stem is Jǐ,
so mǎo and yǒu belong to Jǐ.
Gèn is the youngest son.
After mǎo comes chén,
so the first six of its hexagram obtains Qián’s chén.
After yǒu comes xū,
and the fourth six obtains Qián’s xū.
Gèn’s stem is Bǐng,
so chén and xū belong to Bǐng.
Duì is the youngest daughter.
After chén comes sì,
so the first nine of its hexagram obtains Kūn’s sì.
After xū comes hài,
and the fourth nine obtains Kūn’s hài.
Duì’s stem is Dīng,
so sì and hài belong to Dīng.
The six children take stems
that are the remainder of Qián and Kūn.
When taking branches,
they all derive from Qián and Kūn.
Yang takes from Qián,
yin takes from Kūn.
All are received from the parents,
so the six children together govern the twelve earthly branches.
Human nà yīn
all follows from this.
Jiǎ, Yǐ, Rén, and Guǐ
are not used for nà yīn
because they belong to Qián and Kūn.
Someone may ask:
When the six children use stems,
they take those unused by the parents;
when using branches, why are they entirely the same as the parents?
The answer is:
Stems are yang,
and yang substance is odd,
so they are precisely divided for one-time use.
Branches are yin,
and yin substance is even,
so they are used repeatedly.
Moreover, turtle shell divination uses days,
thus directly seeking from stems.
Therefore, the revealed signs are divided into ten parts.
Yarrow stalk divination uses the earthly branches,
directly seeking from branches,
so the flying and hidden six lines
all discuss the twelve earthly branches.
Although the substance is not combined,
they must be paired to clarify the meaning.
Stems are honored.
Thus, they must be established first and then the branches sought.
Although yarrow stalk divination does not directly use stems,
it still requires stem assistance
to reveal its tendency.
Just as turtle shell divination judges the twelve earthly branches,
although the sign’s body has no branch imagery,
it must be inferred and discussed.
Although yarrow stalk divination lacks three Jiǎ, three Rén, three Yǐ, and three Guǐ,
it also infers the virtual to seek the actual.
Moreover, when setting stems,
one starts first from the parents,
and then proceeds to the six children.
Assign Jiǎ to Qián,
Yǐ to Kūn,
Bǐng to Gèn,
Dīng to Duì,
Wù to Kǎn,
Jǐ to Lí,
Gēng to Zhèn,
Xīn to Xùn,
going through the eight trigrams.
Rén returns to Qián,
then Guǐ returns to Kūn.
The ten stems’ positions in the six lines:
Qián and Kūn hold honored positions,
so taking their beginning and end is logical.
Each substance obtains two stems.
Branches are directly used on the lines,
so each hexagram is fully equipped.
Yang trigrams take yang branches,
yin trigrams take yin branches.
Four trigrams are yang together,
four trigrams are yin together,
not exactly the same as the parents.
When Fúxī drew the eight trigrams as three lines,
he encompassed heaven, earth, and man.
Thus, when dividing stems,
each trigram takes three,
with Qián and Kūn at the beginning,
so they take Jiǎ and Yǐ.
Later, Shénnóng doubled them,
making them eight pure trigrams.
There is a principle of doubling.
Thus, the six stems of the hexagrams are all the same as the parents,
with no duality in meaning.
Therefore, the later hexagrams take Rén and Guǐ.
As for Jiǎ, Yǐ, Rén, and Guǐ,
each missing three,
they are all arranged among the virtual uses.
They are not entirely absent
because yin has the meaning of following yang.
The Nine Palaces:
they are divided above into the heavens,
and distinguished below on the earth,
each occupying nine positions.
In the heavens, there are the twenty-eight lunar mansions
and the nine stars of the Northern Dipper.
On the earth, there are the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and the center.
They are distributed across the nine regions,
and are called "palaces"
because they are all places where spirits roam and dwell.
Hence they are named "palaces."
Zhèng Sīnóng states:
"Tàiyī moves through the palaces of the eight trigrams,
every four steps entering the center.
The center
is where the earth spirits reside,
thus it is called the Nine Palaces."
The "Qián Záo Dù" of the Yì Wěi states:
"The Yì says: 'One yīn and one yáng is called the Dào.'
Therefore, Tàiyī takes its numbers
to move through the Nine Palaces.
The Yì says:
Heaven is one, earth is two;
heaven is three, earth is four;
heaven is five, earth is six;
heaven is seven, earth is eight;
heaven is nine, earth is ten.
The numbers of heaven and earth
sum to fifty-five.
In the use of the Nine Palaces,
heaven subtracts one,
earth subtracts two,
and humanity subtracts three.
The remainder is forty-nine,
which corresponds to the number of yarrow stalks.
Further, the four seasons subtract four,
leaving forty-five.
The five represents the Five Phases;
the forty represents the completed numbers of the Five Phases.
Combined, they form the number of one season.
Distributed among the five directions,
each direction having nine
represents the ninety days of one season,
and the four directions complete the four seasons.
Three palaces facing each other,
summing to fifteen,
represent the number of one solar term,
forming the twenty-four solar terms."
The "Hóng Fàn" chapter of the Shàng Shū states:
"The first is called
the Five Phases.
Its position is in the north,
where yang energy begins,
and all things are about to sprout.
The second is called
reverently applying the five affairs.
Its position is in the southwest,
where humility approaches virtue,
and court audiences bring auspicious celebrations.
The third is called
diligently applying the eight policies.
Its position is in the east,
where all grains are cultivated,
and hemp, flax, silkworms, and mulberries thrive.
The fourth is called
harmoniously applying the five calendars.
Its position is in the southeast,
where the sun, moon, stars, and constellations,
clouds, and rain all arise.
The fifth is called
establishing the use of the royal standard.
Its position is in the central palace,
where officials set up standards,
and governance transforms the lords and ministers.
The sixth is called
governing with the three virtues.
Its position is in the northwest,
where violence is suppressed and subdued,
and legal disputes are adjudicated.
The seventh is called
illuminating with the examination of doubts.
Its position is in the west,
where auspicious and inauspicious outcomes are determined,
and doubts are distinguished.
The eighth is called
contemplating with the various omens.
Its position is in the northeast,
where reverence for virtue is upheld,
and arrogance and disorderly conduct are restrained.
The ninth is called
encouraging with the five blessings,
and warning with the six extremes. Its position is in the south,
where all things are full and mature,
yin energy is disseminated,
the seasons complete the annual virtue,
yin and yang are harmoniously balanced,
and the Five Phases are without error."
Thus, the Yellow Emperor's Nine Palaces Classic states:
Wear nine and tread one,
Three on the left and seven on the right,
Two and four form the corners,
Six and eight form the feet,
Five occupies the central palace,
Overall governing gains and losses.
The numbers are: Kǎn one,
Kūn two,
Zhèn three,
Xùn four,
Central palace five,
Qián six,
Duì seven,
Gěn eight,
Lí nine.
Tàiyī traverses the nine palaces,
Starting from one,
From few to many,
Following its sequence.
Matching calculations says:
The center and the four cardinal directions,
Each divides nine calculations.
It is commanded:
Wood falls and returns to its root,
Dividing six to Hài.
Thus take six calculations from Zhèn,
To place at Qián.
Water flows toward the end,
Dividing eight to Chǒu.
Thus take eight calculations from Kǎn,
To place at Gěn.
Metal is righteous and firm,
Dividing two returns to Wèi.
Thus take two calculations from Duì,
To place at Kūn.
Fire's nature is blazing and flourishing,
It remains in its own region.
Thus Lí's calculations do not move.
Earth rules the four seasons,
Its root is born at Sì.
Thus divide four calculations from the central palace,
To place at Xùn.
Thus forming the position of wearing nine and treading one.
Also, the initial method of forming the eight trigrams,
Commands the calculations of the directions.
First take nine calculations from the north.
Command:
Water generates wood,
One calculation on Mǎo,
One calculation on Chén.
Also horizontally place one calculation on Jiǎ,
One calculation on Yǐ.
Next take nine calculations from the east.
Command:
Wood generates fire in the south,
Distribute five positions.
Then take the calculations from the south.
Command:
Fire generates earth in the center.
One calculation in the northwest for Wù,
One calculation in the southwest for Jǐ.
Then take the calculations from the center.
Command:
Earth generates metal in the west,
Distribute five positions.
Then take the calculations from the west.
Command:
Metal generates water in the north,
After distributing the positions of the ten heavenly stems and twelve earthly branches across the five directions,
Then add one each of the yīn stems.
Command:
Yīn numbers are even.
Next add one each of the yáng branches.
Command:
The branch substance originally adds its beginning.
The remaining calculations are for the numbers of the twelve months.
Place one calculation in the northwest.
Command:
The beginning of Qián.
Place two calculations in the southwest.
Command:
The beginning of Kūn.
Also place the remaining nine calculations in the center,
As the image of change.
Command:
Qián governs Jiǎ and Rén,
Then take the calculations on Jiǎ and Rén,
To form the Qián trigram.
Also command:
Kūn governs Yǐ and Guǐ,
Next take the calculations on Yǐ and Guǐ,
To form the Kūn trigram.
The parent trigrams,
Once the line images are determined,
Next come the six children.
First start with the eldest son.
Command:
Zhèn governs Gēng, Zǐ, and Wǔ,
Then take the calculations on Gēng, Zǐ, and Wǔ,
To form the Zhèn trigram.
Next the eldest daughter.
Command:
Xùn governs Xīn, Chǒu, and Wèi,
Next take the calculations on Xīn, Chǒu, and Wèi,
To form the Xùn trigram.
Next the middle son.
Command:
Kǎn governs Wù, Yín, and Shēn,
Next take the calculations on Wù, Yín, and Shēn,
To form the Kǎn trigram.
Next the middle daughter.
Command:
Lí governs Jǐ, Mǎo, and Yǒu,
Next take the calculations on Jǐ, Mǎo, and Yǒu,
To form the Lí trigram.
Next the youngest son.
Command:
Gěn governs Bǐng, Chén, and Xū,
Next take the calculations on Bǐng, Chén, and Xū,
To form the Gěn trigram.
Next the youngest daughter.
Command:
Duì governs Dīng, Sì, and Hài,
Next take the calculations on Dīng, Sì, and Hài,
To form the Duì trigram.
Once the eight trigrams are formed.
Question:
From where do the eight trigrams begin?
Answer:
They arise from the five phases.
Also asked:
From what do the five phases arise?
Answer:
They arise from heaven and earth.
From what do heaven and earth arise?
Answer:
They arise from Tàiyī.
From what does Tàiyī arise?
Answer:
It arises from change.
Thus it is said:
In change there is the Supreme Ultimate,
Which generates the two modes.
Thus change the character "change" to "Tàiyī".
Change the character "Tàiyī" to "heaven".
Heaven generates one,
Earth generates two.
Change the character "heaven" to "water".
Heaven generates water.
Change the character "water" to "wood".
Water generates wood.
Change the character "wood" to "fire".
Wood generates fire.
Change the character "fire" to "earth".
Fire generates earth.
Change the character "earth" to "metal".
Earth generates metal.
Change the character "metal" to the eight trigrams characters.
The eight trigrams arise from the five phases.
Change the eight trigrams characters to the twelve months characters.
The months governed by the eight trigrams.
Change the twelve months characters to "earth".
All things emerge and ultimately return to earth.
Thus the method of creating the nine palaces and eight trigrams is fully presented.
The Nine Palaces number one,
begins from the north.
Kǎn one due north,
corresponds to the beginning of heaven.
The beginning has no second, hence one.
The north is the beginning of the Five Phases,
therefore the Five Phases are in the north.
Hence it is said,
the beginning of yang qi,
all things are about to sprout.
The Five Affairs number two,
are in the southwest.
The Five Affairs are appearance, speech, sight, hearing, and thought.
Explained separately in a later chapter.
Because of the Five Phases, there are the Five Affairs,
next in order, hence two.
Also it is said,
Kūn two is in the southwest.
Corresponds to the number of earth.
The southwest is the pitch pipe of Línzhōng,
the second in order of qi.
The Five Affairs are the foremost of human affairs.
Therefore it is said,
humility approaches virtue,
court audiences and auspicious celebrations.
These are what the Five Affairs govern.
The Eight Regulations number three,
are in the east.
The Eight Regulations are food, goods, sacrifices, Minister of Works, Minister of Education, Minister of Justice, guests, and army.
Since there are the Five Affairs,
next cultivate the Eight Regulations,
hence three.
Also it is said,
Zhèn three due east,
corresponds to the number of humans,
the meaning of the three powers is complete.
The east is spring,
the beginning of agriculture.
Food refers to plowing, planting, cooking, and boiling.
Goods refer to accumulation, storage, and exchange,
coins, cloth, metal, and weapons.
Sacrifices refer to sacrificial rites and offerings to spirits.
The Minister of Works is for land and fields.
The Minister of Education is for population, households, and numbers.
The Minister of Justice is for prohibiting and preparing against thieves and robbers,
investigating and inspecting irregularities.
Guests refer to registering comings and goings,
receiving and accommodating auspicious celebrations.
The army is for instructing and regulating farmers,
setting up plows and methods.
Therefore it is said,
cultivating all grains,
hemp, silk, and mulberry.
The Five Calendars number four,
are in the southeast.
The Five Calendars are year, month, day, seasons, and calendar numbers.
Since the Eight Regulations are cultivated,
without years, seasons, months, and days,
there is no means to spread planting.
Next in order, hence four.
Also it is said,
Xùn four southeast,
wind moves through the four seasons,
to correspond to the number of the four seasons.
The southeast is Sì,
pure Qián in charge,
Qián governs heaven,
Xùn governs commands.
Therefore located in the southeast.
Year,
because the four seasons have order, flourishing and decline, beginning and end.
Month and day,
illuminate all things, climate, far and near.
Seasons,
means looking up to the king's transformation,
must establish achievements and offer treasures.
Day and hour,
order yin and yang,
decide and produce things.
Calendar numbers,
record and mark degrees,
farmers watch and wait,
taxes and levies according to the time.
Therefore it is said,
the king is like the year.
Tax numbers are grasped and completed,
to transform those below.
Ministers and officials are like the month,
following transformation and practicing the Way to establish treasures.
Masters and assistants are like the day,
arranging various duties,
creating and making all things.
Year, month, day,
time does not change.
Cultivate tasks and respect time,
to follow the calendar.
Therefore it is said,
sun, moon, stars, and constellations,
clouds and rain arise together.
The Royal Standard number five,
is in the center.
The royal king establishes ten thousand states,
resides in the center, distinguishing the four directions.
All officials thereby govern,
all affairs are fully managed,
years and seasons achieve completion,
duties and tributes are equal.
Land taxes and the five grains,
to supply the king's affairs.
Therefore it is in the center.
The central number is originally five.
Also it is said,
earth resides in the center,
corresponds to the number of the Five Phases.
If the king's actions do not attain the center,
then he cannot establish all affairs.
Therefore it is said,
the royal not reaching the ultimate,
is called not establishing.
Therefore it is said,
all officials set up standards,
governance transforms dukes and ministers.
The Three Virtues number six,
are in the northwest.
The Three Virtues are uprightness, overcoming by firmness, overcoming by softness. Qián is the heavenly position,
the image of the ruler.
Exceeding five, hence number six.
Also it is said,
Qián is in the northwest,
yin and yang qi divide in the northwest,
therefore corresponds to the number of the six pitch pipes.
The northwest is where Qián is situated,
therefore the ruler resides there.
Uprightness is human virtue.
The noble person is square and upright with righteousness,
without any crookedness or selfishness.
Therefore it is said,
peaceful and upright.
Do not doubt his virtue.
Overcoming by firmness is heavenly virtue.
Laws and measures are not lost,
light and heavy crimes are submitted to.
Therefore it is said,
deep and hidden, overcoming by firmness.
Overcoming by softness is earthly virtue.
Having virtue, ranks, and emoluments,
stabilizing all duties,
rewarding and bestowing upon all states.
Therefore it is said,
high and bright, overcoming by softness.
Therefore it is said,
suppressing and subduing the violent and strong,
deciding and judging lawsuits and disputes.
Examining Doubts number seven,
is in the west.
Examining Doubts means,
establishing divination and milfoil,
inquiring about doubts and choosing the good,
observing the signs of heaven and earth,
to determine good and bad fortune.
Milfoil is round, hexagrams are square.
Turtle and milfoil together know what is possible and what is not.
Three persons divine,
follow the words of two.
In ancient times, the sages,
careful in planning and valuing beginnings,
moving in affairs and undertaking tasks,
planting roots and opening foundations,
resolving suspicions and settling doubts.
Must plan with the wise and knowing,
with the elders,
and consult with milfoil and turtle.
Therefore actions have no faults,
considerations have no miscalculations.
Barbarians, although lacking the order of ruler and minister,
also have divination for resolving doubts,
sometimes using metal and stone,
sometimes using wood and grass.
Therefore know that examining doubts is a matter
esteemed by the sages,
because it follows after Qián,
hence number seven.
Also it is said,
Duì due west.
Mǎo and Yǒu are the gates of heaven and earth.
Mǎo governs beginning,
Yǒu governs end.
Therefore when the Dipper points to Mǎo,
then all things come out,
points to Yǒu,
then all things enter.
Duì corresponds to the number of the seven stars.
Duì is metal, governs joy and speech,
therefore in the west.
Therefore it is said,
determining good and bad fortune,
distinguishing doubts.
Various Signs number eight,
are in the northeast,
Various Signs means many signs.
The king down to the common people,
none should fail to examine their faults inwardly
and observe the signs and omens outwardly.
By following the signs and understanding the opportunities,
then there will be no calamities or disasters.
If one does not scrutinize their faults,
nor consider the various signs,
then when disaster arrives, they will not realize it,
and ruin and collapse are not far off.
Those who witness signs of opportunity
must reverently serve the Supreme Deity,
so that their actions are without fault;
then blessings and responses will be bestowed upon them.
The Book of Songs says:
"Brightly serving the Supreme Deity,
truly they embrace many blessings."
If one does not respectfully uphold goodness,
nor fear the Supreme Deity,
the multitude of spirits will become angry,
and there will surely be reprimands and punishments.
The number eight
follows after seven.
It is also said:
"Gèn is eight, located in the northeast."
Gèn signifies stopping.
Gèn represents the small paths.
All things emerge greatly from Zhèn,
and emerge in small measure from Gèn.
Zhèn is the eldest among the many male [trigrams],
Gèn is the youngest among the many male [trigrams].
Thus it corresponds to the number of the eight trigrams.
Since Gèn means to stop,
it commands to cease evil and turn to good.
Therefore it is in the northeast.
Hence it is said:
"Solemnly respect the virtuous direction;
wild presumption leads to chaotic conduct."
The five blessings and six extremities, number nine,
are in the south.
The five blessings are longevity, wealth, health and peace, love of virtue, and a good end to one's life.
Longevity means
when filial piety, fraternal duty, and the virtues of the Way are complete,
then one cultivates the divine elixir,
to prolong life and extend years.
Wealth means the transformative influence of virtue reaches all,
and abundance and plenty are without lack.
Health and peace mean
the state's transformation brings peace and tranquility,
lasting joy and freedom from troubles.
Love of virtue means
discussing principles, comparing categories,
promoting the good and restraining the evil.
A good end to one's life means
following the times to accomplish tasks,
so that one's lifespan can fully manifest good virtue.
The six extremities are:
misfortune, premature death, sickness, sorrow, wickedness, and poverty/weakness.
Misfortune and premature death refer to
beheading, displaying severed heads, execution, dismemberment—great crimes.
Sickness refers to
flogging, caning, beating, striking, lying ill, nursing, and observation.
Sorrow,
means discussing, acting, gazing anxiously, and facing the morning sun.
Wickedness,
means head-shaving, foot-shackling, wearing red [convict's clothes], flaying, killing, humiliation, imprisonment, and abandonment.
Poverty,
means repaying bribes, confiscated property, taxes, and seizure of assets.
Weakness,
means expulsion from the city and villages, banishment to borderlands,
to warn those who come after.
The principle of these crimes and punishments resides afterward,
hence the number nine.
It is also said:
"Lí is already in the wǔ [south],
considered as the opposite of zǐ [north].
At the extreme, it returns back.
Therefore Lí is at the very end,
representing the number of the Nine Palaces.
Lí represents brightness;
the ruler faces south to administer governance,
symbolizing the brightness of Lí.
Punishments and penalties require clarity,
hence they are in the south.
Therefore it is said:
"All things generally reach fullness and fruition."
There are only nine palaces.
The reason they are not ten is that
the eight directions and the center
culminate in the number nine.
Above, they correspond to the nine heavens, nine stars, and twenty-eight lunar mansions;
below, they correspond to the five sacred mountains, four great rivers, and nine provinces.
The Nine Palaces Classic states:
One governs Héngshān;
two governs the Sānjiāng;
three governs Tàishān;
four governs the Huái;
five governs Sōnggāo;
six governs the Hé;
seven governs Huàshān;
eight governs the Jǐ;
nine governs Huòshān.
Furthermore, one is Jìzhōu;
two is Jīngzhōu;
three is Qīngzhōu;
four is Xúzhōu;
five is Yùzhōu;
six is Yōngzhōu;
seven is Liángzhōu;
eight is Yǎnzhōu;
nine is Yángzhōu.
The names of the nine provinces
have undergone mutual changes.
The nine provinces of the Tribute of Yǔ
correspond to those of the Táng period.
Those with the same names
are because Yáo commanded Yǔ
to control the floods and divide the land into nine provinces,
and they remained unchanged thereafter.
Therefore, the Zhōu and Yú periods had twelve provinces,
