adding Yōu, Bìng, and Yíng.
Shùn, because Qīngzhōu extended across the sea,
separated Qí to form Yíngzhōu.
Jìzhōu was too vast north to south,
so Wèi was separated to form Bìngzhōu.
North of Yān was separately established as Yōuzhōu.
During the Yīn period, the nine provinces included Yōu and Yíng,
but not Qīng and Liáng.
The Zhōu official system's nine provinces included Yōu and Bìng,
but not Xú and Liáng.
The Hàn established twelve provinces,
adding Jiāo and Yì.
As for Jìzhōu,
the Explanation of Names says:
Jìzhōu takes its name from the land,
having both perilous and easy terrain,
where emperors and kings established their capitals.
The Tàikāng Geographical Records states:
Jì means near.
Its qi is close and similar.
Its territory extends from east of Tàiháng
to Jiéshí, Wángwū, and Dǐzhù.
The Tribute of Yǔ states:
Jì was thus established.
The Annals of Lǚ Bùwéi states:
Between the two rivers is Jìzhōu.
Directly to the north,
Jīngzhōu:
the Explanation of Names says:
Jīng means to alert.
The southern barbarians frequently rebelled and invaded,
so the province's defenses were first strengthened,
requiring constant vigilance.
Its territory borders Jīngshān to the north,
and extends south to the southern side of Héngshān.
The Tribute of Yǔ states:
From Jīng to Héngyáng is Jīngzhōu.
The Ěryǎ states:
South of the Hàn is called Jīngzhōu.
Lǚ's work states:
Jīng is Chǔ.
As for Qīngzhōu,
the Explanation of Names says:
Qīng is in the east, where life is generated.
The Tàikāng Geographical Records states:
The color of the lesser yang is qīng (blue-green);
it is the beginning of the year and the start of affairs,
hence it is used as the name.
Its territory borders the sea to the northeast,
and Dài to the west.
The Tribute of Yǔ states:
From the sea to Dài is Qīngzhōu.
Lǚ's work states:
The eastern sea coast is Qīngzhōu, Qí.
As for Xúzhōu,
the Explanation of Names says:
Xú means relaxed.
The earth's qi is gentle and unhurried.
Its territory extends east to the sea,
north to Dài,
and south to the Huái.
The Tribute of Yǔ states:
From the sea, Dài, and the Huái,
is Xúzhōu.
Lǚ's work states:
Above the Sì is Xúzhōu, Lǔ.
The Ěryǎ states:
East of the Jǐ is called Xúzhōu.
As for Yùzhōu, the Explanation of Names says:
Yù is in the center of the nine provinces,
meaning peaceful and content.
The Tàikāng Geographical Records states:
It receives the harmonious central qi,
its nature and principle are tranquil and relaxed.
Its territory borders Jīng to the south,
and the Hé to the north.
The Tribute of Yǔ states:
From Jīng to the Hé is Yùzhōu.
Lǚ's work states:
Between the Hé and the Hàn is Yùzhōu.
The Ěryǎ states:
South of the Hé is called Yùzhōu.
As for Yōngzhōu,
the Tàikāng Geographical Records states:
Yōng occupies the northwestern position,
where yang does not reach,
and yin qi is obstructed and stifled,
hence it is used as the name.
Its territory borders the Hēishuǐ to the west,
and the Xīhé to the east.
The Tribute of Yǔ states:
From the Hēishuǐ to the Xīhé,
is Yōngzhōu.
Lǚ's work states:
Yōngzhōu is Qín.
The Ěryǎ states:
West of the Hé is called Yōngzhōu.
As for Liángzhōu,
the Tàikāng Geographical Records states:
Liáng means strong.
It takes the strong, metallic qi of the west,
and uses it as the name.
Its territory borders Huàshān to the east,
and the Hēishuǐ to the west.
The Tribute of Yǔ states:
South of Huà and the Hēishuǐ,
is Liángzhōu.
As for Yǎnzhōu,
the Explanation of Names says:
It takes its name from the Yǎnshuǐ.
The Tàikāng Geographical Records states:
It distinguishes the meaning of practicing faithfulness and upholding integrity.
Its territory borders the Jǐ to the southeast,
and the Hé to the northwest.
The Tribute of Yǔ states:
Between the Jǐ and the Hé is Yǎnzhōu.
As for Yángzhōu,
the Explanation of Names says:
Yángzhōu has much water,
and its water waves surge (yáng).
Its territory borders the Huái to the north,
and the sea to the east.
The Tribute of Yǔ states:
From the Huái to the sea is Yángzhōu.
Lǚ's work states:
Yángzhōu is Yuè.
The Ěryǎ states:
South of the Jiāng is called Yángzhōu.
Now, according to the positions of the nine palaces:
Jìzhōu, directly north, is in the Kǎn palace.
Jīngzhōu, southwest, is in the Kūn palace.
Qīngzhōu, directly east, is in the Zhèn palace.
Xúzhōu, southeast, is in the Xùn palace.
Yùzhōu, the center, is in the central palace.
Yōngzhōu, northwest, is in the Qián palace.
Liángzhōu, directly west, is in the Duì palace.
Yǎnzhōu, northeast, is in the Gèn palace.
Yángzhōu, directly south, is in the Lí palace.
These positions are similar to this explanation.
Tàiyī places Yǎnzhōu in the directly northern Kǎn position,
Qīngzhōu in the northeastern Gèn position,
Xúzhōu in the directly eastern Zhèn position,
Yángzhōu in the southeastern Xùn position,
Jīngzhōu in the directly southern Lí position,
Liángzhōu in the southwestern Kūn position,
Yōngzhōu in the directly western Duì position,
Jìzhōu in the northwestern Qián position.
These all follow the original qi of the Five Phases.
The northwest is the Hài position,
so Kǎn water resides there.
The northeast is the Yín position,
so Zhèn wood resides there.
The southeast is the Sì position,
so Lí fire resides there.
The southwest is the Shēn position,
so Duì metal resides there.
Qián is metal,
so it follows the original metal position.
Xùn is wood,
so it follows the original wood position.
Kūn and Gèn are both earth,
so they take the meridians of the earth,
residing directly south and directly north.
These all follow the initial positions of the Zhōulǐ's Office of Regions.
Although the palace positions slightly shift,
the qi of the Five Phases is one.
These nine regions
correspond above to the Nine Heavens,
which are divided into twenty-eight lunar mansions.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
The central heaven is Jūntiān,
its number is five,
its stars are Jiǎo, Kàng, and Dī.
They correspond to the regions of Hán and Zhèng.
Jūn means the pivot.
It extends the pivot to the four directions,
and is also called Jítiān.
It is the master of the four movements,
corresponding to the central palace and Yùzhōu.
The eastern heaven is Cāngtiān,
its number is three,
its stars are Fáng, Xīn, and Wěi.
Fáng and Xīn correspond to the region of Sòng,
Wěi corresponds to the region of Yān.
The color of the east is blue-green.
It corresponds to the Zhèn palace and Qīngzhōu.
The northeast heaven is Biàntiān,
its number is eight,
its stars are Jī, Dǒu, and Niú.
Jī corresponds to the region of Yān,
Dǒu corresponds to the region of Wú,
Niú corresponds to the region of Dài.
It is the end phase of Water,
when yin energy is exhausted and yang energy begins to act,
and all things are about to change.
It corresponds to the Gèn palace and Yǎnzhōu.
The northern heaven is Xuántiān,
its number is one,
its stars are Nǚ, Xū, Wēi, and Shì.
Nǚ corresponds to the region of Yuè,
Xū and Wēi correspond to the region of Qí,
Shì corresponds to the region of Wèi.
The color of Water is black,
hence it is called Xuántiān.
It corresponds to the Kǎn palace and Jìzhōu.
The northwest heaven is Yōutiān,
its number is six,
its stars are Bì, Kuí, and Lóu.
Bì corresponds to the region of Wèi,
Kuí and Lóu correspond to the region of Lǔ.
It is the end phase of Metal,
which is the deep darkness of the Great Yin.
It corresponds to the Qián palace and Yōngzhōu.
The western heaven is Hàotiān,
its number is seven,
its stars are Wèi, Mǎo, and Bì.
Wèi corresponds to the region of Lǔ,
Bì and Mǎo correspond to the region of Zhào.
The color of Metal is white,
hence it is called Hàotiān.
It corresponds to the Duì palace and Liángzhōu.
The southwest heaven is Zhūtiān,
its number is two,
its stars are Zī, Shēn, and Jǐng.
Zī and Shēn correspond to the region of Jìn,
Jǐng corresponds to the region of Qín.
It occupies the end phase of Fire.
The color of yang is vermilion.
It corresponds to the Kūn palace and Jīngzhōu.
The southern heaven is Yántiān,
its number is nine,
its stars are Guǐ, Liǔ, and Xīng.
Guǐ corresponds to the region of Qín.
Liǔ and Xīng correspond to the region of Zhōu.
The nature of Fire is to blaze upward.
Hence it is called Yántiān.
It corresponds to the Lí palace and Yángzhōu.
The southeast heaven is Yángtiān,
its number is four,
its stars are Zhāng, Yì, and Zhěn.
Zhāng corresponds to the region of Zhōu,
Yì and Zhěn correspond to the region of Chǔ.
It is the end phase of Wood,
and is about to become the Great Yang,
hence it is called Yángtiān.
It corresponds to the Xùn palace and Xúzhōu.
These Nine Heavens also belong to the number of the nine stars of the Northern Dipper,
thus they correspond below to the Nine Regions.
Yántiān, number nine,
belongs to the first pivot star of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Lí palace and Yángzhōu.
Biàntiān, number eight,
belongs to the second rotating star of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Gèn palace and Yǎnzhōu.
Hàotiān, number seven,
belongs to the third jade star of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Duì palace and Liángzhōu.
Yōutiān, number six,
belongs to the fourth balance star of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Qián palace and Yōngzhōu.
Jūntiān, number five,
belongs to the fifth equilibrium star of the Dipper,
corresponding to the central palace and Yùzhōu.
Yángtiān, number four,
belongs to the sixth Kāiyáng star of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Xùn palace and Xúzhōu.
Cāngtiān, number three,
belongs to the seventh Yáoguāng star of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Zhèn palace and Qīngzhōu.
Zhūtiān, number two,
belongs to the eighth star of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Kūn palace and Jīngzhōu.
Xuántiān, number one,
belongs to the ninth star of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Kǎn palace and Jìzhōu.
The eighth and ninth stars of the Dipper
are yin and invisible,
because they correspond to yin palaces.
Furthermore, Guō Pú's Yì Zhān states:
Qián is one, Kūn is two,
Zhèn is three, Xùn is four,
Kǎn is five, Lí is six,
Gèn is seven, Duì is eight.
When divining numbers for people or things,
all follow this standard.
This is because they are arranged in the order of parents, sons, and daughters.
These are the numbers of the Nine Palaces and Eight Trigrams.
Therefore, they are fully explained here.
Composed by Xiāo Jí, Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments with Equipage, Duke of the Founding of Chéngyáng Commandery.
The scripture states:
Heaven generates one,
beginning with northern Water.
Earth generates two,
beginning with southern Fire.
Human generates three,
beginning with eastern Wood.
Time generates four,
beginning with western Metal.
The Five Phases generate five,
beginning with central Earth.
It also says:
When it is said Heaven begins by generating one,
it means that because of one, Heaven is generated,
not that Heaven generates one.
Therefore it is said:
One generates two,
two generates three,
three generates the myriad things.
Earth generates two
also means that because of two, Earth is generated;
because of three, humans are generated;
because of four, time is generated.
The Five Phases all arise from one,
and the numbers reach five.
Earth comes last.
Obtaining five, it generates the Five Phases.
The Five Phases emerge together but at different times because,
upon emerging, they leave their origin,
and find their mates.
For example, humans are also born from the same primordial energy,
but each comes from a different family,
they are paired as husband and wife,
and give birth to children.
Thus, the Five Phases all depend on each other to complete.
The Five Phases share the same origin but reside separately,
there is merely a sequence of earlier and later.
Now, the Five Phases all rely on yin and yang energies to be born.
Therefore it is said:
Moist energy generates Water,
warm energy generates Fire,
strong energy generates Wood,
hard energy generates Metal,
harmonious energy generates Earth.
Thus we know the Five Phases arise simultaneously,
relying on their meanings to generate each other.
A commentary says:
The Five Phases arise together,
each distinguished by its name.
However, since the Five Phases are distinguished by name,
they alternately take charge,
rotating in cycles of rest and dominance.
Thus they generate each other.
Yǐng Róng states:
Whenever the Five Phases generate each other,
it refers to different categories transforming each other.
Just as men and women of different surnames can achieve reproduction.
If water is added to water,
no fine flavor is produced.
Prince Xiàn of Héjiān
asked Lord Dǒng of Wēnchéng, saying,
"Filial piety is the constant principle of Heaven,
the righteousness of Earth—what does this mean?"
He replied,
"Heaven has the Five Phases,
which are wood, fire, earth, metal, and water.
Wood produces fire,
fire produces earth,
earth produces metal,
metal produces water,
water produces wood.
Wood corresponds to spring.
Spring governs birth,
summer governs growth and nourishment,
autumn governs harvest,
winter governs storage.
Storage is what is accomplished in winter.
Therefore, what the father begets,
his son grows;
what the father grows,
his son nourishes;
what the father nourishes,
his son completes.
One dares not fail to fulfill the father's intent,
thus exhausting the way of being human.
Therefore, the Five Phases are the Five Constants.
The Báihǔ Tōng states:
'Wood produces fire'
because wood's nature is warm,
fire lies hidden within it,
and emerges through drilling and friction.
Thus wood produces fire.
'Fire produces earth'
because fire is hot and thus can burn wood;
when wood is burned, it becomes ash.
Ash is earth.
Thus fire produces earth.
'Earth produces metal'
because metal resides in stone,
born from the moisture of mountains.
Earth accumulates to form mountains,
and mountains necessarily produce stone.
Thus earth produces metal.
'Metal produces water'
because the energy of lesser yīn
moistens and flows with fluidity;
melting metal also becomes water.
Therefore, mountain clouds arise from moisture.
Thus metal produces water.
'Water produces wood'
because through water's moisture, wood can grow.
Thus water produces wood.
The Yuánmìng Bāo states:
'Yang exhales, yīn transforms.
Thus water produces wood.'
The Chūnqiū Fánlù states:
'The east is wood.
Wood is the foundation of agriculture.
The Minister of Agriculture
manages the five grains and livestock;
the Minister of War consumes them.
Thus wood produces fire.
Fire originally corresponds to the Minister of War,
who should understand.
When celestial signs and omens are not yet apparent,
he alone sees clearly.
Once the world is at peace,
he secures the ruler and ministers.
Thus fire produces earth.
Earth is the ruler,
who should be trustworthy.
He achieves through timely might and strength.
The Grand Minister of Justice.
Thus earth produces metal.
Metal is the Minister of Works, upholding righteousness.
Borders are peaceful and secure,
bandits and thieves do not arise,
cities have no lawsuits or disputes,
then there is peace.
The Minister of Justice enforces the law.
Thus metal produces water.
Water is the Minister of Justice enforcing the law.
He upholds ritual.
Ruler and ministers have their proper positions,
elders and youth have their order.
All artisans work in season,
completing the year's provisions.
Tools and equipment, once made, are supplied
to the Minister of Agriculture, the field official.
Thus water produces wood.'
Though the two explanations differ in details and meaning,
their mutual production is the same.
The Five Phases each have fixed forms.
Only fire emerges through drilling and friction
because fire is the energy of great yang.
It is warm, thus it is born.
What emerges from drilling wood
still relies on and attaches to the myriad things.
Just as the sage has no name,
yet can order the myriad things,
he still takes the myriad things as his name.
Yang energy is supremely divine.
Therefore, it has hidden and manifest aspects.
The Five Phases differ in substance,
and their places of birth and death are not the same;
they circulate through the twelve months and twelve earthly branches, appearing and disappearing.
Wood receives energy at Shēn,
is conceived at Yǒu,
nourished at Xū,
born at Hài,
bathed at Zǐ,
capped and belted at Chǒu,
enters office at Yín,
flourishes at Mǎo,
declines at Chén,
sickens at Sì,
dies at Wǔ,
and is buried at Wèi.
Fire receives energy at Hài,
is conceived at Zǐ,
nourished at Chǒu,
born at Yín,
bathed at Mǎo,
capped and belted at Chén,
enters office at Sì,
flourishes at Wǔ,
declines at Wèi,
sickens at Shēn,
dies at Yǒu,
and is buried at Xū.
Metal receives energy at Yín,
is conceived at Mǎo,
nourished at Chén,
born at Sì,
bathed at Wǔ,
capped and belted at Wèi,
enters office at Shēn,
flourishes at Yǒu,
declines at Xū,
sickens at Hài,
dies at Zǐ,
and is buried at Chǒu.
Water receives energy at Sì,
is conceived at Wǔ,
nourished at Wèi,
born at Shēn,
bathed at Yǒu,
capped and belted at Xū,
enters office at Hài,
flourishes at Zǐ,
declines at Chǒu,
sickens at Yín,
dies at Mǎo,
and is buried at Chén.
Earth receives energy at Hài,
is conceived at Zǐ,
nourished at Chǒu,
temporarily moves at Yín,
born at Mǎo,
bathed at Chén,
capped and belted at Sì,
enters office at Wǔ,
flourishes at Wèi,
declines and sickens at Shēn,
dies at Yǒu,
and is buried at Xū.
Xū is the tomb of Fire.
Fire is its mother;
mother and child should not be buried together.
Proceeding to Chǒu,
Chǒu is the tomb of Metal.
Metal is its child;
this is also inappropriate in principle.
Considering returning to Wèi,
Wèi is the tomb of Wood.
Wood is the ghost of Earth;
fearing it, one dares not enter.
Resting and settling in Chén,
Chén is the tomb of Water.
Water is its wife;
this is appropriate in principle.
Thus, it was buried in Chén.
In ancient times, Shùn was buried in Cāngwú,
and his two consorts did not accompany him.
Hence, it is known that joint burial is not an ancient practice.
However, Jì Wǔzǐ said,
"Since the time of Zhōu Gōng,
this has not been changed."
The Book of Songs says,
"In life, we dwell in separate rooms;
in death, we share the same grave."
This is to emphasize the principle
of reuniting bones and flesh in the same return,
with water and soil sharing the same tomb,
precisely drawing from this.
Also, using the four seasons to explain,
the rationale returns to this.
Gāotáng Lóngyǐ said,
"Earth is born in Wèi,
flourishes in Xū,
strengthens in Chǒu,
and ends in Chén."
Chén is the tomb of water and soil.
Therefore, on Chén days, there is no weeping,
because Chén days are associated with heavy mourning.
The grief of baring the chest and leaping in mourning
surely does not require waiting for the day to pass.
What Gāotáng said
is superficial.
The theory of its birth and kingly influence
is another school altogether.
The Wǔxíng Shū says,
"Although Earth is temporarily supported in the realm of Fire,
born in Sì,
buried in Chén,
Earth divides its kingly influence among the four seasons,
each having its own places of birth and death.
Chén Earth receives its vital energy in Shēn and Yǒu,
is conceived in Xū,
nurtured in Hài,
born in Zǐ,
bathed in Chǒu,
capped and belted in Yín,
assumes office in Mǎo,
reigns in Chén,
declines and sickens in Sì,
dies in Wǔ,
and is buried in Wèi.
Wèi Earth receives its vital energy in Hài and Zǐ,
is conceived in Chǒu,
nurtured in Yín,
born in Mǎo,
bathed in Chén,
capped and belted in Sì,
assumes office in Wǔ,
reigns in Wèi,
declines and sickens in Shēn,
dies in Yǒu,
and is buried in Xū.
Xū Earth receives its vital energy in Yín and Mǎo,
is conceived in Chén,
nurtured in Sì,
born in Wǔ,
bathed in Wèi,
capped and belted in Shēn,
assumes office in Yǒu,
reigns in Xū,
declines and sickens in Hài,
dies in Zǐ,
and is buried in Chǒu.
Chǒu Earth receives its vital energy in Sì and Wǔ,
is conceived in Wèi,
nurtured in Shēn,
born in Yǒu,
bathed in Xū,
capped and belted in Hài,
assumes office in Zǐ,
reigns in Chǒu,

The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì says,
"The Five Elements produce Earth's benefits,
to supply the world."
The Guījīng says,
"When Wood and Earth move, it is Chén Earth;
when Fire moves, it is Wèi Earth;
when Metal moves, it is Xū Earth;
when Water moves, it is Chǒu Earth."
It also says,
"Jiǎ, Yǐ, Yín, and Mǎo correspond to Chén Earth;
Bǐng, Dīng, Sì, and Wǔ correspond to Wèi Earth;
Gēng, Xīn, Shēn, and Yǒu correspond to Xū Earth;
Rén, Guǐ, Hài, and Zǐ correspond to Chǒu Earth."
Generally, each of the Five Elements reigns
for seventy-two days.
Earth resides in the last month of each season for eighteen days,
totaling seventy-two days.
This illustrates that Earth has different places of birth and death in the four directions.
This is used in divination.
When discussing the fixed positions of reign, flourishing, and places of birth and death,
all take the last month of summer, the sixth month,
as the time when Earth reigns.
The Book of Rites says,
"Central Earth
is after the last month of summer,
which is the midpoint of the year,
situated at the center of the four seasons."
The celestial altar, earth spirits, and human ghosts
are also all in Wèi.
Kūn is also in Wèi.
The hexagram is governed by Earth.
Therefore, it is said,
"Earth's virtue is in Wèi,
and ends in Chǒu."
The Book of Changes says,
"In the southwest, one gains companions;
in the northeast, one loses companions."
This clarifies that Earth's reign is fixed in Wèi,
and its tomb is fixed in Chén.
Among the Five Elements, all are born when their parents are in office,
taking the meaning of being strong and capable of nurturing.
Only Metal is born in Fire:
Sì contains strong Earth,
which can produce Metal.
Metal, without Fire,
cannot transform its shape.
Therefore, Metal is born in the position of Fire.
It is also said that Metal is born in the ghost position:
Metal's father is Earth,
and Wù and Jǐ are temporarily governed by Bǐng and Dīng.
The father cannot nurture alone;
the mother is also needed.
Metal in the south encounters Sì Fire.
Metal transforms only when it meets Fire,
and when Metal transforms, Water is produced.
Wù and Jǐ Earth have transformative Water,
so Metal does not fear Fire.
Jǐ contains Water's energy,
making it Metal's stepmother.
Among the Five Elements, all receive vital energy in the month after burial,
because after death, they return to life,
and their spiritual energy never ceases.
The principles of waxing and waning have
three categories in total.
The first distinguishes the waxing and waning of the five agents' substance;
the second discusses the waxing and waning of the heavenly stems and earthly branches;
the third discusses the waxing and waning of the eight trigrams.
Regarding the waxing and waning of the five agents' substance:
In spring, wood waxes;
fire assists;
water rests;
metal is imprisoned;
earth perishes.
In summer, fire waxes;
earth assists;
wood rests;
water is imprisoned;
metal perishes.
In the sixth month, earth waxes;
metal assists;
fire rests;
wood is imprisoned;
water perishes.
In autumn, metal waxes;
water assists;
earth rests;
fire is imprisoned;
wood perishes.
In winter, water waxes;
wood assists;
metal rests;
earth is imprisoned;
fire perishes.
Regarding the waxing and waning of the heavenly stems and earthly branches:
In spring, Jiǎ, Yǐ, Yín, and Mǎo wax;
Bǐng, Dīng, Sì, and Wǔ assist;
Rén, Guǐ, Hài, and Zǐ rest;
Gēng, Xīn, Shēn, and Yǒu are imprisoned;
Wù, Jǐ, Chén, Xū, Chǒu, and Wèi perish.
In summer, Bǐng, Dīng, Sì, and Wǔ wax;
Wù, Jǐ, Chén, Xū, Chǒu, and Wèi assist;
Jiǎ, Yǐ, Yín, and Mǎo rest;
Rén, Guǐ, Hài, and Zǐ are imprisoned;
Gēng, Xīn, Shēn, and Yǒu perish.
In the sixth month, Wù, Jǐ, Chén, Xū, Chǒu, and Wèi wax;
Gēng, Xīn, Shēn, and Yǒu assist;
Bǐng, Dīng, Sì, and Wǔ rest;
Jiǎ, Yǐ, Yín, and Mǎo are imprisoned;
Rén, Guǐ, Hài, and Zǐ perish.
In autumn, Gēng, Xīn, Shēn, and Yǒu wax;
Rén, Guǐ, Hài, and Zǐ assist;
Wù, Jǐ, Chén, Xū, Chǒu, and Wèi rest;
Bǐng, Dīng, Sì, and Wǔ are imprisoned;
Jiǎ, Yǐ, Yín, and Mǎo perish.
In winter, Rén, Guǐ, Hài, and Zǐ wax;
Jiǎ, Yǐ, Yín, and Mǎo assist;
Gēng, Xīn, Shēn, and Yǒu rest;
Wù, Jǐ, Chén, Xū, Chǒu, and Wèi are imprisoned;
Bǐng, Dīng, Sì, and Wǔ perish.
Regarding the waxing and waning of the eight trigrams:
At the Beginning of Spring, Gèn waxes;
Zhèn assists;
Xùn is in gestation;
Lí is submerged;
Kūn perishes;
Duì is imprisoned;
Qián is discarded;
Kǎn rests.
At the Spring Equinox, Zhèn waxes;
Xùn assists;
Lí is in gestation;
Kūn is submerged;
Duì perishes;
Qián is imprisoned;
Kǎn is discarded;
Gèn rests.
At the Beginning of Summer, Xùn waxes;
Lí assists;
Kūn is in gestation;
Duì is submerged;
Qián perishes;
Kǎn is imprisoned;
Gèn is discarded;
Zhèn rests.
At the Summer Solstice, Lí waxes;
Kūn assists;
Duì is in gestation;
Qián is submerged;
Kǎn perishes;
Gèn is imprisoned;
Zhèn is discarded;
Xùn rests.
At the Beginning of Autumn, Kūn waxes;
Duì assists;
Qián is in gestation;
Kǎn is submerged;
Gèn perishes;
Zhèn is imprisoned;
Xùn is discarded;
Lí rests.
At the Autumn Equinox, Duì waxes;
Qián assists;
Kǎn is in gestation;
Gèn is submerged;
Zhèn perishes;
Xùn is imprisoned;
Lí is discarded;
Kūn rests.
At the Beginning of Winter, Qián waxes;
Kǎn assists;
Gèn is in gestation;
Zhèn is submerged;
Xùn perishes;
Lí is imprisoned;
Kūn is discarded;
Duì rests.
At the Winter Solstice, Kǎn waxes;
Gèn assists;
Zhèn is in gestation;
Xùn is submerged;
Lí perishes;
Kūn is imprisoned;
Duì is discarded;
Qián rests.
Each trigram follows the qi of the eight nodes,
each lasting forty-five days.
In the period when an element is in its "king" phase,
it is always the case that its "son" element serves as the "minister" phase,
because the "son" element is then in its prime,
capable of assisting in governance and affairs.
The "parents" are in the "rest" phase,
because the "son" element is at the peak of its "king" energy,
while the "parents" are old and weak,
unable to manage affairs.
This is like when Yáo grew old and entrusted the governance of the state to Shùn.
What is feared is the "death" phase,
because the "king" phase of the body can control and kill it.
What is carved is the "imprisoned" phase,
because the "son" element serves as the "minister,"
capable of imprisoning enemies.
Liǔ Shìlóng said:
When wood is in its "king" phase, it manifests as forests, gardens, bamboo, and trees;
in its "minister" phase, as reeds, rushes, grasses, and weeds;
in its "rest" phase, as rafters, pillars, boats, and carts;
in its "imprisoned" phase, as firewood, kindling, thickets, and stumps;
in its "death" phase, as coffins, rotten wood, and decaying stumps.
When fire is in its "king" phase, it manifests as pottery, kilns, and blazing light;
in its "minister" phase, as lamps and candles;
in its "rest" phase, as smoke and vapor.
In its "imprisoned" phase, as charcoal and ashes;
in its "death" phase, as ashes.
When earth is in its "king" phase, it manifests as states, cities, mountains, and peaks;
in its "minister" phase, as walls, altars, hills, and mounds;
in its "rest" phase, as fields and dwellings;
in its "imprisoned" phase, as walls and enclosures;
in its "death" phase, as manure and soil.
When metal is in its "king" phase, it manifests as gold, jade, and precious vessels;
in its "minister" phase, as silver, copper, and sharp blades;
in its "rest" phase, as lead, tin, plows, and hoes;
in its "imprisoned" phase, as scorched vessels, cauldrons, and spades;
in its "death" phase, as sand, gravel, and broken iron.
When water is in its "king" phase, it manifests as seas and great rivers;
in its "minister" phase, as lakes, marshes, ponds, and springs;
in its "rest" phase, as ditches and channels;
in its "imprisoned" phase, as wine and broth;
in its "death" phase, as dried-up ponds and wells.
All these are because the energy is at its peak during the "king" phase,
hence manifesting as grand and vast things.
During the "minister" phase, the energy is inferior,
so the manifestations gradually become smaller.
During the "rest" phase, the energy declines,
so the manifestations become even more subtle.
During the "imprisoned" phase, it worsens further,
hence the lowest manifestations.
During the "death" phase, it is discarded and unused,
thus manifesting as withered and decayed things.
Zhào Yí said:
In the positions of the five elements,
when an element is in its proper direction, it is at its peak;
when it is in the direction of what it fears, it reaches its end.
Thus, wood fears metal.
Jiǎ gives his younger sister Yǐ in marriage to Gēng.
Gēng obtains wood energy.
Thus, wood is conceived in the direction of metal,
born in the direction of water,
flourishes in its proper direction,
and declines in the direction of fire.
Fire contains the birth of metal,
so it ends in Wèi.
It reaches its end in the western direction,
because metal is in its "king" phase there.
Bǐng gives his younger sister Dīng in marriage to Rén.
Rén obtains fire energy.
Thus, fire is conceived in the direction of water,
born in the direction of wood,
flourishes in its proper direction,
and declines in the direction of metal.
It reaches its end in the northern direction,
because water is in its "king" phase there.
Wù gives his younger sister Jǐ in marriage to Jiǎ.
Jiǎ obtains earth energy.
Thus, earth is conceived in the direction of wood,
born in the direction of fire,
flourishes in its proper position,
and declines in the direction of water.
It reaches its end in the eastern direction,
because wood is in its "king" phase there.
Gēng gives his younger sister Xīn in marriage to Bǐng.
Bǐng obtains metal energy.
Thus, metal is conceived in the direction of wood,
born in the direction of fire,
flourishes in its proper direction,
and declines in the direction of water.
It reaches its end in the eastern direction,
because there is the birth of fire there.
Rén gives his younger sister Guǐ in marriage to Wù.
Wù obtains water energy.
Thus, water is conceived in the direction of earth,
born in the direction of metal,
flourishes in its proper direction,
and declines in the direction of wood.
It reaches its end in the southern direction,
because there is strong earth there.
This illustrates the principle of mutual generation and mutual fear among them,
an unbroken cycle of beginning and end.
The meaning of the stems and branches
involves many combinations.
Here, we briefly discuss their directional positions and pairings.
Stems do not stand alone,
branches are not empty designations.
They must be paired and combined
to determine years, months, days, and times for use.
Like rulers and ministers, husbands and wives,
they must be paired to achieve completion.
In summary,
from Jiǎ to Guǐ is yang,
representing the stems,
and the days.
From Yín to Chǒu is yin,
representing the branches,
and the hours.
Distinguishing further,
among the stems, Jiǎ, Bǐng, Wù, Gēng, and Rén are yang;
Yǐ, Dīng, Jǐ, Xīn, and Guǐ are yin.
Among the branches, Yín, Chén, Wǔ, Shēn, Xū, and Zǐ are yang;
Mǎo, Sì, Wèi, Yǒu, Hài, and Chǒu are yin.
Yang represents hardness,
the ruler,
the husband,
the superior,
the external,
the surface,
movement,
advancement,
rising,
looking upward,
the front,
the left,
virtue,
giving,
and opening.
Yin represents softness,
the minister,
the wife,
the concubine,
wealth,
the inferior,
the internal,
the interior,
stillness,
retreat,
hiding,
position,
the rear,
the right,
punishment,
storing,
and closing.
The analogies for yin and yang
are numerous and broad,
but the general outline is as described.
Jiǎ, yǐ, yín, mǎo are wood.
Their positions are in the east.
Bǐng, dīng, sì, wǔ are fire.
Their positions are in the south.
Wù, jǐ, chén, xū, chǒu, wèi are earth.
Their position is in the center,
ruling over the four seasons,
and temporarily governing with bǐng and dīng.
Gēng, xīn, shēn, yǒu are metal.
Their positions are in the west.
Rén, guǐ, hài, zǐ are water.
Their positions are in the north.
Jiǎ is the first of the heavenly stems,
zǐ is the first of the earthly branches,
and they are paired.
The qi of the great yang
stirs beneath the Yellow Springs,
in the month when zǐ is established.
The pitch of huángzhōng,
as the source of qi, resides in zǐ,
therefore zǐ is taken as the first.
All things emerge in the month when yín is established,
all becoming visible in form.
Jiǎ belongs to this month,
therefore jiǎ is taken as the first and paired with zǐ.
What is visible is yang,
therefore it follows the stems.
What is not yet visible is yīn,
therefore it follows the branches.
This is why jiǎ and zǐ are paired,
as the beginning of the sexagenary cycle.
Since there are ten stems,
and twelve branches,
they rotate and pair with each other,
ending with guǐhài,
thus there are sixty days.
Ten days make one xún,
therefore there are six xún.
One xún completes one cycle from jiǎ to guǐ.
Thus, starting with jiǎ paired with zǐ,
the stems are exhausted until guǐyǒu.
Then the stems are exhausted, and the remaining branches are xū and hài.
Again, start with jiǎ paired with xū,
exhaust the stems until guǐwèi,
the remaining branches are shēn and yǒu.
Again, start with jiǎ paired with shēn,
exhaust the stems until guǐsì,
the remaining branches are wǔ and wèi.
Again, start with jiǎ paired with wǔ,
exhaust the stems until guǐmǎo,
the remaining branches are chén and sì.
Again, start with jiǎ paired with chén,
exhaust the stems until guǐchǒu,
the remaining branches are yín and mǎo.
Again, start with jiǎ paired with yín,
exhaust the stems until guǐhài.
The ten stems paired with the twelve branches,
complete a cycle and return to starting from jiǎzǐ.
Thus, the six jiǎ rotate,
ending at sixty days.
Ten days make one xún.
Within one xún,
the two branches that have no stem to pair with
are called "gū" (orphaned).
The branches opposite to them
are called "xū" (empty).
This is what divination refers to as "kōngwáng" (empty void).
Because the branches are orphaned without stems,
therefore it is named "kōngwáng".
"Wáng" means "nonexistent".
Having no stem, therefore it is "wáng".
What is opposite to them,
is completely empty,
therefore it is called "kōng".
The calculation method places the twelve branches horizontally in the four directions,
places the eight stems vertically in the four directions,
and places wù and jǐ in the center.
For example, in the jiǎzǐ xún,
take the stem jiǎ to pair with the branch zǐ.
Proceeding in this order of pairing,
until wùchén.
Its position is in the center.
Earth is the master of the four phases,
and cannot be moved.
Therefore, take the branches chén and sì,
enter the center,
and pair them with wù and jǐ.
The rest all pair stems with branches.
Until xū and hài have no stems to pair with.
Being alone, they are therefore "gū".
The positions of chén and sì,
have neither branch nor stem.
Therefore they are named "xū".
The branches of kōngwáng,
speaking from the perspective of the five phases,
such as the jiǎzǐ xún lacking xū and hài.
Water and earth are half kōngwáng.
Because xū is earth,
hài is water,
not completely lacking hài and zǐ,
therefore it is said "half".
The jiǎxū xún lacks shēn and yǒu.
This is metal fully kōngwáng,
because both branches of metal are lacking.
The jiǎshēn xún lacks wǔ and wèi.
This is fire and earth half kōngwáng,
because sì and wǔ are not completely lacking.
The jiǎwǔ xún lacking chén and sì is also like this.
The jiǎchén xún lacks yín and mǎo.
Also said to be wood fully kōngwáng.
The jiǎyín xún lacks zǐ and chǒu.
Also water and earth half kōngwáng.
All because the two branches are not both lacking.
Military texts say,
yang is born in jiǎzǐ,
deficient in xū and hài.
Still, it is the Gate of Heaven.
Yīn is born in jiǎwǔ,
deficient in chén and sì.
Still, it is the Gate of Earth.
The yang boundary is jiǎyín,
deficient in zǐ and chǒu.
Still, it is the Gate of Ghosts.
The yīn boundary is jiǎshēn,
deficient in wǔ and wèi.
Still, it is the Gate of Humans.
Yang flourishes in jiǎchén,
with mǎo as its barrier.
Yīn rises in jiǎxū,
with yǒu as its barrier.
These are all the empty branches of the six jiǎ.
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo says,
the earth is deficient in the southeast.
Moving to the right ends and enters the empty gate.
This clarifies that in jiǎzǐ, gū is at xū and hài,
and xū is at chén and sì.
One stem and one branch make one day,
because the celestial sphere is 365 and 1/4 degrees,
and the sun travels one degree each day,
therefore exactly one stem and one branch
govern one day.
Three xún make one month,
because the moon travels 13 and 1/4 degrees per day,
and three xún complete the celestial sphere.
Twelve months make one year,
because each of the four seasons has three months,
the functions of growth and killing are complete,
and it cycles through the twelve branches.
One year totals 360 days,
because six times six is thirty-six,
which is the number of the six jiǎ.
Between the six jiǎ are the days of two months,
to complete the odd and even numbers of yīn and yang.
Yang is odd,
yīn is even.
All things and categories,
the principles of fortune and misfortune,
are made manifest by this.
The pairing of stems and branches
is the same for years, months, days, and hours.
Establishing the origin of the year
begins from the first epoch jiǎzǐ.
Establishing the origin of the month
begins from the eleventh month jiǎzǐ of the year with stems jiǎ or jǐ.
Establishing the origin of the day
begins from jiǎzǐ in the sexagenary cycle.
Establishing the origin of the hour
begins after the two solstices of winter and summer,
on the midnight of the day with stems jiǎ or jǐ,
starting from jiǎzǐ.
All four matters take jiǎzǐ as the beginning.
Regarding its correspondence above to the nine stars and
below to the nine provinces:
The Huángdì Bīngjué states:
Starting from the first star of the Dipper's bowl on the jiǎzǐ day,
count forward to the gēngwǔ day,
which corresponds to the seventh strong star.
Upon reaching the xīnwèi day,
return and count backward from the sixth star to the bǐngzǐ day.
Then, starting from the first star again, count forward through the entire cycle of the six jiǎ.
As for its correspondence below to the nine provinces:
Historical records state:
Jiǎ corresponds to Qí,
yǐ to the Eastern Yí,
bǐng to Chǔ,
dīng to the Southern Yí,
wù to Wèi,
jǐ to Hán,
gēng to Qín,
xīn to the Western Yí,
rén to Yān,
guǐ to the Northern Yí.
The "Treatise on the Five Phases" in the Book of Hàn states:
Jiǎ and yǐ correspond to regions beyond the seas,
where the sun and moon do not govern.
Bǐng and dīng correspond to the Jiāng-Huái region, the sea, and Mount Dài.
Wù and jǐ correspond to the Central Provinces, the Hé River, and the Jì River.
Gēng and xīn correspond to the area west of Mount Huà.
Rén and guǐ correspond to the area north of Mount Cháng.
Zǐ corresponds to Zhōu,
chǒu to Dí,
yín to Chǔ,
mǎo to Zhèng,
chén to Hándān,
sì to Wèi,
wǔ to Qín,
wèi to Zhōngshān and Sòng,
shēn to Qí,
yǒu to Lǔ,
xū to Yuè,
hài to Yān.
The Lóngshǒu Jīng states:
Zǐ corresponds to Qí and Qīngzhōu,
chǒu to Wú, Yuè, and Yángzhōu,
yín to Yān and Yōuzhōu,
mǎo to Sòng and Yùzhōu,
chén to Jìn and Yǎnzhōu,
sì to Chǔ and Jīngzhōu,
wǔ to Zhōu and Sānhé,
wèi to Qín and Yōngzhōu,
shēn to Shǔ and Yìzhōu,
yǒu to Liángzhōu,
xū to Xúzhōu,
hài to Wèi and Bìngzhōu.
Regarding the positions of the earthly branches,
the historical records of Shǐ and Hàn are relatively close.
In terms of stellar correspondences,
the Lóngshǒu Jīng is considered appropriate.
Regarding its correspondence to the human body:
Jiǎ and yǐ correspond to the head,
bǐng and dīng to the chest and flanks,
wù and jǐ to the heart and abdomen,
gēng and xīn to the thighs,
rén and guǐ to the hands and feet.
Thus, zǐ corresponds to the head,
chǒu and hài to the chest and arms,
yín and xū to the hands,
mǎo and yǒu to the waist and flanks,
chén and shēn to the buttocks and upper arms,
sì and wèi to the shins,
wǔ to the feet.
In all these, the beginning corresponds to the head,
and the end corresponds to the feet.
Regarding correspondence to the five viscera:
Among the heavenly stems, jiǎ and yǐ correspond to the liver,
bǐng and dīng to the heart,
wù and jǐ to the spleen,
gēng and xīn to the lungs,
rén and guǐ to the kidneys.
Among the earthly branches, yín and mǎo correspond to the liver,
sì and wǔ to the heart,
chén, xū, chǒu, and wèi to the spleen,
shēn and yǒu to the lungs,
hài and zǐ to the kidneys.
These are all assigned according to the Five Phases.
Furthermore, among the heavenly stems, jiǎ and yǐ correspond to skin and hair,
bǐng and dīng to claws and sinews,
wù and jǐ to flesh,
gēng and xīn to bones,
rén and guǐ to blood vessels.
Among the earthly branches, yín and mǎo correspond to skin and hair,
sì and wǔ to claws and sinews,
chén, xū, chǒu, and wèi to flesh,
shēn and yǒu to bones,
hài and zǐ to blood vessels.
Wood grows upon the earth,
hence it corresponds to skin and hair.
Fire possesses fierceness and vigor,
hence it corresponds to sinews and claws.
Earth has the capacity to support and bear,
hence it corresponds to flesh.
Metal's nature is hard and firm,
hence it corresponds to bones.
Water's fundamental nature is flowing and moistening,
hence it corresponds to blood vessels.
These are all correspondences of the stems and branches,
hence they are explained here for completeness.
Generally, the Five Phases are evenly distributed,
permeating all things,
and one cannot rigidly adhere to a single interpretation.
Now, first, we discuss the inherent complexity within each Phase.
However, its qì circulates universally,
applied according to circumstances.
If one claims there is no complexity,
then Water should only be one.
Why then are there said to be five, yet also six?
Fire, Metal, Wood, and Earth are likewise.
One should understand that the generative numbers are fundamental,
while the completer numbers involve complexity.
Since complexity exists,
a single Phase in its own substance
inherently possesses five meanings.
For example, Wood has the quality of bending and straightening,
this is its Wood aspect.
Wood contains fire within it,
this is its Fire aspect.
Wood can be made into weapons,
having the capacity to strike and impact,
this is its Metal aspect.
Wood contains moisture within it,
this is its Water aspect.
Wood puts forth blossoms, leaves, seeds, and fruits,
this is its Earth aspect.
Fire's external yang is its Fire aspect.
Its internal yīn is its Water aspect.
Its capacity to kill is its Metal aspect.
Its capacity to ripen is its Wood aspect.
Its capacity to generate is its Earth aspect.
Earth's capacity to generate is its Earth aspect.
Its capacity to contain is its Water aspect.
Its capacity to bring to completion is its Wood aspect.
Its capacity to defend makes it its Metal aspect.
Containing yang is its Fire aspect.
Metal's capacity to cut is its Metal aspect.
Its capacity to follow and change (be molded) is its Wood aspect.
Containing fire is its Fire aspect.
Having impurity is its Water aspect.
Its capacity to generate is its Earth aspect.
Water's external yīn is its Water aspect.
Its internal yang is its Fire aspect.
Its capacity to nourish and foster is its Wood aspect.
Its moistening and life-giving quality is its Earth aspect.
Its capacity to kill is its Metal aspect.
These all use meaning to explain how a single Phase communicates with the five qì.
To discuss principles based on specific matters,
it is not so.
Some exist, some do not.
Those with weak substance,
then their bodies can accommodate each other.
Those with strong substance,
then their bodies cannot accommodate each other.
There is no wood within metal,
there is no metal within wood.
Because metal and wood directly harm each other.
There is no fire within water,
there is no water within fire.
Because these two elements directly harm each other.
Also, there is no metal within water,
but there is water within metal.
There is also water within wood,
there is also fire within wood,
there is also fire within stone.
And since water can generate wood,
then there is water within wood.
Water is generated from metal,
so there is water within metal.
Fire is generated from wood,
so there is fire within wood.
Water again is generated from metal,
so there is water within metal.
Water can generate wood.
There is fire within wood.
Fire engraves metal,
how can stone also have fire?
This is because the nature of fire is weak,
so the weak can enter the strong.
But there is no metal within fire,
this is because the strong cannot enter the weak.
Wood is generated from water,
so wood contains water.
Metal can generate water,
so metal contains water.
The reason there is no metal or wood within water,
is that metal and wood are in water,
but one cannot say the substance of water has metal or wood.
Moisture is within wood and stone,
so wood and stone can have the meaning of water.
This is also the weak being able to enter the strong,
the strong cannot enter the weak.
In Yánzhōu there are trees,
that grow within fire.
This is not fire being able to generate trees.
It is that fire cannot burn these trees.
Nor is fire within the trees,
rather it is the trees being within fire,
yet their substances do not intermingle.
No different from metal being in water,
yet unable to intermix with the substance of water.
Also like the hidden fire that smolders in the sea.
This is fire within water,
but it is not the substance of water intermixing with fire.
This slightly touches upon the mystical and strange,
and is also not the constant standard of the Five Phases.
Also, there is fire within wood,
and fire can still burn wood.
This is because the generated fire is at its peak,
so it can burn wood.
There is fire within stone,
but fire does not burn stone.
This is because fire has reached the realm of metal,
its energy has already declined,
so it cannot burn stone.
As for using fire to melt metal,
one also takes its peak state,
so it can melt metal.
One does not take declining fire,
just as metal can overcome wood,
but lead and tin cannot cut it.
This is because it is not strong metal.
The nature of earth is all-encompassing,
there is nothing it does not receive.
Therefore, within earth, water, metal, wood, and fire are all present.
Fire is not solely yang energy,
just as the ground burning in Fànyáng,
is yin.
Earth and fire do not harm each other.
Although it is not always so,
one cannot say it does not exist.
Since all are among the four phases,
why is this alone so?
Earth resides in the ground,
and the ground is yin.
Fire is the energy of the great yang,
therefore it cannot always be present.
Regarding the mixing of the Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches,
the Wǔxíng Shū says:
Jiǎ gives his younger sister Yǐ,
in marriage to Gēng as a wife.
Therefore, Yǐ contains mixed metal.
At the beginning of spring, wood is dominant.
Jiǎ summons Yǐ back,
Yǐ returns carrying metal energy.
Therefore, in mid-spring, elm seeds turn white and fall.
Bǐng gives his younger sister Dīng,
in marriage to Rén as a wife.
Therefore, Dīng contains mixed water.
At the beginning of summer, fire is dominant.
Bǐng summons Dīng back,
Dīng returns carrying water energy.
Therefore, in mid-summer, mulberries ripen and turn black.
Wù gives his younger sister Jǐ,
in marriage to Jiǎ as a wife.
Therefore, Jǐ contains mixed wood.
At the end of summer, earth is dominant.
Wù summons Jǐ back,
Jǐ returns carrying wood energy.
Therefore, at the end of summer, there are green fruits.
Gēng gives his younger sister Xīn,
in marriage to Bǐng as a wife.
Therefore, Xīn contains mixed fire.
At the beginning of autumn, metal is dominant.
Gēng summons Xīn back,
Xīn returns carrying fire energy.
Therefore, in mid-autumn, dates ripen and turn red.
Rén gives his younger sister Guǐ,
in marriage to Wù as a wife.
Therefore, Guǐ contains mixed earth.
At the beginning of winter, water is dominant.
Rén summons Guǐ back,
Guǐ returns carrying earth energy.
Therefore, in mid-winter, plants and trees all turn yellow.
Jiǎ, Bǐng, Wù, Gēng, Rén are male,
strong and firm.
Therefore, they inherently possess virtue and are not mixed.
Yǐ, Dīng, Jǐ, Xīn, Guǐ are female,
soft and weak.
They do not act independently but follow their husbands.
Therefore, they are mixed.
Just like a married woman,
who takes her husband's surname,
and when she returns for a visit,
brings her children along,
thus the clan lineage becomes mixed.
The Wǔxíng Shí Zá says:
Jiǎ is wood,
Yǐ is timber,
Bǐng is fire,
Dīng is ash,
Wù is earth,
Jǐ is mud,
Gēng is metal,
Xīn is furnace slag,
Rén is water,
Guǐ is turbid filth.
These all signify mixed meanings.
Yín and Mǎo are wood,
spring carries fire,
therefore Mǎo is pure wood,
Yín is mixed wood.
Sì and Wǔ are fire,
summer carries earth,
therefore Wǔ is pure fire,
Sì is mixed fire.
Shēn and Yǒu are metal,
autumn carries water,
therefore Yǒu is pure metal,
Shēn is mixed metal.
Hài and Zǐ are water,
winter carries wood,
therefore Zǐ is pure water,
Hài is mixed water.
Earth resides in the center,
governing the four energies separately,
therefore Chén contains residual wood,
Wèi contains residual fire,
Xū contains residual metal,
Chǒu contains residual water,
each for twelve days.
Therefore, the four beginning months (Sì Mèng) are where the pregnant generative energy originates,
the four middle months (Sì Zhòng) are where peak vigor is established,
the four end months (Sì Jì) are where burial and sending-off reside.
Pregnancy and burial,
both have the meaning of mixture.
The Five Phases are not merely pure in their inherent nature;
within each direction, there is also the principle of intermingling.
The east corresponds to Jiǎ, Yǐ, Yín, Mǎo, and Chén.
Jiǎ is Wood.
Within Yǐ, there is intermingled Metal.
Within Yín, there is nascent Fire.
Chén is Earth.
Within Mǎo, there is dead Water.
The south corresponds to Bǐng, Dīng, Sì, Wǔ, and Wèi.
Bǐng is Fire.
Within Dīng, there is intermingled Water.
Within Sì, there is nascent Metal.
Wèi is Earth.
Within Wǔ, there is dead Wood.
The west corresponds to Gēng, Xīn, Shēn, Yǒu, and Xū.
Gēng is Metal.
Within Xīn, there is intermingled Fire.
Within Shēn, there is nascent Water.
Xū is Earth.
Furthermore, within Yǒu, there is embryonic Wood.
The north corresponds to Rén, Guǐ, Hài, Zǐ, and Chǒu.
Rén is Water.
Within Guǐ, there is intermingled Earth.
Within Hài, there is nascent Wood.
Within Zǐ, there is embryonic Fire.
Within Chǒu, there is dead Metal.
These are all instances where each direction possesses its own distinct Five Phases.
Yín, Wǔ, and Xū constitute the position of Fire.
Within Yín, there is nascent Fire—
located in the east.
Within Wǔ, there is ruling Fire—
located in the south.
Within Xū, there is dead Fire—
located in the west.
Hài, Mǎo, and Wèi constitute the position of Wood.
Within Hài, there is nascent Wood—
located in the north.
Within Mǎo, there is ruling Wood—
located in the east.
Within Wèi, there is dead Wood—
located in the south.
Shēn, Zǐ, and Chén constitute the position of Water.
Within Shēn, there is nascent Water—
located in the west.
Within Zǐ, there is ruling Water—
located in the north.
Within Chén, there is dead Water—
located in the east.
Sì, Yǒu, and Chǒu constitute the position of Metal.
Within Sì, there is nascent Metal—
located in the south.
Within Yǒu, there is ruling Metal—
located in the west.
Within Chǒu, there is dead Metal—
located in the north.
This illustrates how the substance of a single phase
is intermingled across three directions.
Wèi, Chén, Chǒu, and Xū constitute the position of Earth.
Within Wèi, there is ruling Earth;
within Chén, there is dead Earth;
within Chǒu, there is declining Earth;
within Xū, there is robust Earth.
This shows the substance of Earth intermingled across the four directions.
Zhào Yí states:
"The Five Phases intermingle
like brocade and damask."
This statement
is indeed apt.
Dé (virtue) means to obtain.
It benefits all things,
each according to its desires,
without regret or stinginess;
therefore, it is called Dé.
The Wǔxíng Shū (Book of the Five Phases) states:
"If one possesses a single Dé,
it can ward off a hundred calamities."
In all matters governed by Yīn and Yáng,
encountering Dé is auspicious,
and it is called fúdé (blessing virtue).
Because it provides aid and rescue,
all affairs become auspicious,
and disasters and harms vanish.
Dé has four types:
three are discussed in terms of the Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches,
and one is discussed in terms of the monthly qi.
The three types related to Stems and Branches are:
first, Stem Dé;
second, Branch Dé;
third, Combined Stem and Branch Dé.
Regarding the Virtue of the Heavenly Stems:
Jiǎ's virtue resides in itself;
Yǐ's virtue resides in Gēng;
Bǐng's virtue resides in itself;
Dīng's virtue resides in Rén;
Wù's virtue resides in itself;
Jǐ's virtue resides in Jiǎ;
Gēng's virtue resides in itself;
Xīn's virtue resides in Bǐng;
Rén's virtue resides in itself;
Guǐ's virtue resides in Wù.
Among these ten stems,
Jiǎ, Bǐng, Wù, Gēng, and Rén are yang;
being honorable, their virtue resides in themselves.
Yǐ, Dīng, Jǐ, Xīn, and Guǐ are yīn;
being humble, they pair their virtue with yang,
embodying the principle of following the husband,
and thus do not possess virtue in themselves.
Yáng Zǐ states:
"In the way of pairing with the days,
there are precisely five pairs:
Jiǎ and Jǐ correspond to wood;
Bǐng and Xīn correspond to fire;
Wù and Guǐ correspond to earth;
Yǐ and Gēng correspond to metal;
Dīng and Rén correspond to water."
The principle of yīn and yang
necessarily involves mutual pairing,
following the principles of ruler and subject, husband and wife.
Jiǎ is the ruler,
the husband;
Jǐ is the subject,
the wife.
The ruler's position resides in itself;
the subject's position derives from the ruler.
Therefore, Jǐ's virtue resides in Jiǎ,
and Yǐ's virtue resides in Gēng.
The remaining four pairs are likewise,
following the way of yīn submitting to yang.
Regarding the Virtue of the Earthly Branches:
Zǐ's virtue resides in Sì;
Chǒu's virtue resides in Wǔ;
Yín's virtue resides in Wèi;
Mǎo's virtue resides in Shēn;
Chén's virtue resides in Yǒu;
Sì's virtue resides in Xū;
Wǔ's virtue resides in Hài;
Wèi's virtue resides in Zǐ;
Shēn's virtue resides in Chǒu;
Yǒu's virtue resides in Yín;
Xū's virtue resides in Mǎo;
Hài's virtue resides in Chén.
These are all based on the place where their husband generates and assists.
Zǐ takes Sì as its virtue because
Zǐ is water,
taking earth as its husband,
and Sì contains generating earth.
Chǒu takes Wǔ as its virtue because
Chǒu is earth,
taking wood as its husband,
and Wǔ contains dead wood.
Yín takes Wèi as its virtue because
Yín is wood,
taking metal as its husband,
and Wèi contains capped metal.
Mǎo takes Shēn as its virtue because
Mǎo is wood,
taking metal as its husband,
and Shēn contains waxing metal.
Chén takes Yǒu as its virtue because
Chén is earth,
taking wood as its husband,
and Yǒu contains embryonic wood.
Sì takes Xū as its virtue because
Sì is fire,
taking water as its husband,
and Xū contains capped water.
Wǔ takes Hài as its virtue because
Wǔ is fire,
taking water as its husband,
and Hài contains waxing water.
Wèi takes Zǐ as its virtue because
Wèi is earth,
taking wood as its husband,
and Zǐ contains bathing wood.
Shēn takes Chǒu as its virtue because
Shēn is metal,
taking fire as its husband,
and Chǒu contains nourishing fire.
Yǒu takes Yín as its virtue because
Yǒu is metal,
taking fire as its husband,
and Yín contains generating fire.
Xū takes Mǎo as its virtue because
Xū is earth,
taking wood as its husband,
and Mǎo contains flourishing wood.
Hài takes Chén as its virtue because
Hài is water,
taking earth as its husband,
and Chén contains dead earth.
Someone may ask:
"Regarding the principle of following the husband,
if the husband is alive, there is virtue,
enabling harmony and nourishment,
thus one follows.
If dead, there is separation and opposition,
unable to harmonize and follow;
why then does the dead still constitute virtue?"
The answer is:
"A woman does not remarry;
once she descends to marry a man,
she is called by his clan name.
Even in death, she follows his clan;
how could she be called by it in life
and abandon it in death?
Therefore, yīn's submission to yang
endures through life and death."
Regarding the Combined Virtue of Stems and Branches:
Zǐ's virtue resides in Jiǎ;
Chǒu's virtue resides in Xīn;
Yín's virtue resides in Bǐng;
Mǎo's virtue resides in Dīng;
Chén's virtue resides in Gēng;
Sì's virtue resides in Jǐ;
Wǔ's virtue resides in Wù;
Wèi's virtue resides in Xīn;
Shēn's virtue resides in Rén;
Yǒu's virtue resides in Guǐ;
Xū's virtue resides in Gēng;
Hài's virtue resides in Yǐ.
These all take the son as virtue.
This means the son can support his mother,
possessing the nature of filial care,
and thus constitutes virtue.
In general, stems are yang,
branches are yīn.
The yang substance is firm and self-sufficient;
the yīn substance is gentle and submissive to yang.
A woman has the ritual of three obediences;
she never has the principle of self-determination.
When the husband dies, she obeys the son;
therefore, she takes the son as virtue.
If stems and branches each had their own virtue,
they would all follow their husbands.
But now stems and branches share virtue,
thus departing from the husband's position,
and so they follow the son.
Zǐ's virtue residing in Jiǎ
is because water is the mother of wood.
All other cases are analogous.
Regarding Taking the Monthly Qi as Virtue:
Virtue does not stand alone;
it is paired with punishment.
Virtue is yang,
following Qián;
punishment is yīn,
following Kūn.
It is like human governance:
both punishment and virtue are applied.
Virtue involves celebration, rewards, and bestowal of rank,
thus matching yang.
Punishment involves execution, penalties, reduction, and seizure,
thus matching yīn.
Therefore, when a king
sees a solar eclipse, he cultivates virtue;
when he sees a lunar eclipse, he cultivates punishment.
Dǒng Zhòngshū's *Chūnqiū Fánlù* states:
"The constant way of Heaven
is one yang, one yīn.
Yang is Heaven's virtue;
yīn is Heaven's punishment.
Through yīn and yang's movement over the year,
one observes what Heaven favors and entrusts,
and can see the application of virtue and punishment.
However, Heaven favors yang, not yīn;
it prefers virtue, not punishment.
Thus yang emerges and accumulates in summer,
entrusting virtue with the year's affairs;
yīn emerges and accumulates in winter,
setting aside punishment in an empty place."
Tàigōng states:
"When a ruler undertakes affairs,
if good, Heaven responds with virtue;
if evil, Heaven responds with punishment."
These all illustrate the pairing of yīn and yang:
virtue does not govern alone,
but must be paired with punishment.
Regarding the qi of the two hexagrams Qián and Kūn:
In the tenth month, the Kūn hexagram is in effect.
From the eleventh month, yang qi stirs,
and the yin lines transform.
In the fourth month, the Qián hexagram is in effect.
From the fifth month, yin qi stirs,
and the yang lines transform.
Therefore, Huángzhōng and Ruíbīn
mark the beginning of yin and yang qi.
Virtue and punishment reside therein.
In the month of Jiànzǐ,
the first six line of Kūn
transforms into yang.
The Fù hexagram is in effect.
Yang qi stirs beneath the Yellow Springs,
while yin qi spreads above the azure sky.
Virtue is in the chamber,
and punishment is in the wilds.
In the month of Jiànchǒu,
the second six line of Kūn
transforms into yang.
The Lín hexagram is in effect.
Yang qi gradually emerges,
and all things sprout buds.
Yin qi is about to descend,
and its fierce wrath has already diminished.
Virtue is in the hall,
and punishment is in the street.
In the month of Jiànyín,
the third six line of Kūn
transforms into yang.
The Tài hexagram is in effect.
Yang qi has already reached forth,
and yin qi descends inward.
Yin and yang interact harmoniously,
and all things draw out their buds and leaves.
Virtue is in the courtyard,
and punishment is in the lane.
In the month of Jiànmǎo,
the fourth six line of Kūn
transforms into yang.
The Dàzhuàng hexagram is in effect.
Yang qi ascends to the heavens,
while yin qi descends into the earth.
Yin and yang qi interact,
and all things mature and emerge.
Virtue and punishment both gather at the gate.
In the month of Jiànchén,
the fifth six line of Kūn
transforms into yang.
The Guài hexagram is in effect.
Yang qi ascends and reaches forth,
while yin qi declines and weakens.
Virtue is in the lane,
and punishment is in the courtyard.
In the month of Jiànsì,
the top six line of Kūn
transforms into yang.
Pure yang is in effect.
Yang qi is greatly abundant,
and yin qi is eliminated and removed.
All things rejoice and grow robust,
with no further punishment or killing.
Virtue is in the street,
and punishment is in the hall.
In the month of Jiànwǔ,
the first nine line of Qián
transforms into yin.
The Gòu hexagram is in effect.
Yin qi stirs beneath the Yellow Springs,
while yang qi spreads above the azure sky.
Virtue is in the wilds,
and punishment is in the chamber.
In the month of Jiànwèi,
the second nine line of Qián
transforms into yin.
The Dùn hexagram is in effect.
Yin qi gradually rises,
and yang qi is about to diminish.
All things reach the peak of robustness,
and all begin to age and decline.
Virtue is in the street,
and punishment is in the hall.
In the month of Jiànshēn,
the third nine line of Qián
transforms into yin.
The Pǐ hexagram is in effect.
Yang qi sinks and retreats,
while yin qi advances and rises.
Yin and yang are blocked and separated,
and the power of killing is at its peak.
Virtue is in the lane,
and punishment is in the courtyard.
In the month of Jiànyǒu,
the fourth nine line of Qián
transforms into yin.
The Guān hexagram is in effect.
Yang qi enters inward,
while yin qi extends outward.
Yin and yang contend and combine,
and all things transform and decline.
Virtue is at the gate,
and punishment again gathers at the gate.
In the month of Jiànxū,
the fifth nine line of Qián
transforms into yin.
The Bō hexagram is in effect.
Yang qi is about to be exhausted,
while yin qi ascends and reaches forth.
All things wither and fade,
and killing and harm prevail.
Virtue is in the courtyard,
and punishment is in the lane.
In the month of Jiànhài,
the top nine line of Qián
transforms into yin,
and pure Kūn returns to its position.
Yang qi is eliminated and removed,
and yin qi is greatly abundant.
All things are stored and collected,
with no signs of punishment or offense.
Virtue is in the hall,
and punishment is in the street.
These two matters of punishment and virtue
move in and out, advancing and retreating,
and are all applied accordingly.
Do not forget to grasp the chisel.
Encountering virtue brings auspiciousness,
while meeting punishment brings inauspiciousness.
Therefore, this is explained here.
Confucius said:
Qián is yang,
Kūn is yin,
and yin and yang combine their virtues.
The foundation of the five phases
receives life from heaven,
and then receives completion from earth.
They receive qi from yang
and determine form from yin.
The body is not established in partiality,
so each has its own pairing.
Speaking in general terms,
the stems are yang and belong to heaven,
while the branches are yin and belong to earth.
Speaking in specific terms,
the stems themselves have yin and yang:
Jiǎ is yang,
Yǐ is yin,
Bǐng is yang,
Dīng is yin,
Wù is yang,
Jǐ is yin,
Gēng is yang,
Xīn is yin,
Rén is yang,
Guǐ is yin.
The branches also themselves have yin and yang:
Zǐ is yang,
Chǒu is yin,
Yín is yang,
Mǎo is yin,
Chén is yang,
Sì is yin,
Wǔ is yang,
Wèi is yin,
Shēn is yang,
Yǒu is yin,
Xū is yang,
Hài is yin.
Each symbolizes heaven and earth
and pairs with one another on their own,
embodying the way of husband and wife.
Regarding the heavenly stem combinations:
Jǐ is the wife of Jiǎ,
therefore Jiǎ combines with Jǐ.
Xīn is the wife of Bǐng,
therefore Bǐng combines with Xīn.
Guǐ is the wife of Wù,
therefore Guǐ combines with Wù.
Yǐ is the wife of Gēng,
therefore Yǐ combines with Gēng.
Dīng is the wife of Rén,
therefore Rén combines with Dīng.
The Jì family's theory of yīn and yáng states:
Wood (eight) fears Metal (nine),
so it gives its younger sister Yǐ to Gēng as a wife.
Gēng's energy resides in autumn,
harmonized with wood energy,
hence shepherd's purse and wheat are born in autumn,
which is the meaning of the wife coming.
Fire (seven) fears Water (six),
so it gives its younger sister Dīng to Rén as a wife.
Rén obtains the hot energy of fire,
hence coltsfoot blooms in winter.
Metal (nine) fears Fire (seven),
so it gives its younger sister Xīn to Bǐng as a wife.
Bǐng obtains metal energy,
hence at the beginning of summer, delicate grasses and shepherd's purse die,
therefore after the summer solstice,
the three Gēng days mark the fu period,
due to the fear of fire.
Earth (five) fears Wood (eight),
so it gives its younger sister Jǐ to Jiǎ as a wife.
Earth carries the combination of yīn and yáng,
marrying its female to wood,
thus it can generate living things.
Water (six) fears Earth (five),
so it gives its younger sister Guǐ to Wù as a wife.
The five phases harmonize with each other,
this is their combination.
Regarding the earthly branch combinations:
They are the points where the paths of the sun and moon meet.
In the first month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Zōuzī.
Zōuzī is Hài.
Also called Shǐwéi.
The Dipper points to Yín,
therefore Yín combines with Hài.
In the second month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Jiànglóu.
Jiànglóu is Xū.
The Dipper points to Mǎo,
therefore Mǎo combines with Xū.
In the third month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Dàliáng.
Dàliáng is Yǒu.
The Dipper points to Chén,
therefore Chén combines with Yǒu.
In the fourth month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Shíchén.
Shíchén is Shēn.
The Dipper points to Sì,
therefore Sì combines with Shēn.
In the fifth month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Chúnshǒu.
Chúnshǒu is Wèi.
The Dipper points to Wǔ,
therefore Wǔ combines with Wèi.
In the sixth month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Chúnhuǒ.
Chúnhuǒ is Wǔ.
The Dipper points to Wèi,
therefore Wèi combines with Wǔ.
In the seventh month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Chúnwěi.
Chúnwěi is Sì.
The Dipper points to Shēn,
therefore Shēn combines with Sì.
In the eighth month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Shòuxīng.
Shòuxīng is Chén.
The Dipper points to Yǒu,
therefore Yǒu combines with Chén.
In the ninth month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Dàhuǒ.
Dàhuǒ is Mǎo.
The Dipper points to Xū,
therefore Xū combines with Mǎo.
In the tenth month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Zhémù.
Zhémù is Yín.
The Dipper points to Hài,
therefore Hài combines with Yín.
In the eleventh month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Xīngjì.
Xīngjì is Chǒu.
The Dipper points to Zǐ,
therefore Zǐ combines with Chǒu.
In the twelfth month, the sun and moon meet at the station of Xuánxiāo.
Xuánxiāo is Zǐ,
also called Tiānyuán.
The Dipper points to Chǒu,
therefore Chǒu combines with Zǐ.
Xuánxiāo:
Xuán means black,
Xiāo means exhaustion.
Yīn energy is abundant,
so the myriad things begin to stir,
yet have not been born.
The world is empty and void,
thus it is called exhaustion.
Xīngjì:
Jì means to govern and unify.
It leads the beginning and end of the myriad things.
Zhémù:
The myriad things begin to sprout,
distinguishing water and wood.
Dàhuǒ:
It is the wood of the east,
the Heart constellation is in Mǎo,
fire emerges from the heart of wood.
Shòuxīng:
The myriad things begin to reach forth,
each fulfilling its destiny.
Chúnwěi:
It is the southern constellation of the Vermilion Bird,
with the Chariot as its tail.
Chúnhuǒ:
Yáng energy is grand and abundant,
the Fire Star culminates at dusk,
located at the place of the Seven Stars of the Vermilion Bird.
Chúnshǒu:
It is a southern constellation,
its form resembles a bird,
with the Well as its crown,
and the Willow as its mouth.
Shíchén:
Yīn energy is heavy and sinking,
descending its substance into things.
Dàliáng:
Means strong.
White dew has already descended,
and the myriad things are firm and strong.
Jiànglóu:
Jiàng means to descend,
Lóu means bent.
Yīn energy encroaches upwards,
and the myriad things wither and bend.
Zōuzī:
Yīn is abundant and yáng lies hidden,
and the myriad things are sorrowful and mournful.
Generally, when yīn and yáng are paired,
good and evil are balanced in principle.
The inauspicious is not entirely inauspicious,
the auspicious is not solely auspicious.
Auspiciousness ends in inauspiciousness,
inauspiciousness ends in auspiciousness.
Therefore, combination is not exclusively combination,
but also contains the meaning of separation.
Regarding the pairing of stems and branches with days and hours,
there are thus the Five Combinations and the Five Separations.
The Five Combinations:
As the Hé Tú says:
Jiǎyín and Yǐmǎo are the combination of Heaven and Earth,
Bǐngyín and Dīngmǎo are the combination of Sun and Moon,
Wùyín and Jǐmǎo are the combination of People,
Gēngyín and Xīnmǎo are the combination of Metal and Stone,
Rényín and Guǐmǎo are the combination of Rivers.
The Five Separations:
Jiǎshēn and Yǐyǒu are the separation of Heaven and Earth,
Bǐngshēn and Dīngyǒu are the separation of Sun and Moon,
Wùshēn and Jǐyǒu are the separation of People,
Gēngshēn and Xīnyǒu are the separation of Metal and Stone,
Rénshēn and Guǐyǒu are the separation of Rivers.
Yín and Mǎo are where yáng ascends,
able to generate the myriad things.
The sun often rises there,
and the moon is full and rises again.
It is the place in the east where lesser yáng grows,
where things joyfully gather,
therefore it is considered combination.
Shēn and Yǒu are where yīn converges,
the direction of stern execution.
Both the sun and moon set there.
It is the place in the west where lesser yīn ages and declines,
which things detest,
therefore it is considered separation.
Jiǎ and Yǐ are the heads of the heavenly stems,
their trigrams belong to Qián and Kūn,
thus they are likened to Heaven and Earth.
Bǐng and Dīng are the height of sunlight,
thus they represent the Sun and Moon.
Wù and Jǐ reside in the center,
able to complete the myriad things,
thus they are analogous to People.
Gēng and Xīn are inherently Metal and Stone.
Rén and Guǐ are naturally Rivers.
In all matters,
if auspicious, follow combination;
if inauspicious, follow separation.
Encountering combination brings rest,
encountering separation brings obstruction.
Selecting days and determining times,
the use of divination,
is widely applied.
"Fú" (support) means to assist.
"Yì" (restraint) means to halt and retreat.
Once the Five Phases are established,
prosperity and decline occur at their proper times,
and nobility and humility alternate,
thus there are those that support and restrain each other.
This describes their interaction.
When the mother obtains the child, it is support;
when the child encounters the mother, it is restraint.
The child has the principle of filial care and obedient assistance,
hence it is support.
The mother has the way of dignity, instruction, and control,
hence it is restraint.
Supporting relationships:
Wood supports Water,
Water supports Metal,
Metal supports Earth,
Earth supports Fire,
Fire supports Wood.
These are all cases where the mother obtains the child.
Restraining relationships:
Wood restrains Fire,
Fire restrains Earth,
Earth restrains Metal,
Metal restrains Water,
Water restrains Wood.
These are all cases where the child encounters the mother.
Liǔ Shìlóng's *Guī Jīng* says:
Support means longevity; restraint means not.
Support means rising; restraint means stopping.
Support means looking up; restraint means bowing down.
Support means advancing; restraint means retreating.
Support means moving; restraint means halting.
Support means auspicious; restraint means inauspicious.
Regarding this, further consideration is needed.
In general, when parents have qì, they are true parents;
when without qì, they are ancestral spirits.
With qì, they bring blessings and assistance to the son;
without qì, they bring wealth and merit.
Therefore, support is necessarily good; restraint is evil.
During the time of flourishing and kingship, there is qì;
during the time of death and extinction, there is no qì.
Having qì or not having qì further has two aspects.
If one encounters harmonious virtue, even restraint is not harmful.
If one meets punishment and overcoming, it is inauspicious.
A further question:
Regarding the mother's way of instruction and control over the child,
calling it inauspicious—this is not yet understandable.
Dignity, instruction, and control,
teaching with righteousness and proper methods,
wishing for the child to become a proper person—
why should this be considered evil instead?
Answer:
The previous explanation already mentioned two aspects.
If one encounters harmonious virtue, even restraint is not harmful.
Having qì as true parents—this is wishing for the child to become a proper person.
However, during the time of instruction,
the interaction with the child may not go as desired,
which is also an obstruction,
let alone encountering punishment and overcoming.
Even Shùn, with his utmost filial piety,
still fled from the heavy staff.
Wáng Xiáng knocking on ice,
Mèng Zōng weeping for bamboo shoots—
were these teachings of righteousness and proper methods?
Without qì as spirits—
when spirits come,
they mostly wish to cause hauntings.
Only through prayers and supplications
can blessings be obtained.
What about this restraint?
Question:
The explanation says having qì is parents,
without qì is spirits—
this also raises doubt.
Although spirits reside in obscurity and subtlety,
they still are entities.
With essence and spiritual resonance,
fortune and misfortune thus respond.
If it is said they are without,
then upon what do ancestral temple sacrifices rely?
Answer:
What is meant by having or not having
precisely discusses life and death.
In life, the form exists, thus there is;
in death, the qì scatters, thus there is not.
It does not speak of the obscure and subtle;
why is this doubtful?
Question:
If death is thus explained as being without,
then without—what is there to consider,
that it can cause restraint?
Answer:
Although spirits have no visible form or substance,
they have good and evil that can be sought.
Therefore, they can cause restraint.
Question:
If they can cause restraint,
then there is the meaning of existence.
Answer:
Regarding restraint, there is;
speaking of form, there is not.
Now explaining "without"—
discussing in terms of qì,
it is not completely without.
But there is no flourishing and kingly qì,
only death and extinction qì.
When flourishing and kingly qì comes, it is auspicious;
when death and extinction qì comes, it is inauspicious.
What is meant by without qì
is without flourishing and kingly qì.
Although the Five Phases correspond to ruler and minister, father and son,
their flourishing and kingliness differ.
They follow taboos and overcome each other.
Overcoming means to control and punish.
Because the strong can control the weak:
Wood overcomes Earth,
Earth overcomes Water,
Water overcomes Fire,
Fire overcomes Metal,
Metal overcomes Wood.
The *Báihǔ Tōng* says:
Wood overcomes Earth because the concentrated overcomes the scattered.
Earth overcomes Water because the solid overcomes the empty.
Water overcomes Fire because the many overcome the few.
Fire overcomes Metal because the refined overcomes the hard.
Metal overcomes Wood because the rigid overcomes the soft.
The *Chūnqiū Fánlù* says:
Wood is the farmer.
If farmers are disobedient as if in rebellion,
the Minister of Education punishes their leaders to correct them.
Therefore Metal overcomes Wood.
Fire is the court having slanderous and wicked ministers
who confuse their ruler;
according to law, they are punished.
Therefore Water overcomes Fire.
Earth is the ruler.
If greatly extravagant, exceeding measure, and losing propriety,
the people rebel against him to the extreme.
Therefore Wood overcomes Earth.
Metal is the Minister of Education.
If weak and unable to command the masses,
then the Minister of War punishes him.
Therefore Fire overcomes Metal.
Water is the law enforcer.
If partial and unjust,
then the Minister of Justice punishes him.
Therefore Earth overcomes Water.
The victor is the ruler,
the husband,
the official,
the clerk,
the ghost.
The defeated is the minister,
the wife,
wealth.
The ruler with awe-inspiring dignity is exalted.
The husband with virtue and righteousness is esteemed.
The official with ability has rewards and punishments.
The clerk with penal law decides judgments.
The ghost with overcoming and killing brings illness and mourning.
All these are the victors.
The minister fears and submits to his superior.
The wife respects and follows her husband.
Wealth rests on being controlled and used by others.
All these are the defeated.
Whenever the superior overcomes the subordinate, it is called compliance;
whenever the subordinate overcomes the superior, it is called stripping.
This is analogous to how a ruler possesses the law to punish his ministers,
while ministers have no principle to offend their ruler;
a father has the way to instruct his son,
but a son has no method to teach his father.
Therefore, when the superior overcomes the subordinate,
it follows principle in action;
when the subordinate overcomes the superior,
it violates principle in overcoming.
Hence, the Báihǔ Tōng states:
Yang represents the ruler,
Yin represents the minister.
Water, with the energy of Great Yin,
controls the fire of Great Yang;
Metal, with the energy of Lesser Yin,
controls the wood of Lesser Yang.
This is analogous to a ruler who has lost the Way,
such as Shāng Tāng exiling Jié,
or Zhōu Wǔ attacking Zhòu.
These are all cases of punishing the guilty.
In all divination, obtaining what overcomes one is inauspicious,
while obtaining what is controlled by one is auspicious.
According to the Way of the Five Elements,
the son can rescue the father from calamity.
Thus, when Metal goes to overcome Wood,
Fire takes revenge for it.
Once Fire consumes Metal,
Water avenges its disgrace.
However, when an element is in a declining phase,
it is instead controlled by the ruling element.
This is like water in a cauldron being boiled by fire.
The Báihǔ Tōng states:
Fire is hot, Water is cold.
There is warm water,
but why is there no cold fire?
This clarifies that a minister can become a ruler,
but a ruler cannot become a minister.
When fire boils water into soup,
its form is not altered,
only its name is changed.
When water extinguishes fire into charcoal,
both form and name are completely gone.
This is also like a ruler being deposited and ceasing to exist,
or a minister committing a crime and retiring from office.
In the mutual overcoming of the Five Elements,
when Wood pierces Earth, it is not destroyed;
when Fire burns Metal, it is not destroyed—
this is because Yang energy is benevolent,
favoring life.
When Metal attacks Wood or
Water extinguishes Fire, it is an offense—
this is because Yin energy is greedy,
favoring killing.
As for events like mountain collapses and river drying up,
disasters caused by wood and stone,
heavenly fire flowing down,
human fire blazing upward,
simultaneous floods and droughts,
harm from wind and frost—
these are all due to failures in human governance,
with Heaven and Earth issuing reprimands.
This is what is called the mutual conflict of the Five Elements,
meaning disharmony and conflict.
Because their energies clash in conflict,
it is not called overcoming.
Conflict also means abandonment.
For Wood, it is the shaking of Nángōng Jí;
for Water, it is the drying up of the Three Rivers;
for Fire, it is disasters in palaces and houses;
for Metal, it is the shaking of the Nine Tripods;
for Earth, it is mountain collapses in Qí and Chǔ.
When Wood, Metal, Water, and Fire all conflict with Earth,
it results in earthquakes and splitting of the earth,
which is this phenomenon.
Therefore, when the energies of the Five Elements clash,
there are six types of conflict,
generally as described.
Now, punishment
is named for killing and penalizing.
Naturally, it is applied to the unjust;
it is not intentionally inflicted upon each other.
The Five Elements each reside in one direction;
cold and heat shift and change,
moving in response to the seasons,
not losing their proper timing,
