each not offending the other,
and none should uniquely receive punishment.
However, they must be used without severity to achieve order.
They cannot be discarded and left unused.
Therefore, they all reciprocally punish each other.
Just as using Metal to work Metal
creates implements,
and using humans to govern humans
creates state administration.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
Punishments cannot be abolished in a state,
nor can whipping and scolding be abandoned in a family.
Thus, the three thousand categories of the Five Punishments
all fundamentally derive from the Five Elements.
The Zhōushū states:
Based on the mutual overcoming of the Five Elements,
the Five Punishments were created.
These are tattooing, cutting off the nose, cutting off the feet, castration, and death.
Fire can change the color of Metal,
hence tattooing changes the flesh.
Metal can overcome Wood,
hence cutting off the feet removes the bone joints.
Wood can overcome Earth,
hence cutting off the nose removes the nose.
Earth can block Water,
hence castration cuts off licentiousness.
Water can extinguish Fire,
hence death ends life.
Up to the time of Hàn Wén,
he abolished the mutilating punishments,
replacing them with flogging.
Subsequently, beheading, decapitation, exile, strangulation, and penal servitude
still did not exceed the number five.
The Shàngshū states:
Exile is a leniency for the Five Punishments.
Moreover, the five exiles are separated
by five hundred lǐ each.
The counts for flogging
start from ten,
accumulating up to one hundred,
also following the numbers of the Ten Heavenly Stems.
The Shàngshū Xíngdé Kǎo states:
Death resembles the punishment of Heaven.
The number for redemption is three thousand,
corresponding to Heaven, Earth, and Humanity.
The punishments of days, celestial stems, and earthly branches
also have three types.
Therefore, the punishments of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity
share the same principle.
The three types are:
first, branches punishing each other;
second, branches punishing stems;
third, stems punishing branches.
Branches punishing each other means:
Zǐ punishes at Mǎo,
Mǎo punishes at Zǐ;
Chǒu punishes at Xū,
Xū punishes at Wèi,
Wèi punishes at Chǒu;
Yín punishes at Sì,
Sì punishes at Shēn,
Shēn punishes at Yín;
Chén, Wǔ, Yǒu, and Hài each punish themselves.
The Hànshū, in Yì Fèng’s memorial, states:
Wood falls and returns to its root,
hence Hài, Mǎo, Wèi—the positions of Wood—
are punished in the north:
Hài punishes itself,
Mǎo punishes at Zǐ,
Wèi punishes at Chǒu.
Water flows toward its end,
hence Shēn, Zǐ, Chén—the positions of Water—
are punished in the east:
Shēn punishes at Yín,
Zǐ punishes at Mǎo,
Chén punishes itself.
Metal is hard, Fire is strong,
each returns to its homeland;
hence Sì, Yǒu, Chǒu—the positions of Metal—
are punished in the west:
Sì punishes at Shēn,
Yǒu punishes itself,
Chǒu punishes at Xū.
Yín, Wǔ, Xū—the positions of Fire—
are punished in the south:
Yín punishes at Sì,
Wǔ punishes itself,
Xū punishes at Wèi.
When the Earthly Branches punish the Heavenly Stems:
Yín punishes Gēng,
Mǎo punishes Xīn,
Chén punishes Jiǎ,
Sì punishes Guǐ,
Wǔ punishes Rén,
Wèi punishes Yǐ,
Shēn punishes Bǐng,
Yǒu punishes Dīng,
Xū punishes Jiǎ,
Hài punishes Jǐ,
Zǐ punishes Wù,
Chǒu punishes Yǐ.
When the Heavenly Stems punish the Earthly Branches:
Jiǎ punishes Shēn,
Yǐ punishes Yǒu,
Bǐng punishes Zǐ,
Dīng punishes Hài,
Wù punishes Yín,
Jǐ punishes Mǎo,
Gēng punishes Wǔ,
Xīn punishes Sì,
Rén punishes Chén and Xū,
Guǐ punishes Chǒu and Wèi.
In all these cases, punishment is determined by what overcomes what.
In all divination practices,
encountering punishment is not auspicious.
However, for some matters sought,
they cannot be obtained without punishment.
The Shǐ Sū Turtle Shell Classic states:
"When something should succeed but does not,
examine the cracks for signs of mutual punishment."
Another question asks:
"The Six Harmonies are auspicious, yet
why do Shēn and Sì conflict with each other?"
The answer is:
"Metal carries Water, born within Fire.
Fire is the 'ghost' of Metal,
Water is the 'ghost' of Fire.
Metal and Water together are born within Fire,
thus it is the 'ghost' mother and child within the body.
Shēn is the position of Metal,
and also contains Water.
Sì is the position of Fire,
and also generates Metal.
They mutually oppose each other,
hence it is considered punishment.
However, punishment has an upper and lower aspect.
For example, Yín punishes Sì:
Sì is the upper punishment,
Yín is the lower punishment.
The remaining examples follow this pattern.
Therefore, the Military Manual states:
"When wind comes from the direction of the upper punishment,
those seated must rise urgently,
those walking must stop urgently."
This refers to exactly that.
Speaking of the Three Punishments:
such as Yín punishing Sì,
and Sì punishing Shēn.
On a Yín day at a Shēn hour,
if wind arises from the Sì direction,
or an omen appears in the Sì direction,
it is called the Three Punishments.
Others also follow this principle.
There is also punishment based on following the Qi,
which stands in opposition to Virtue.
This has already been explained previously.
Therefore, it will not be explained again.
Mutual Harm:
Moving counterclockwise, they meet at the twelve Earthly Branches,
forming pairs that harm each other,
named the Six Harms.
Xū and Yǒu,
Hài and Shēn,
Zǐ and Wèi,
Chǒu and Wǔ,
Yín and Sì,
Mǎo and Chén—
these are the Six Harms.
This signifies killing and injury.
Now, these six harms
may represent ruler and minister, father and son,
or husband and wife.
In principle, they should not harm each other.
The Classic of Filial Piety states:
"One who does not love his own parents,
yet loves others,
is called one who violates virtue."
Since they violate their nature of kindness and love,
there is a principle of anger and slaughter.
What the Five Agents detest
lies in destruction and conflict.
The present mutual harm
arises from combining with destruction and conflict. Hence,
the father loses his kindness,
the son violates his filial piety,
the wife lacks respect and obedience,
the husband abandons harmony and unity.
All combine in hatred and resentment,
forming the principle of mutual harm.
As for cases like
awaiting bear's paws while starving, or probing for fledgling birds when hungry,
Chóng'ěr fleeing abroad,
Shēnshēng receiving the decree of death,
within Hé Nèi, husband and wife harm each other,
beyond the frontier, ruler and minister kill and seize—
are these not examples of harm?
Regarding Chén and Mǎo harming each other:
Mǎo combines with Xū,
and Xū destroys Chén.
Chén Earth is the wife of Mǎo Wood.
Xū and Chén share enmity.
Mǎo combining with Xū
is essentially abandoning [Chén].
Chén combines with Yǒu,
and Yǒu conflicts with and destroys Mǎo.
Chén is Mǎo's wife,
Yǒu is Mǎo's enemy.
Chén combining with Yǒu,
where Yǒu can overcome Mǎo,
is the image of a wife committing adultery with an outsider
and killing her original husband.
Sì combines with Shēn,
and Shēn conflicts with Yín.
Sì is the child of Yín.
Shēn can overcome Yín.
Sì combining with Shēn
represents a child acting rebelliously.
Regarding Chǒu and Wǔ harming each other:
Chǒu combines with Zǐ,
and Zǐ conflicts with and destroys Wǔ.
Wǔ combines with Wèi,
and Wèi destroys Chǒu.
This also signifies the principle of father and son harming each other.
Regarding Wèi and Zǐ harming each other:
Wèi combines with Wǔ,
and Wǔ conflicts with and destroys Zǐ.
Wèi Earth is the ruler,
Zǐ Water is the minister.
Wǔ Fire is the wealth of Zǐ Water.
This is the image of a ruler using wealth to harm his minister.
Zǐ combines with Chǒu,
and Chǒu is destroyed by Wèi.
Chǒu is also Earth.
Zǐ combining with Chǒu
desires to draw in an external ruler to jointly harm its own lord.
This is the image of a minister fleeing into exile.
Regarding Shēn and Hài harming each other:
Hài combines with Yín,
and Yín conflicts with Shēn.
Shēn combines with Sì,
and Sì conflicts with Hài.
This also signifies the principle of father and son harming each other.
That which generates does not necessarily generate,
that which harms does not necessarily harm.
Just as fire can burn things,
yet there is the fire of Yánzhōu,
which cannot burn things;
water can moisten and nourish,
but when floods suddenly arrive,
they also cause grasses and trees to wither and yellow.
This is an instance of generation turning into harm,
and harm turning into generation.
Drilling wood produces fire,
while clouds, rain, lightning, and thunder
arise from mutual causation.
This is harm turning into generation.
Water inherently harms fire,
yet when grease soaks a wick,
the lamp’s flame grows brighter—
this too is harm turning into generation.
Yin, yang, the five phases, and the myriad things exist,
and the responses of fortune and misfortune
are each spoken of according to their categories.
Sometimes there is misfortune within fortune,
and fortune within misfortune.
In misfortune, observe what rescues it;
in fortune, observe what harms it.
If misfortune has rescue,
it does not reach the point of disaster.
If fortune has harm,
it does not attain full celebration.
Pure misfortune brings great disaster;
pure fortune brings deep blessings.
For example, Chǒu and Wǔ harm each other;
if Zǐ clashes and breaks Wǔ,
and Zǐ contains Rén water,
this is pure misfortune.
If Wèi is broken by Chǒu,
and Chǒu contains the wood that desires to assist,
able to restrain Wèi earth,
then there is rescue.
Wèi and Zǐ harm each other;
if Wèi clashes and breaks Zǐ,
and Zǐ is Rén water,
water restrains Wǔ fire,
so there is fortune within misfortune.
Zǐ combines with Chǒu,
but Chǒu earth in turn restrains Zǐ water—
this is misfortune within fortune.
The principle of generation and harm
follows examples like these.
As for clashing and breaking,
it is due to their energies opposing and confronting each other.
Clashing energy is light,
breaking energy is heavy.
The branches and stems each have their own mutual oppositions.
Therefore, each has clashing and breaking.
For stem clashing and breaking:
Jiǎ and Gēng clash and break,
Yǐ and Xīn clash and break,
Bǐng and Rén clash and break,
Dīng and Guǐ clash and break,
Wù and Rén, Jiǎ and Wù, Yǐ and Jǐ
also clash and break.
These are all direct clashes and breaks.
Moreover, their inherent natures mutually overcome,
making it even heavier.
For branch clashing and breaking:
Zǐ and Wǔ clash and break,
Chǒu and Wèi clash and break,
Yín and Shēn clash and break,
Mǎo and Yǒu clash and break,
Chén and Xū clash and break,
Sì and Hài clash and break.
This also takes from mutual opposition.
Their lightness or heaviness
is all spoken of in terms of life and death.
The Four Mèng have life but no death,
so they clash directly but do not break.
The Four Jì have death but no life,
so they break directly without clashing.
The Four Zhòng have both death and life arising,
therefore they have both clashing and breaking.
The Four Mèng have life but no death,
so they only have clash, not break—
Yín has living fire,
Sì has living metal,
Shēn has living water,
Hài has living wood.
The Four Zhòng have both death and life:
Mǎo has flourishing wood and dead water,
Wǔ has flourishing fire and dead wood,
Yǒu has flourishing metal and dead fire,
Zǐ has flourishing water and dead metal.
The Four Jì have death but no life:
Chén has dead water,
Wèi has dead wood,
Xū has dead fire,
Chǒu has dead metal.
Death energy is heavy,
therefore it can break.
Life energy is light,
therefore it clashes.
Furthermore, Jiǎ moving toward Gēng is clash;
Gēng moving toward Jiǎ is break.
This is because the strong controls the weak.
As for clashing and breaking,
all involve positions directly opposing each other,
which is most inauspicious.
Also, mutually moving toward clashing positions—
if I am at Gēng and cause the enemy to reside at Jiǎ—
is because the strong controls the weak.
A question says:
"Lì energy is mutual clash,
yet now you explain clashing and breaking
without calling it lì—
this is not yet understandable."
The answer says:
"The mutual lì of the five phases
becomes heavy due to changes in events;
it is not constant.
If there is attack, it appears;
if there is no disaster, it ceases.
What is explained now
is simply the positions of the branches and stems,
constantly opposing each other on their own,
the hard and soft clashing.
It does not inquire into mutations and anomalies;
how could it be called such?"
Composed by Xiāo Jí, Duke of Kāiguó of Chéngyáng Commandery, with the honorary title of Yítóng Sānsī.
In the Zuǒzhuàn,
Zǐchǎn said:
"They manifest as the five colors."
Cài Bójiē said:
"That which communicates with the eye are the five colors."
The Huángdì Sùwèn says:
"The nature of plants has five aspects."
To distinguish them as the five colors:
Eastern wood is the bluish-green color,
the generation and growth of the myriad things—
the color of gentleness and softness.
Southern fire is the red color,
resembling the appearance of blazing yang and flames.
Central earth is the yellow color;
yellow is the color of earth.
Therefore it is said, "Heaven is dark and earth is yellow."
Western metal’s color is white;
autumn is the killing energy,
white dew becomes frost.
White is the image of mourning.
Northern water’s color is black;
from afar it looks dark and deep—
the image of shadowy darkness.
The vast and boundless dark sea,
profound and dark without end.
Water is the thing of the great yin,
therefore it is shadowy and dark.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì states:
"The essence of earth is yellow,
the essence of wood is green,
the essence of fire is red,
the essence of metal is white,
the essence of water is black."
The Chūnqiū Kǎoyìyǒu says:
"The qì of the northern Dí people generates Yōudū.
Its color is black,
like herds of livestock and felt tents.
The qì of the southern Yí people generates Jiāozhǐ.
Its color is red,
gathered at corners like banners and bird heads.
The qì of the eastern Yí people generates Láizhù.
Its color is bluish-green,
scattered and spread out,
like forest trees.
The qì of the western Yí people generates Shāqiū.
Its color is white,
sharp and accumulated like floating blades.
The central earth gathers;
its color is yellow,
like the shape of city walls.
Yellow qì fills the four borders,
the essence of earth expands."
These five are the correct colors.
Their changing colors are also five.
Yǐng Zǐyán's "Explanations of the Spring and Autumn Annals" states:
The classics mention the Red Dí and the White Dí.
Thus, the east is blue-green,
the north is black,
the center is yellow,
all of which are the standard colors.
Earth (Wù) fears Wood,
therefore, it gives its younger sister Jǐ in marriage to Jiǎ,
mixing yellow into blue-green,
thus the intermediate color of the east is green.
The Book of Songs says:
"Green, oh the robe, oh!"
This criticizes intermediate colors disrupting the standard colors.
Metal (Gēng) fears Fire,
therefore, it gives its younger sister Xīn in marriage to Bǐng,
mixing white into red,
thus the intermediate color of the south is pink.
The Analects, "Xiāng Dǎng" chapter, says:
"Pink and purple are not used for informal garments."
Wood (Jiǎ) fears Metal,
therefore, it gives its younger sister Yǐ in marriage to Gēng,
mixing blue-green into white,
thus the intermediate color of the west is pale blue.
Fire (Bǐng) fears Water,
therefore, it gives its younger sister Dīng in marriage to Rén,
mixing red into black,
thus the intermediate color of the north is purple.
Confucius said:
"I detest purple for usurping the place of vermilion."
Water (Rén) fears Earth,
therefore, it gives its younger sister Guǐ in marriage to Wù,
mixing black into yellow,
thus the intermediate color of the center
is dark yellow.
The "Wǔxíng Shū" states:
Jiǎ is blue-green,
Jǐ is green,
Bǐng is red,
Xīn is pink,
Gēng is white,
Yǐ is pale blue,
Rén is black,
Dīng is purple,
Wù is yellow,
Guǐ is dark yellow.
In these cases, the husband represents the standard color,
and the wife represents the mixed color.
Liǔ Shìlóng states:
The Eight Trigrams each have their own colors:
Zhèn is blue-green,
Lí is red,
Duì is white,
Kǎn is black.
These are all the standard colors of their respective directions.
Qián is purple,
Gèn is pink,
Xùn is green,
Kūn is yellow.
These are all intermediate colors.
Kūn takes the standard color of the Wèi Earth.
The "Jiǎyǐ Jīng" states:
Blue-green like kingfisher feathers,
black like crow feathers,
red like a rooster's comb,
yellow like a crab's belly,
white like pig fat.
These five colors indicate the presence of vital energy.
Blue-green like growing grass,
black like water moss,
yellow like unripe bitter orange,
red like clotted blood,
white like dried bones.
These five colors indicate the presence of deathly energy.
The "Xiàng Jīng" states:
When blue-green energy first arrives,
it is like sprouting wheat;
at its peak,
it is like the green of tree leaves;
when about to depart,
it is like moss on water.
When red energy first arrives,
it is like a reddish-brown pillar;
at its peak,
it is like cinnabar;
when about to depart,
it is like dried blood.
When yellow energy first arrives,
it is like silk from a silkworm;
at its peak,
it is like a gaming board;
when about to depart,
it is like withered leaves.
When white energy first arrives,
it is like a jade seal;
at its peak,
it is like light on powder;
when about to depart,
it is like verdigris on coins.
When black energy first arrives,
it is like the liver of a dead horse;
at its peak,
it is like the sheen of lacquer;
when about to depart,
it is like mossy grime.
The "Book of Rites" states:
When a gentleman wears mourning garments,
he has a sorrowful countenance;
when he wears ceremonial cap and robes, he has a respectful countenance.
When in armor and helmet, he has an inviolable countenance.
The "Dà Dài Lǐ" states:
Confucius said:
"A gentleman has three kinds of countenance.
Brightly joyful,
the countenance of bells and drums.
With a composed spirit,
the countenance of grief and mourning.
Fiercely agitated,
the countenance of weapons and armor."
The "Guān Rén" chapter of the "Dà Dài Lǐ" states:
Humans have five inherent dispositions:
joy, anger, desire, fear, and sorrow.
When joy is stored within,
even if one wishes to conceal it,
the yang joy will inevitably show.
The other four dispositions are the same.
The five energies reside sincerely within,
and manifest outwardly in form.
Human emotions cannot be hidden.
A joyful countenance appears naturally;
an angry countenance appears flushed with indignation;
a desirous countenance appears radiant with pleasure;
a fearful countenance appears pale and subdued;
a sorrowful countenance
appears startled and still.
Genuine wisdom necessarily has a countenance of profound depth;
genuine benevolence necessarily has a countenance worthy of respect;
genuine courage necessarily has a countenance difficult to intimidate;
genuine loyalty necessarily has a countenance that is endearing;
genuine purity necessarily has a countenance difficult to defile;
genuine authenticity necessarily has a countenance worthy of trust.
One's natural countenance is bright and serene;
a false countenance is tangled, chaotic, and agitated.
Now, a joyful countenance is yellow;
an angry countenance is red;
a sorrowful countenance is blue-green;
a mourning countenance is white;
a grieving countenance is black.
These are all the colors of the five constant virtues,
stirred within the five viscera,
and manifested externally,
corresponding to the goodness, evil, flourishing, and decline of one's actions.
This is what the gentleman observes,
and therefore it is explained here.
Zǐ Chǎn said,
Zhang established the five tones.
Cài Bójiē stated,
That which reaches the ear is called sound.
Blue produces the jué tone,
white produces the shāng tone,
black produces the yǔ tone,
red produces the zhǐ tone,
yellow produces the gōng tone.
The Treatise on Harmonics and Calendrics says,
Jué means to touch.
The yang qi stirs,
and all things touch the earth and are born.
Zhǐ means prosperity.
All things flourish greatly and multiply in prosperity.
Gōng means center.
It dwells in the center, extends to the four directions,
initiates and gives life,
and is the warp of the four tones.
Shāng means to manifest.
Things become manifest and clear.
Yǔ means space.
Things are stored, gathered, and covered by space.
The Wei on Music says,
When the qi of spring is harmonious, the jué tone is in tune;
when the qi of summer is harmonious, the zhǐ tone is in tune;
when the qi of late summer is harmonious, the gōng tone is in tune;
when the qi of autumn is harmonious, the shāng tone is in tune;
when the qi of winter is harmonious, the yǔ tone is in tune.
The Record of Music says,
Gōng corresponds to the ruler;
therefore, if the gōng is disordered, it becomes wild,
and the ruler becomes arrogant.
Shāng corresponds to the minister;
if the shāng is disordered, it becomes biased,
and the minister becomes corrupt.
Zhǐ corresponds to affairs;
if the zhǐ is disordered, it becomes sorrowful,
and affairs become laborious.
Yǔ corresponds to things;
if the yǔ is disordered, it becomes perilous,
and resources become depleted.
Jué corresponds to the people;
if the jué is disordered, it becomes anxious,
and the people become resentful.
If these five are not disordered,
then the world is peaceful and harmonious,
with no corrupt or decaying sounds.
The Sùwèn says,
The wood tone is jué,
and in sound, it is a shout.
The fire tone is zhǐ,
and in sound, it is laughter.
The earth tone is gōng,
and in sound, it is singing.
The metal tone is shāng.
and in sound, it is weeping.
The water tone is yǔ,
and in sound, it is groaning.
The Record of Music says,
Music is that from which sounds are born.
Its root lies in the human heart being moved by things.
Therefore, when a sorrowful heart is moved,
its sound is hurried and cut off;
when a joyful heart is moved,
its sound is expansive and relaxed;
when a delighted heart is moved,
its sound is released and scattered;
when an angry heart is moved,
its sound is rough and fierce;
when a steadfast heart is moved,
its sound is straight and pure;
when a loving heart is moved,
its sound is harmonious and gentle.
These six are not inherent nature,
but are moved by things and then activated.
Examine the sound to know the tone,
examine the tone to know the music,
examine the music to know governance,
and the way of governance is complete.
Therefore, the Preface to the Book of Songs says,
When sounds form patterns,
it is called tone.
The tones of a well-governed age
are peaceful and joyful,
and its governance is harmonious.
The tones of a chaotic age
are resentful and angry,
and its governance is perverse.
The tones of a perished state
are sorrowful and pensive,
and its people are distressed.
The chapter "Observing People" in the Dàdài Lǐjì says,
Sincerity lies within,
and must manifest externally.
Use what is seen to infer what is hidden,
use the small to infer the great.
Sound resembles its reality.
When qi first generates things,
things, once born, have sound.
Sounds have hardness and softness, clarity and turbidity, goodness and badness,
all expressed through sound.
Therefore, those whose heart-qi is boastful and deceptive
have sounds that are scattered and diffuse;
those whose heart-qi is compliant and trustworthy
have sounds that are smooth and rhythmic;
those whose heart-qi is base and perverse
have sounds that are foul and ugly;
those whose heart-qi is broad and gentle
have sounds that are warm and harmonious.
Therefore, the sage listens to their sounds,
observes their countenance,
and knows their goodness or evil.
That which is singly emitted is called sound,
that which is harmoniously combined is called tone.
The Preface to the Máo Shī says: "When sounds form patterns, it is called tone."
Therefore, based on the five tones, there are the eight musical sounds.
The Wei on Music says,
Things are completed by three,
and established by five.
Three and five make eight,
therefore, musical sounds are eight.
The eight musical sounds are metal, stone, silk, bamboo, earth, wood, gourd, and leather,
used to produce gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ.
Metal corresponds to bells,
stone corresponds to chimes,
silk corresponds to strings,
bamboo corresponds to pipes,
earth corresponds to xūn (ocarina),
wood corresponds to zhùyǔ (percussion instruments),
gourd corresponds to shēng (mouth organ),
leather corresponds to drums.
Drums govern zhèn,
shēng govern xùn,
zhùyǔ govern qián,
xūn govern gèn,
pipes govern kǎn,
strings govern lí,
chimes govern kūn,
bells govern duì.
The "Diagrams and Portents" chapter of the Yuè Wěi states:
Kǎn governs the winter solstice.
The gōng note is the symbol of the ruler;
when people have a ruler,
then the myriad things achieve completion.
When the vital force has the gōng note of the Yellow Bell,
then the myriad things are harmonized,
which is how proper order begins in the world.
One who can share the same norms as Heaven and Earth,
and unite his virtue with the spirits and the luminous,
will then have the seven beginnings and eight endings [of music]
each attain their proper place,
and the Son of Heaven will be reverent and majestic,
the four quarters will take him as their beginning.
Therefore, for music, the guǎn (pipe) is used.
Gèn governs the beginning of spring.
The yang qi begins to emerge;
it is said thunder stirs within a hundred lǐ,
and the sage, in granting land to the people,
also does not exceed one hundred mǔ.
This is the division of Heaven and Earth,
the measure of the Yellow Bell.
Nine [parts] harmonize the eight tones.
Therefore, the sage uses nine qǐng [of land]
to establish eight families.
The superior farmer feeds nine mouths,
the middling one feeds seven mouths,
the inferior one feeds five mouths.
This ensures the wealthy are not overly extravagant,
and the poor have no worry of hunger or starvation.
In three years, there is a surplus of one year's store;
in nine years, a surplus of three years' store.
This is what the Yellow Bell accomplishes,
through the harmony of waxing and waning.
Therefore, for music, the xūn (ocarina) is used.
Zhèn governs the spring equinox.
Heaven and Earth, yin and yang, are divided equally.
Therefore, the sage king models himself on Heaven's inheritance
to establish the five jūn (equalities/regulations).
The five jūn
are also the jūn (tuning) of the pentatonic scale by the pitch-pipes.
Though musical notes are extremely numerous,
the basic tones do not exceed five.
Though things are extremely abundant,
the jūn (regulations) do not exceed five.
So that the rich consider the poor,
the strong do not encroach upon the weak,
the wise do not deceive the foolish,
the market has no double prices,
the myriad things share equality,
the four seasons constantly obtain [their due],
the public treasury has surplus,
kindness reaches all under heaven,
sharing the same virtue as Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, for music, the drum is used.
Xùn governs the beginning of summer.
It is said the myriad things, long and short, each have their differences.
Therefore, the sage king models himself on Heaven's inheritance
to pattern the assigning of affairs.
The noble and the humble each have their ranks;
among the officers, then there is righteous deference and ritual propriety;
ruler and minister have distinction;
superior and inferior are all ordered;
the way of governance proceeds.
Therefore, for music, the shēng (mouth organ) is used.
Lí governs the summer solstice.
Yang begins to descend,
and yin completes things.
Therefore, the sage king models himself on Heaven's inheritance
to pattern the assigning of regulations for clothing and measures,
in order to clarify ritual and righteousness, and make noble and base manifest,
illuminating their virtue brightly,
leading them by measure.
Then women's work has distinctions,
and men's conduct has ritual propriety.
Therefore, for music, stringed instruments are used.
Kūn governs the beginning of autumn.
Yang qi is just entering,
and yin qi holds sway.
Insects first seek their burrows, desiring to hibernate.
Therefore, the sage king models himself on this,
assigning measures and dimensions for palaces and houses.
Also, regulations and systems are made appropriate,
large and small have their patterns,
noble and base have their distinctions,
superior and inferior have their proper sequence.
Therefore, for music, the qìng (chime stone) is used.
Duì governs the autumn equinox.
Heaven, Earth, the myriad things, and human achievements are all settled.
Therefore, the sage king models himself on Heaven's inheritance
to fix ranks and emoluments.
Ranks and emoluments do not exceed one's ability.
Gōng is the ruler;
shāng is the minister.
Shāng means to display.
It means the minister displays and makes clear the ruler's merit and virtue.
Noble and base have their positions;
positions have their corresponding things;
things have their appropriateness.
Those who achieve merit receive rank and reward;
those who fail in merit receive punishment and penalty.
Therefore, for music, the zhōng (bell) is used.
Qián governs the beginning of winter.
Yin and yang end and begin again;
the myriad things die and are revived.
Therefore, the sage king models himself on Heaven's inheritance
to establish penal laws.
Punishing one moves a thousand;
executing one affects ten thousand.
So that the dead bear no resentment,
and the living bear no grievance.
Therefore, for music, the zhùyǔ (wooden percussion box and tiger) are used.
The Guóyǔ says:
Earthenware and silk (stringed instruments like) qín and sè emphasize the gōng note;
metal bells emphasize the yǔ note;
stone chimes emphasize the jué note;
gourd and bamboo emphasize the zhǐ note;
leather and wood emphasize the shāng note.
The lǜ pitches are used to harmonize music;
the pitch-pipes are used to level the tones.
Metal and stone are used to stir it;
silk and bamboo are used to carry it forward;
song is used to chant it;
gourd is used to spread it;
earthenware is used to support it;
leather and wood are used to regulate it.
When things attain their constancy, it is called music;
what is seized is called striking;
mutual support is called harmony;
fine and great not overstepping is called balance.
Earthenware and silk both belong to fire,
therefore they emphasize gōng.
This is the principle of mother and child responding to each other.
Metal bells emphasizing yǔ is also like this.
Stone emphasizing jué:
stone is metal.
With jué, it is the meaning of female and male harmonizing.
Gourd is earth.
Bamboo is wood.
Emphasizing zhǐ is also the principle of mother and child responding.
Leather and wood both belong to jué,
emphasizing shāng is also due to female and male harmonizing.
The gōng tone is harmonious and舒缓 (soothing);
its harmony is broad and gentle,
affecting the spleen.
The shāng tone is dispersed and bright;
its harmony is warm and empty,
affecting the lungs.
The jué tone is guarded and restrained;
its harmony is tranquil and clear,
affecting the liver.
The zhǐ tone is defeated and rapid;
its harmony is even and balanced,
affecting the heart.
The yǔ tone is rapid and empty;
its harmony is short and dispersed,
affecting the kidneys.
The Huángdì Bīng Jué states:
When two armies are facing each other,
send a man to a point
one hundred and twenty paces from the enemy camp,
and use a tube pressed to the ear to listen.
If you hear a rumbling like carts,
like thunder or drum sounds, it is gōng.
Their general will be tolerant, harmonious, and trustworthy.
If you hear metal and stone harmonizing,
a booming sound of attack,
like bells, chime stones, or thunderclaps, it is shāng.
Their general will be威严 (awe-inspiring), wrathful, fond of killing,
and it is suitable to frequently provoke his anger.
If you hear a sound like galloping horses, flaming cannons, or rending and splitting, it is zhǐ.
Their general will be fierce, brave, and courageous,
difficult to contend with directly.
If you hear a rustling, soughing sound,
like trees moving,
or like people calling out sorrowfully, it is jué.
Their general will be benevolent and cannot be deceived.
If you hear a gurgling sound like flowing water raising waves,
or agitated air sounding like laughter, it is yǔ.
Their general will be greedy, covetous, and full of treacherous schemes.
Examine these five tones to know the enemy's nature.
The sounds of awaiting the wind
are also all like this.
This together discusses the manifestations of musical sounds,
therefore it is provided here for explanation.
Zǐ Chǎn said,
Qi forms the five flavors.
Zhèng Xuán said,
What enters the mouth are the five flavors,
what enters the nose are the five odors.
The Lǐjì Yuèlìng says,
In the days of spring,
its flavor is sour,
its odor is gamy,
which are the smell and flavor of wood.
Shuōwén says,
Gamy means the odor of sheep.
The qi of spring things
resembles that of sheep.
The reason wood is sour
symbolizes the birth of all things in the east.
Sour means to drill.
It means all things drill through the earth to be born.
The five flavors obtain sourness,
and thus are conveyed.
Yuánmìngbāo says,
Sour means the beginning.
Qi begins to generate and concentrate,
the mind naturally becomes upright.
The Lǐjì says,
In the days of summer,
its flavor is bitter,
its odor is scorched.
The reason fire is bitter
is because the south governs growth and nourishment.
Bitterness is what nourishes growth.
The five flavors require bitterness,
in order to be nourished.
Yuánmìngbāo says,
Bitterness means toil and hardship,
only then can it nourish.
Fāngyán says,
Bitterness means satisfaction.
The odor scorched
is because yang qi steams and moves,
it is the qi of blazing fire.
Xǔ Shèn said,
Scorched means things burned by fire,
have the odor of scorching and burning.
Summer qi is the same.
The Lǐjì says,
In the days of late summer,
its flavor is sweet,
its odor is fragrant.
The reason earth's flavor is sweet
is because the center is harmonious and balanced.
Sweet means delicious.
Yuánmìngbāo says,
Sweet means eating as usual,
it speaks of being content with its flavor.
Sweet flavor is the master of the five flavors,
just as earth harmonizes and completes the four agents.
The odor fragrant
is the local qi of earth,
fragrance is the master.
Xǔ Shèn said,
Earth obtains the harmonious and balanced qi,
therefore it is fragrant.
The Lǐjì says,
In the days of autumn,
its odor is fishy,
its flavor is pungent.
The west,
has a killing qi that is fishy.
Xǔ Shèn said,
The qi of being unripe,
is fishy.
The qi of western metal,
symbolizes this flavor pungent,
things obtain pungency,
and then wither and are killed.
It is also said,
Pungency of the old and new.
Old things are all exhausted,
new things have already formed,
therefore it is called new.
Yuánmìngbāo says,
Yin harms, therefore pungent,
killing in principle, therefore pungent,
piercing yin qi makes it so.
The Lǐjì says,
In the days of winter,
its flavor is salty,
its odor is rotten.
Rotten is the qi of water.
As if existing, as if not existing,
it means the qi is subtle.
It is also said,
Water receives filth and turbidity,
therefore its odor is decayed and rotten.
Xǔ Shèn said,
The odor of rot and decay,
northern qi is the same.
This flavor salty is of northern things.
Salty is what hardens them,
just as the five flavors obtain saltiness and then become firm.
Xǔ Shèn said,
Salty means to hold.
Yuánmìngbāo says,
Salty means sickle.
Sickle means clear.
The qi of extreme cold,
therefore makes it clear and salty.
Zhèng Xuán said,
Of the five flavors, vinegar is sour,
wine is bitter,
honey is sweet,
ginger is pungent,
salt is salty.
Huángdì Jiǎyǐ Jīng says,
Among grains, rice is sweet,
hemp is sour,
soybean is salty,
wheat is bitter,
millet is pungent.
One says,
rice is pungent.
Among fruits, jujube is sweet,
plum is sour,
chestnut is salty,
apricot is bitter,
peach is pungent.
Among vegetables, mallow is sweet,
leek is sour,
bean leaves are salty,
Chinese chive is bitter,
scallion is pungent.
Among domestic animals, ox is sweet,
dog is sour,
pig is salty,
sheep is bitter,
chicken is pungent.
Běncǎo says,
Among stones, jade is sweet,
metal is pungent,
realgar is bitter,
azurite is sour,
red halloysite is salty.
Among herbs, poria is sweet,
cinnamon heartwood is pungent,
asparagus root is bitter,
schisandra is sour,
figwort is salty.
Among insects, ephemera are sweet,
millipedes are pungent,
python is bitter,
pill bugs are sour,
lizard is salty.
Examples of medicinal and edible things are many,
here only a general outline is given.
They are matched with the five flavors like this.
All are generated by the qi of the five agents,
the qi is partial,
therefore their flavors are distinct.
In summary,
among the five grains, the awned ones correspond to wood,
the scattered ones correspond to fire,
the podded ones correspond to metal,
the narrow ones correspond to water,
and the clustered ones correspond to earth.
Awned grains include wheat and barley,
scattered grains include millet and broomcorn millet,
podded grains include sesame,
narrow grains include soybeans and other beans,
and clustered grains include millet and foxtail millet.
The awned ones are chosen for their sharp, slender awns,
symbolizing wood emerging from the earth,
like sharp points.
Scattered refers to spreading out.
It symbolizes the warm energy of fire,
causing things to spread out.
Podded means square or regular.
It symbolizes metal's ability to cut and shape,
with a square and upright form.
Narrow means slender.
It symbolizes water flowing long and narrow.
Clustered means gathered together.
It symbolizes all things gathering in the earth,
where they become useful.
Among the five fruits, the seeded ones correspond to wood,
the pitted ones correspond to fire,
the thick-skinned ones correspond to metal,
the hard-shelled ones correspond to water,
and the clustered ones correspond to earth.
Seeded fruits include pears and crabapples,
pitted fruits include peaches, plums, and apricots,
thick-skinned fruits include oranges and tangerines,
hard-shelled fruits include walnuts and chestnuts,
and clustered fruits include grapes.
Seeded fruits are chosen for their moist, glossy appearance,
like the glossy growth of wood,
with seeds and fruits flourishing.
Pitted fruits are chosen for their inedible pits inside the flesh,
which are unfit to eat,
like the hidden yin within fire,
incapable of containing anything.
Thick-skinned fruits are chosen for their tough, tight skin,
like the aging energy of metal,
where things shrink and tighten in the west.
Hard-shelled fruits are chosen for their edible flesh inside the shell,
like the yang within water,
capable of containing and holding.
Clustered fruits are chosen for their clustered growth,
like all things gathering in the earth.
This is a general discussion of grains and fruits,
corresponding to the five flavors,
as roughly explained earlier.
The Yuèlìng states:
In spring, eat wheat and mutton.
Wheat has a husk,
thus it belongs to wood.
Sheep are fire animals;
the qi of spring is still cold,
so these are used to calm one's nature.
In summer, eat beans and chicken.
Beans have a husk and are firm,
aligning with water.
Chickens belong to wood animals.
Therefore, they are eaten during the hot season.
In the center (late summer), eat millet and beef.
Millet is the chief among grains.
Cattle are earth animals;
due to their sweet and harmonious nature,
they correspond to the season.
In autumn, eat hemp and dog.
Hemp belongs to metal;
dogs are also metal animals,
hence they follow autumn.
In winter, eat glutinous millet and pork.
Glutinous millet is dispersing and belongs to fire.
Pigs are water animals.
Combining their fire and water
makes them suitable for winter consumption.
These five types of food
have different principles.
In spring, when it is still cold, eat warm foods;
in summer, when it is hot, eat cold foods.
This reasoning is understandable.
Bitter and sweet flavors harmonize,
thus they are suitable according to the season;
this is also understandable.
As for the two foods of autumn and winter,
they should logically be hot,
yet they are not hot.
What is the reason for this?
If following Cài Yōng's explanation,
simply stating that the food flavors are mutually suitable,
then there is no further doubt.
If following Zhèng Xuán's explanation,
it is indeed not fully comprehensive.
Now, expanding on Zhèng's words:
Lesser Yang and Greater Yang
have qi that is dispersing;
Lesser Yin and Greater Yin
have qi that is constricting and closing.
Thus, Héshàng Gōng,
explaining Lǎozǐ's words, said:
When agitated qi is above,
and yang qi lies hidden below,
that is why it is cold.
When calm qi is above,
and yin qi lies hidden below,
that is why it is hot.
The human body's yin and yang
follow the same principle.
In spring and summer, qi disperses,
and yang qi expands.
It is suitable to use warm foods to harmonize yin qi.
In autumn and winter, qi constricts and closes,
with yang qi inside the body;
it is suitable to use cold foods
to regulate yang qi.
Winter combines water and fire,
differing from autumn.
Precisely because it is a time of storage and closure,
more so than autumn,
it balances both water and fire.
Now, also considering the Jiǎyǐ [text],
to compare with Zhèng's meaning,
there are slight discrepancies.
The Jiǎyǐ states that both mutton and wheat are bitter,
both being fire flavors.
Zhèng Xuán says mutton is a fire animal, which aligns.
But he considers wheat to belong to wood.
This is based on its husked form.
The use of warmth remains the same.
The Jiǎyǐ
states that beans are salty and chicken is pungent.
Zhèng Xuán says beans align with water, which matches,
but chicken belongs to wood, which differs.
This is because chickens crow near dawn, close to the yín (tiger) wood hour.
Also, they flap their wings,
possessing yang nature.
Yet, as a yǒu (rooster) bird,
it belongs to metal in reality.
The Jiǎyǐ states that both hemp and dog are sour.
Zhèng says both hemp and dog belong to metal.
Sour is a wood flavor,
used to regulate metal qi;
using the flavor of Lesser Yang
to regulate the qi of Lesser Yin
is logically acceptable.
But using metal to regulate metal
may disrupt harmony.
The Jiǎyǐ
states that glutinous millet is pungent and pork is salty.
Zhèng Xuán says pork aligns with water, which matches,
but glutinous millet belongs to fire, which differs.
This is because glutinous millet is red and hot in nature,
thus considered fire.
If following Zhèng's intent,
it is as explained earlier.
If considering the meaning of the Jiǎyǐ's Míngtáng Yuèlìng,
eating cold in summer
aims to regulate the oppressive, toxic qi of intense heat.
Eating cold in winter
removes latent heat stored within.
Using warmth in spring's cold.
Both ideas are not dissimilar.
In autumn, using Lesser Yang to harmonize Lesser Yin
is due to the presence of killing qi.
Thus, using raw flavors to supplement.
Zhèng's view entirely diverges.
The Zhōulǐ, Tiānguān states:
In general harmonization, spring favors more sour,
summer more bitter,
autumn more pungent,
winter more salty,
and adjust with smooth and sweet flavors.
There are two interpretations.
One says:
Follow the seasonal qi;
spring meals should be more sour,
summer meals should be more bitter.
The other says:
"More" means excessive.
If spring meals are overly sour,
reduce salty flavors.
reduce sour flavors.
Hence, the later sentence states:
Adjust with smooth and sweet flavors.
Now, following the former interpretation,
the flavors of the four seasons
each correspond to what is appropriate at the time.
Thus, salty and bitter flavors in each season
suit nourishing the body.
Earth, being central,
encompasses all four resources.
Therefore, the flavors of the four seasons
must also include sweet flavors for harmonization.
It also states:
For harmonizing what is suitable in meals:
Beef pairs with tú,
tú being rice.
Mutton pairs with glutinous millet;
pork pairs with millet;
dog pairs with fine millet;
fowl pairs with wheat;
fish pairs with gū.
Gū is wild rice.
All gentlemen's meals should generally follow this.
Generally, sour medicines nourish the bones;
bitter ones nourish the qi;
sweet ones nourish the flesh;
pungent ones nourish the sinews;
salty ones nourish the vessels.
This expresses the principle of mutual support.
The Hétú states:
If a person consumes salt without limit,
it causes the kidney qi to become excessive
and the heart qi to decline,
making the person manic,
prone to nosebleeds and vomiting blood,
and unsettled in spirit.
Consuming pungent flavors without limit
causes the lung qi to become excessive
and the liver qi to decline,
making the person timid, cowardly, sorrowful, and worried,
with blindness and white hair.
Consuming sweet flavors without limit
causes the spleen qi to become excessive
and the kidney qi to decline,
making the person foolish and lustful,
with seminal emission, lower back pain,
and discharge of pus and blood.
Consuming bitter flavors without limit
causes the heart qi to become excessive
and the lung qi to decline,
making the person decisive and reckless with life,
with cough, rebellious qi, and chest fullness.
Consuming sour flavors without limit
causes the liver qi to become excessive
and the spleen qi to decline,
making the person unable to digest grains,
with dim vision, deafness, and obstinate masses.
This expresses the principle of mutual restraint among the five viscera.
The Huángdì Yǎngshēng Jīng states:
Sour enters the liver;
pungent enters the lungs;
bitter enters the heart;
sweet enters the spleen;
salty enters the kidneys.
When disease is in the sinews,
do not eat sour.
When disease is in the qi,
do not eat pungent.
When disease is in the bones,
do not eat salty.
When disease is in the blood,
do not eat bitter.
When disease is in the flesh,
do not eat sweet.
If one indulges the mouth and consumes them,
they must not be taken in excess,
for they will surely harm oneself.
Therefore they are called the five thieves.
It also says:
For liver disease, avoid pungent;
for heart disease, avoid salty;
for spleen disease, avoid sour;
for lung disease, avoid bitter;
for kidney disease, avoid sweet.
These are all flavors that are disliked,
hence they are avoided.
It also says:
For lung disease, it is suitable to eat glutinous rice,
beef, jujubes, and mallows.
For heart disease, it is suitable to eat wheat, mutton, apricots, and jiàotou.
For kidney disease, it is suitable to eat soybeans, yellow millet, pork, and huò leaves.
For liver disease, it is suitable to eat hemp seeds, dog meat, plums, and leeks.
For spleen disease, it is suitable to eat chicken, peaches, millet, and scallions.
These are the five suitable foods.
The liver, heart, and kidneys are the three solid viscera,
therefore each is supplemented with its own fundamental flavor.
The spleen and lungs are hollow,
therefore they are nourished by the mother-child relationship.
The Chūnqiū Qiántán Bā states:
The five flavors generate the five viscera:
salty generates the liver;
sour generates the heart;
bitter generates the spleen;
sweet generates the lungs;
pungent generates the kidneys.
The Yǎngshēng Jīng states:
The liver's color is green;
it is suitable to eat salty foods:
rice, beef, and jujubes.
The heart's color is red;
it is suitable to eat vinegar:
dog meat and plums.
The lungs' color is white;
it is suitable to eat sweet foods:
wheat, mutton, and apricots.
The spleen's color is yellow;
it is suitable to eat bitter foods:
soybeans, pork, and millet.
The kidneys' color is black;
it is suitable to eat pungent foods:
millet and chicken.
These five foods all use what generates them
to nourish their child.
It also says:
When the five flavors enter the mouth,
each goes to a specific place,
and each causes specific ailments.
Sour goes to the sinews;
eating too much of it
causes urinary retention.
Salty goes to the blood;
eating too much of it
causes thirst.
Pungent goes to the qi;
eating too much of it
causes a hollow feeling in the heart.
Bitter goes to the bones;
eating too much of it
causes changes in the person.
Sweet goes to the skin;
eating too much of it
causes nausea.
Pungent disperses;
sour contracts;
sweet relaxes;
bitter firms;
salty moistens.
The five grains are for nourishment;
the five fruits are for assistance;
the five domestic animals are for benefit.
Combine the flavors and qi and consume them,
following what is suitable for the four seasons and the five viscera.
It also says:
People with a yellow complexion should eat sweet;
those with a green complexion should eat sour;
those with a black complexion should eat salty;
those with a red complexion should eat bitter;
those with a white complexion should eat pungent.
These are all based on what is suitable for the fundamental constitution.
The Jiāyǔ says:
Those who feed on water
are good at swimming and can endure cold.
Those who feed on earth
have no heart and do not rest.
Those who feed on wood
are strong but untamable.
Those who feed on grass
are good at running but foolish.
Those who feed on mulberry leaves
spin silk and become moths.
Those who feed on flesh
are brave and fierce.
Those who feed on qi
are spiritually bright and long-lived.
Those who feed on grains
are intelligent and skillful.
Those who do not eat
do not die and become spirits.
These are all categories based on qi and flavor,
hence they are appended and discussed here.
Examples of the resolution of the five flavors
are mostly not listed.
What the medical classics clarify and can be explained is as above.
The viscera and bowels
are formed from the five phases and six qi.
The viscera number five,
receiving from the five phases to constitute the five natures.
The bowels number six,
based on the six qi,
which are called the six emotions.
The emotions, natures, and qi
will be explained separately later.
Now,
we discuss the principles of correspondence for the viscera and bowels.
The five viscera are:
liver, heart, spleen, lungs, and kidneys.
The six bowels are:
large intestine, small intestine, gallbladder, stomach, triple burner, and bladder.
The liver corresponds to wood,
the heart to fire,
the spleen to earth,
the lungs to metal,
the kidneys to water.
The bladder corresponds to yang,
the small intestine to yin,
the gallbladder to wind,
the large intestine to rain,
the triple burner to obscurity,
the stomach to brightness.
Therefore, Dù Yù of the Spring and Autumn period, Yī Hé, said:
"Excess of yin causes cold diseases,
excess of yang causes heat diseases,
excess of wind causes extremity diseases,
the extremities being the four limbs;
excess of rain causes abdominal diseases,
excess of obscurity causes delusion diseases,
excess of brightness causes heart diseases."
As for the viscera,
because they are stored within the physical form,
they are called 'zàng' (storehouses).
They also can store and receive the five qi,
hence the name 'zàng'.
As for the bowels,
because they transmit, flow, receive, and contain,
they are called 'fǔ' (repositories).
The Báihǔ Tōng states:
"The liver (gān) is so called from 'gǎn' (to ward off).
The lungs (fèi) are so called from 'fèi' (to expend).
This is how emotions move in proper order."
"The heart (xīn) is so called from 'rèn' (to bear responsibility),
bearing responsibility for thought."
"The kidneys (shèn) are so called from 'bīn' (guest),
because they discharge through orifices."
"The spleen (pí) is so called from 'biàn' (to distinguish),
that by which essence receives qi."
The Yuánmìng Bāo states:
"The spleen is for distinguishing."
"The heart obtains it and becomes noble,
the liver obtains it and becomes vigorous,
the lungs obtain it and become great,
the kidneys obtain it and transform."
"The liver corresponds to benevolence,
the lungs to righteousness,
the heart to propriety,
the kidneys to wisdom,
the spleen to faithfulness."
Why does the liver correspond to benevolence?
The liver is the essence of wood.
The benevolent delight in generating life.
The east is yang.
All things begin to be born there,
therefore the liver resembles wood.
Its color is blue-green and it possesses softness.
Why do the lungs correspond to righteousness?
The lungs are the essence of metal.
The righteous are able to make decisive judgments.
The west kills and completes all things,
therefore the lungs resemble metal.
Their color is white and they possess firmness.
Why does the heart correspond to propriety?
The heart is the essence of fire.
In the south, the honored yang is above,
the humble yin is below.
Propriety involves honor and humility,
therefore the heart resembles fire.
Its color is red and it is luminous.
Why do the kidneys correspond to wisdom?
The kidneys are the essence of water.
The wise advance without deviating,
having no doubts or perplexities.
Water also advances without obstruction.
Therefore the kidneys resemble water.
Their color is black; water is yin,
therefore the kidneys are paired.
Why does the spleen correspond to faithfulness?
The spleen is the essence of earth.
Earth governs faithfulness.
It bears the responsibility of nurturing all things,
serving as their model.
In generating things, it shows no partiality;
this is the ultimate faithfulness.
Therefore the spleen resembles earth,
its color is yellow.
Yì Fèng said:
"The nature of the liver is tranquil,
governed by jiǎ and jǐ."
"The nature of the heart is restless,
governed by bǐng and xīn."
"The nature of the spleen is forceful,
governed by wù and guǐ."
"The nature of the lungs is firm,
governed by yǐ and gēng."
"The nature of the kidneys is reverent,
governed by dīng and rén."
Xǔ Shèn's "Different Interpretations of the Five Classics" states:
According to the Xiàhóu and Ōuyáng schools of the "Shàngshū,"
the liver corresponds to wood,
the heart to fire,
the spleen to earth,
the lungs to metal,
and the kidneys to water.
This aligns with the previous view.
The ancient text version of the "Shàngshū" states:
the spleen corresponds to wood,
the lungs to fire,
the heart to earth,
and the liver to metal.
These four organs differ.
According to the "Yuèlìng" chapter of the "Lǐjì,"
in spring, the spleen is offered in sacrifice;
in summer, the lungs;
in late summer, the heart;
in autumn, the liver;
in winter, the kidneys.
All
correspond to their respective seasons,
thus the ancient "Shàngshū" is correct.
Zhèng Xuán refutes this, saying:
This text presents discrepancies and contradictions,
failing to grasp its original intent.
The "Yuèlìng" mentions five sacrifices, all referring to what comes first,
with no mention of what comes after.
Whenever "first" is mentioned, there is an implied "after."
In spring, the household deity is worshipped;
in this sacrifice,
the spleen is offered first,
followed by the kidneys.
In summer, the stove deity is worshipped;
in this sacrifice,
the lungs are offered first, followed by the heart and liver.
In late summer, the central deity of the dwelling is worshipped;
in this sacrifice,
the heart is offered first,
followed by the lungs.
In autumn, the gate deity is worshipped;
in this sacrifice,
the liver is offered first,
followed by the heart and lungs.
In winter, the road deity is worshipped;
in this sacrifice,
the kidneys are offered first,
followed by the spleen.
The meaning of all this
is based on the positions of the four seasons
and the upper and lower locations of the five organs,
arranged accordingly.
Winter occupies the rear position,
and the kidneys are located below.
Summer occupies the front position,
and the lungs are located above.
Spring occupies a slightly forward position,
so the spleen is offered first.
Autumn occupies a slightly receded position,
so the liver is offered first.
The liver, kidneys, and spleen are all below the diaphragm,
while the lungs and heart are above the diaphragm.
Sacrifices must involve three offerings,
hence there is an order of precedence.
This principle differs from that of circulating qi.
The "Eighty-One Questions" states:
All five organs are equal,
so why are the heart and lungs uniquely above the diaphragm?
The response is:
The heart governs qi,
and the lungs govern blood.
Blood circulates within the vessels,
while qi circulates outside the vessels.
They follow each other up and down,
hence they are called yíng and wèi,
which is why the heart and lungs are above the diaphragm.
The "Jiǎyǐ Jīng" states:
Huángdì
asked Qí Bó:
Humans have five organs,
and each organ has five transformations.
The liver is a male organ,
its color is green,
its season is spring,
and its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ.
The heart is a male organ,
its color is red,
its season is summer,
and its days are Bǐng and Dīng.
The spleen is a female organ,
its color is yellow,
its season is late summer,
and its days are Wù and Jǐ.
The lungs are a female organ,
their color is white,
their season is autumn,
and their days are Gēng and Xīn.
The kidneys are a female organ,
their color is black,
their season is winter,
and their days are Rén and Guǐ.
The "Sùwèn" states:
The liver is where the hún resides,
the lesser yang within yīn.
Thus, it connects with spring qi.
The heart is the root of life,
where the shén resides,
the greater yang within yang.
Thus, it connects with summer qi.
The spleen is the root of the granary,
named "promoting transformation,"
capable of transforming waste,
transferring flavors in and out,
belonging to the utmost yīn category.
Thus, it connects with earth qi.
The lungs are the root of qi,
where the pò resides,
the lesser yīn within yang.
Thus, they connect with autumn qi.
The kidneys govern hibernation,
the root of sealing and storing,
where the jīng resides,
the greater yīn within yīn.
Thus, they connect with winter qi.
It also states:
In spring, do not eat liver;
in summer, do not eat heart;
in late summer, do not eat spleen;
in autumn, do not eat lungs;
in winter, do not eat kidneys.
The "Zhōulǐ · Jíyī" states:
The physician in charge of treating the illnesses of ten thousand people,
if he regards the liver as wood,
the heart as fire,
the spleen as earth,
the lungs as metal,
and the kidneys as water,
then diseases will often be cured;
if he reverses this method,
death will result.
The rituals for the central deity in the "Yuèlìng"
are arranged according to the progression and regression of yīn and yáng.
The "Báihǔ Tōng" and medical texts like the "Sùwèn"
use practical circulation as evidence.
Thus, their correspondences are correct.
The "Báihǔ Tōng" also states:
Why does wood float and metal sink?
It is because the child is born from the mother.
Why does the liver sink and the lungs float?
Those with knowledge
honor their mother.
One explanation states:
Jiǎ wood fears metal,
so Yǐ is married to Gēng,
receiving Gēng's transformation.
Wood follows its origin,
directly corresponding to Jiǎ, thus it floats.
The liver follows its transformation,
directly corresponding to Yǐ, thus it sinks.
Gēng metal fears fire,
so Xīn is married to Bǐng,
receiving Bǐng's transformation.
Metal follows its origin,
directly corresponding to Gēng, thus it sinks.
The lungs follow their transformation,
directly corresponding to Xīn, thus they float.
Héshàng Gōng,
in his commentary on the Lǎozǐ, says:
The liver stores the hún (ethereal soul).
The lungs store the pò (corporeal soul).
The heart stores the shén (spirit).
The kidneys store the jīng (essence).
The spleen stores the zhì (will).
If the five viscera are all injured,
then the five spirits depart.
The Dàojīng yì says:
The hún resides in the liver.
The pò is in the lungs.
The shén dwells in the heart.
The jīng is stored in the kidneys.
The zhì is entrusted to the spleen.
This is the same as in the Sùwèn.
The hún corresponds to wood qi.
The shén corresponds to fire qi.
The zhì corresponds to earth qi.
The pò corresponds to metal qi.
The jīng corresponds to water qi.
The hún connects with the eyes.
The shén connects with the tongue.
The zhì connects with the mouth.
The pò connects with the nose.
The jīng connects with the ears.
The Jiǎyǐ Jīng says:
The nose is the orifice of the lungs.
The eyes are the orifices of the liver.
The mouth and lips are the orifices of the spleen.
The tongue is the orifice of the heart.
The ears are the orifices of the kidneys.
Therefore, in lung disease, there is panting and flaring of the nostrils.
In liver disease, the eyes are closed and the canthi are blue.
In spleen disease, the mouth and lips are yellow and dry.
In heart disease, the tongue is curled and shortened, and the face is red.
In kidney disease, the cheeks and face are dark yellow or black, and there is deafness.
These are called the five orifices.
Physiognomy books also call them the five indicators.
Taking the nose and the philtrum as one orifice,
it governs the heart.
The rest are the same.
"Indicator" means
that the favorable or unfavorable colors of the five viscera appear at the five orifices,
allowing one to predict good or bad fortune.
The nose and philtrum
are still part of the mouth region.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì says:
The liver governs benevolence,
hence the eyes see.
The lungs govern righteousness,
hence the nose discerns.
The heart governs propriety,
hence the ears govern.
The kidneys govern trustworthiness,
hence the lower orifices excrete.
The spleen governs wisdom,
hence the mouth instructs.
The Yuánmìngbāo says:
The eyes are envoys of the liver;
the liver's qi is benevolent and shines outward.
The Guǎnzǐ says:
The spleen manifests as the nose.
The liver manifests as the eyes.
The kidneys manifest as the ears.
The lungs manifest as the mouth.
The heart manifests as the lower orifices.
The Daoist Tàipíng Jīng says:
If the liver spirit is absent,
the eyes lack brightness.
If the heart spirit is absent,
the lips are blue-white.
If the lung spirit is absent,
the nose is blocked.
If the kidney spirit is absent,
there is deafness.
If the spleen spirit is absent,
the tongue cannot discern sweet tastes.
Another theory says:
The eyes govern the liver.
The ears govern the kidneys.
The nose governs the heart.
The tongue governs the spleen.
The mouth governs the lungs.
Regarding the liver and kidney viscera,
all the classics agree.
That the liver governs the eyes:
The liver is a wood viscus.
Wood is yang.
It is the region of the east, a place of manifest brightness.
The eyes are also bright and illuminating.
Therefore, they connect with the eyes.
The Daoist Dàshì Jīng says:
Heaven is called "penetrating vision,"
it governs the eyes,
and the eyes govern the liver.
Heaven is yang.
The liver is also yang.
The essence of the eyes and their brightness are also yang.
The light of the eyes is manifest and visible,
and moreover has constant patterns,
like the sun, the yang essence, which is never deficient and is bright.
That the kidneys govern the ears:
The kidneys are a water viscus.
Water is yin.
It is the region of the north, a dark and obscure place.
The ears can hear sounds.
Sound is an image of subtle yin.
Therefore, they connect with the ears.
The Dàshì Jīng says:
Earth is called "penetrating hearing,"
it governs the ears,
and the ears govern the kidneys.
Earth is yin.
The principle of the ear is that when empty, it receives sound.
Water governs emptiness.
Yin governs emptiness.
Yin governs darkness and obscurity.
Sound is also not constant,
like the moon's waxing and waning.
Regarding the spleen, heart, and lungs, these three viscera and their corresponding indicators,
there are various differing theories.
The Jiǎyǐ Jīng correlates the nose with the lungs.
Daoists correlate the nose with the heart.
The Guǎnzǐ correlates it with the spleen.
The Jiǎyǐ Jīng correlates it with the lungs because
the nose, being empty, receives qi,
and the lungs are also empty and receive qi.
Daoists say the nose governs the heart because
it is yang.
The Lǎozǐ Jīng says:
Heaven sends the qi of the five phases
to enter from the nose and be stored in the heart.
The nose, being empty, allows breath to enter and exit.
Its high position resembles heaven.
Therefore, it communicates with heaven,
and the qi is stored in the heart.
The Guǎnzǐ says the spleen is earth,
and the nose is in the center of the face,
therefore it is its indicator.
The Jiǎyǐ Jīng correlates the spleen with the mouth.
Daoists correlate the lungs with the mouth,
which is the same as the Guǎnzǐ.
The Jiǎyǐ Jīng correlates the spleen with the mouth because
the mouth is the gate of intake and output,
and the spleen is the place of reception and transformation.
The mouth can speak and discuss,
and the spleen can digest.
Therefore, they are connected.
Daoists correlate the lungs with the mouth because
the lungs are metal.
Metal can cut and sever.
The mouth has teeth,
which can also make decisions and sever,
which is the image of metal.
The meaning of the Guǎnzǐ
is likely the same.
The Jiǎyǐ Jīng correlates the tongue with the heart.
Daoists correlate the tongue with the spleen.
The Guǎnzǐ correlates the heart with the lower orifices.
The Jiǎyǐ Jīng correlates the tongue with the heart because
for nourishing the body and sustaining life,
nothing surpasses the five flavors.
For discerning, recognizing, and knowing,
nothing surpasses the heart.
When the five flavors enter,
it is as if the tongue knows them.
Regarding the right and wrong of all affairs,
it is as if the heart judges them.
When the heart wishes to express something,
the tongue must speak it.
Therefore, the heart corresponds to the tongue.
Daoists correlate the tongue with the spleen because
the spleen is yin.
The Lǎozǐ Jīng says:
Earth provides humans with the five flavors,
which enter from the mouth and are stored in the stomach.
What the tongue receives
then has moisture and substance.
The substance of earth is inherently material and substantial.
All flavors are produced by the earth.
Therefore, the tongue communicates with earth.
The Guǎnzǐ says the heart corresponds to the lower orifices because
the heart can distinguish good and evil,
therefore it connects with the lower orifices
to eliminate dregs and filth.
The indicators of the five viscera are at the five orifices.
The two orifices of mouth and tongue
share one location.
The others do not share because
the mouth is the indicator of the spleen,
and the spleen is earth.
The tongue is the indicator of the heart,
and the heart is fire.
They share a location because
earth is placed to be governed in the region of fire.
The tongue is inside the mouth because
fire, among the five phases,
is not always visible.
When needed, it is present.
If not used, it remains hidden;
like the tongue within the mouth,
when the mouth opens, it appears,
when the mouth closes, it is concealed.
Moreover, the heart is the master and noble part of the body,
thus it resides within.
Earth governs the four seasons,
hence it is called the union of the four.
The Sùwèn of the Jiǎyǐ,
is a book of diagnosis and prognosis.
Therefore, it is distinguished based on practical application.
The Dàojīng and the Guǎnzǐ,
each follow the interests of their own school.
The six fu organs:
The Hé Tú states:
The lung pairs with the large intestine,
the large intestine is the fu of transmission.
The heart pairs with the small intestine,
the small intestine is the fu of reception and containment.
The liver pairs with the gallbladder,
the gallbladder is the fu of essential purity.
The spleen pairs with the stomach,
the stomach is the fu of the five grains.
The kidney pairs with the bladder,
the bladder is the fu of fluids and humors.
The triple burner stands alone as the fu of internal drainage.
The Jiǎ-Yǐ edition of the Sù Wèn
says the same.
The large intestine being the fu of transmission:
the lung connects to the nose,
the nose is where qi enters and exits,
the large intestine transmits the pathway of the qi of the five grains,
therefore it is its fu.
The small intestine being the fu of reception and containment:
the heart connects to the tongue,
the tongue takes in the five flavors,
the small intestine receives them,
therefore it is the fu of reception and containment.
The gallbladder being the fu of essential purity:
the liver connects to the eyes,
the eyes are organs of clarity and brightness,
and also the masters of essence and spirit,
therefore it is called the fu of essential purity.
The stomach being the fu of the five grains:
the spleen connects to the mouth,
the mouth takes in the five grains,
and the stomach receives them,
therefore it is its fu.
The bladder being the fu of fluids and humors:
the kidney is the water zàng,
the bladder is empty and receives water,
the clear qi of water becomes fluids and humors,
the turbid qi becomes snivel and saliva,
therefore it is considered its fu.
The triple burner being the fu of central drainage:
each of the five zàng pairs with one fu,
the triple burner alone has nothing to pair with,
therefore it is said to stand alone.
It resides among the five zàng,
facilitating the movement of qi upward and downward,
therefore it is the fu of central drainage.
There are five zàng but six fu,
just as the six qì are generated from the five phases.
Also,
like the five natures generating the six emotions.
The Sù Wèn states:
The skin corresponds to the large intestine,
its flourishing is in the hair,
and it is governed by the heart.
The vessels correspond to the small intestine,
their flourishing is in the complexion,
and they are governed by the kidney.
The sinews correspond to the gallbladder,
their flourishing is in the nails,
and they are governed by the lung.
The flesh corresponds to the stomach,
its flourishing is in the lips,
and it is governed by the liver.
The interstices and fine body hair
correspond to the triple burner and bladder,
their flourishing is in the head hair,
and they are governed by the spleen.
The skin corresponding to the large intestine,
its flourishing in the hair,
and being governed by the heart:
the heart is the ruler of the body,
the skin is the city wall of the body,
the body hair is the feathery guard of the body,
the large intestine is the pathway for the transmission of qi.
Therefore they are all interconnected.
The heart is a fire zàng,
the large intestine is a metal fu,
therefore they are paired accordingly.
They are what Bǐng and Xīn govern.
The vessels corresponding to the small intestine,
their flourishing in the complexion,
and being governed by the kidney:
the kidney is water,
the vessels are the ditches and channels of blood,
facilitating the flow of water qi,
the complexion is the radiance of a person.
If blood and qi are abundant,
then the flourishing complexion is robust and cheerful;
if blood and qi are depleted,
then the countenance is withered and haggard.
The kidney is the water zàng,
the small intestine
can both receive and contain,
holding water qi,
and is also a fire fu,
therefore they are paired.
They are what Dīng and Rén govern.
The sinews corresponding to the gallbladder,
their flourishing in the nails,
and being governed by the lung:
the sinews are the firm strength inside the skin,
the nails are the firm sharpness outside the skin,
the lung is a metal zàng,
the gallbladder has the nature of firm purity,
and also,
is a wood fu,
therefore they are paired.
They are what Yǐ and Gēng govern.
The flesh corresponding to the stomach,
its flourishing in the lips,
and being governed by the liver:
the stomach can digest the five grains,
their essential qi becomes flesh,
the five grains enter from the mouth,
therefore their flourishing and moistening is in the lips.
The liver is the wood zàng,
benevolent and able to generate,
the stomach is an earth fu,
therefore they are paired.
They are what Jiǎ and Jǐ govern.
The interstices and fine body hair
corresponding to the triple burner and bladder,
their flourishing in the head hair,
and being governed by the spleen:
the fine body hair relies on the moistening of fluids,
the interstices are inherently open and free-flowing.
The spleen is the place that receives nourishment from flavors;
through this nourishment,
it obtains fluid moistening and free flow;
through fluid moistening and free flow,
hair grows.
It is written:
Hair is the surplus of blood.
The spleen is the earth zàng,
the triple burner and bladder
are both water fu,
therefore they are paired.
They are what Wù and Guǐ govern.
The spleen pairs with two fu,
while the remaining four zàng
each pair with one fu:
the spleen is the earth zàng,
earth represents the way of the ruler,
the ruler is yang,
the number of yang is one,
therefore the zàng is not two.
The triple burner and bladder are both water fu,
water represents the way of the minister,
the minister is yin,
the number of yin is even,
therefore the fu are two.
The Guǎnzǐ says:
The spleen generates bones,
the kidney generates sinews,
the lung generates skin,
the heart generates flesh,
the liver generates nails and hair.
The Yuán Mìng Bāo states:
The liver generates sinews.
The spleen generating bones:
the spleen is earth,
earth can generate wood.
Bones are the foundation of the body,
like wood standing on the ground,
able to form a house,
therefore the spleen generates them.
The kidney generating sinews:
sinews are the channels and network vessels of the bones,
the vessels flow and infuse,
the sinews connect the joints,
and together they facilitate blood and qi.
The kidney is water,
therefore it generates them.
The lung generating skin:
the lung is metal,
metal can cut and sever,
skin also demarcates and defines,
therefore the lung generates it.
The heart generating flesh:
the heart is fire,
flesh is the land of the body,
therefore the heart generates it.
The liver generating nails and hair:
the liver is wood,
nails are the surplus of bones,
hair is the surplus of blood,
both are the qi of water and wood,
therefore the liver generates them.
The Yuán Mìng Bāo stating that the liver generates sinews
also carries the meaning of wood qi;
sinews have branches and twigs,
resembling wood.
The River Chart states:
Benevolence, kindness, and generous giving
are the essence of the liver.
Excessive grief and sorrow
injure the liver.
If the liver is injured,
it causes blurred vision.
Propriety, conduct, and the arrangement of truths
are the essence of the heart.
Extreme joy and anger injure the heart.
If the heart is injured,
it leads to illnesses such as nosebleeds and vomiting.
Harmony, sincerity, and deep trustworthiness
are the essence of the spleen.
Indulgence, greed, and excessive desires
injure the spleen.
If the spleen is injured,
it causes accumulation and failure to transform,
leading to illnesses of obstruction and stagnation.
Righteousness, kindness, firmness, and decisiveness
are the essence of the lungs.
Worry, anxiety, and pent-up anger
injure the lungs.
If the lungs are injured,
it leads to coughing, rebellious qi, and loss of voice.
Wisdom, discernment, strategy, and planning
are the essence of the kidneys.
Overexertion, excessive desires, and pent-up fullness
injure the kidneys.
If the kidneys are injured,
it results in loss of essence and shortened lifespan.
This not only violates the Five Constants
and damages one's years and life,
but also disrupts the Six Emotions,
leading to the loss of family and state.
For example, the two emperors Jié and Zhòu
both perished due to greed and indulgence, losing their states.
The two ministers Liáng and Dòu
also both fell due to extravagance and indulgence, ruining their families.
Although Péngzǐ prolonged his life through indulgence in sensual pleasures,
and the King of Qí dispelled illness through anger,
such divergent paths
all have appropriate ways of regulation.
If regulated, the Four Great Elements gain peace;
if indulged, the Five Viscera become afflicted.
The Sùwèn states:
The liver is the organ of the general,
from which planning and deliberation arise.
The heart is the organ of the sovereign guardian,
from which spirit and clarity arise.
The spleen is the organ of the granary,
from which the five flavors arise.
The lungs are the organ of the minister and mentor,
from which governance and regulation arise.
The kidneys are the organ of exertion and strength,
from which skill and ingenuity arise.
The liver is the organ of the general,
and planning and deliberation arise from it
because the nature of wood is benevolence.
A benevolent person is capable of deep thought and long-term planning,
always seeking to benefit and bring peace to all things.
The general is the leader of military operations,
so planning and deliberation must come first.
Therefore, military texts say:
If troops are raised with benevolence,
then none will fail to follow and achieve it;
if divided with benevolence,
then none will fail to follow and be pleased.
It also says:
If the general lacks strategy,
then the soldiers will worry;
if the general lacks planning,
then the soldiers will desert.
Thus, the liver is the general,
producing planning and deliberation.
The heart is the organ of the sovereign guardian,
and spirit and clarity arise from it
because fire corresponds to the south, where sunlight shines brightly,
symbolizing the ruler.
The spirit is the ruler of the body,
just as the ruler faces south to govern.
The Yìjīng uses Lí to represent fire,
occupying the position of the great sun,
symbolizing the ruler.
Human movement
and the actions of emotions and nature
all originate from the heart.
Thus, it is the organ of the sovereign guardian,
from which spirit and clarity arise.
The spleen is the organ of the granary,
and the five flavors arise from it
because all things are born from the earth
and return to it upon death.
The intake of the five grains
is received by the spleen.
Thus, the emergence of the five flavors
also originates from here.
The lungs are the organ of the minister and mentor,
and governance and regulation arise from them
because metal can judge and decide.
The duty of the minister and mentor
is to understand the way of governance,
ensuring that superiors and subordinates follow teachings
and all adhere to propriety and regulation.
Among the Five Viscera, the lungs
also give rise to governance and regulation.
The Music Apocrypha states:
Shāng means to manifest.
The minister manifests the virtue of the ruler
to harmonize superiors and subordinates.
This is the role of the minister and mentor, related to the kidneys.
The kidneys are the organ of exertion and strength,
and skill and ingenuity arise from them
because the nature of water is wisdom.
Wisdom necessarily brings many abilities,
hence skill and ingenuity.
Ingenuity leads to unceasing self-strengthening.
The Eighty-One Questions asks:
Each of the viscera is single,
so why are the kidneys alone paired?
The left is the kidney,
the right is the Gate of Life.
The Gate of Life
is where essence and spirit converge.
The River Chart states:
The liver and heart emerge on the left,
the spleen and lungs emerge on the right,
while the kidneys and the Gate of Life
both emerge at the chǐ section.
This pertains to pulse examination.
The question is:
The previous explanation
said the kidneys are yīn, hence paired.
Now,
it is said the left is the kidney and the right is the Gate of Life.
Does this not contradict itself?
The answer is:
The Gate of Life and the kidneys
differ in name but are the same in form.
As water viscera, their substance is not different,
hence they are paired.
Named according to yīn numbers,
they are distinguished as left and right,
so each has its own function.
This is similar to how the Triple Burner and the bladder
are both water organs,
yet they can have two different names.
The Classic of Lǎozǐ and the Sùwèn state that the heart stores the spirit.
The spirit is defined by its divine clarity and illumination.
This means the heart can clearly understand all things.
The spirit is the ruler of the body,
symbolized by fire,
as explained previously.
The kidneys store the essence.
Essence is characterized by intelligence, spirituality, and wisdom.
It is also the qi of intelligence and wisdom,
belonging to kidney water.
Because wisdom involves skill,
the essence is stored there.
The spleen stores the will.
Will corresponds to earth.
Earth governs the four phases,
and has many inclinations.
Will is defined by the heart's desires and inclinations,
thus it is stored in the spleen.
