The liver stores the hún (ethereal soul).
Hún is named for its capacity for movement.
The liver is Lesser Yang,
and yang nature is active.
Wood nature is benevolent,
so the hún also governs goodness,
thus it is stored in the liver.
The lungs store the pò (corporeal soul).
Pò is named for its capacity to adhere.
The lungs are Lesser Yin,
and yin nature is tranquil.
Metal governs killing,
and the pò also governs evil.
Therefore it is stored there.
The five viscera govern
the five kinds: spirit, essence, will, hún, and pò.
Discussing them in terms of yin and yang,
there are only two distinctions:
yang is called hún,
yin is called pò.
The Heshanggōng Commentary states:
"The five qi, pure and subtle,
become the spirit, essence, intelligence, and hearing;
the five sounds and the five natures.
Their ghost is called hún;
hún is male.
It governs entry and exit through the nose,
connecting with heaven.
The five flavors, turbid and thick,
become the physical body, bones, flesh,
blood vessels, and the six emotions.
Their ghost is called pò;
pò is female.
It enters and exits through the mouth,
connecting with earth."
The Family Sayings of Confucius records:
Zǎi Wǒ asked Confucius,
"I have heard the names 'ghost' and 'spirit',
but do not know what they refer to."
Confucius said,
"In life, humans have qi.
The qi of the hún is
the flourishing of the spirit.
The qi of the pò is
the flourishing of the ghost.
Humans are born and die;
in death they must return to earth—
this is called 'ghost'.
The qi of the hún returns to heaven—
this is called 'spirit'.
Combining ghost and spirit and making offerings to them
is the ultimate teaching.
The bones and flesh decay below,
transforming into wild earth.
Their qi ascends and spreads above—
this is the manifestation of the spirit.
The sage, following the nature of humans and things,
clarified the designations 'ghost' and 'spirit'
to establish norms for the people.
Burning fat and fragrant herbs
is how we repay the qi.
Offering millet and grain,
preparing the lungs and liver,
adding aromatic wine—
this is how we repay the pò."
The Treatise on the Five Phases in the Book of Hàn states:
"When a person's life ends and the body is interred,
the spirit and essence scatter.
The sages established ancestral temples
to gather the qi of the hún.
Performing spring and autumn sacrifices
is to cultivate filial piety."
Master Shīzǐ said:
"'Ghost' means 'to return'.
In ancient times, they called dead people
'returning people'."
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"A person's spirit and essence
belong to heaven.
The skeleton and bones
belong to earth.
The essence qi enters its gate,
and the bones return to their root."
It also says:
"Heaven's qi is the hún;
earth's qi is the pò."
The "Suburban Sacrifices" chapter of the Book of Rites states:
"In all sacrifices, be cautious regarding these.
The qi of the hún returns to heaven;
the form and pò return to earth.
Therefore, sacrifice seeks the meaning of yin and yang.
Thus, the clear qi is called 'spirit'—
this is the yang hún.
The turbid qi is called 'ghost'—
this is the yin pò."
Yánlíng Jìzǐ,
burying his son between Yíng and Bó, said:
"Bones and flesh return to the earth—
this is fate.
The qi of the hún goes everywhere."
The Records of Yuè states:
The King asked Fànzǐ,
"I have heard that
losing one's hún and pò causes death,
and having them brings life.
All things possess them—
does this apply to humans?"
Fàn Lǐ replied,
"The pò is the sack;
the hún is the source of vital qi."
It also says:
"The hún is the essence of vital qi;
the pò is the dwelling of death qi."
The Hánshī states:
"Zhēn and Wěi are two rivers.
On the third day of the third month,
the state of Zhèng would often, upon these waters,
summon the hún and continue the pò."
The Zuǒzhuàn, 25th year of Duke Zhāo:
The Duke of Sòng held a feast,
had Zhāozǐ Shū sit to his right.
They talked, wept, and were merry.
Confucius said,
"Now, will the ruler and Zǐshū both die?
The refined clarity of the heart
is called the hún and pò.
If the hún and pò depart,
how can one last long?"
All this clarifies that the human body has the two distinctions of hún and pò.
The Classic of Lǎozǐ
states that the hún is stored in the liver
and the pò is stored in the lungs.
Since the hún belongs to heaven,
and heaven's qi is yang,
yang governs goodness and honors the left.
It resides in the liver, in the eastern wood position.
Since the pò belongs to earth,
and earth's qi is yin,
yin governs evil and honors the right.
Thus it resides in the lungs, in the western metal position.
Lǎozǐ said:
"Auspicious affairs honor the left;
inauspicious affairs honor the right."
It also says the five qi are stored in the heart,
and the five flavors are stored in the stomach.
In this discussion,
qi is yang,
and is received and stored.
The heart is the fire viscus,
the place of yang qi.
Flavor is yin,
and is received by the bowels.
The stomach is the bowel of the five grains,
the place of flavors.
The heart governs spirit and essence;
the stomach governs reception and containment.
This does not contradict the principles of hún, pò, yin, and yang.
Furthermore,
it says the hún has three
and the pò has seven.
Yang numbers are odd;
yin numbers are even.
Odd numbers begin with one—
one is the primal qi.
Although the hún is yang,
it is not called the primal beginning.
After one comes three,
therefore the number of the hún is three.
It also says:
Because heaven and earth's two qi combine
to produce humans,
and humans have another qi,
the three materials each have one qi,
therefore the hún has three.
Yin numbers are two—
two is also the beginning of yin.
Although the pò is yin,
Moreover, it is not the primordial beginning,
but the second following the first and the fourth following the third.
Yin does not stand alone,
it must rely on Yang;
taking the three of the hun,
combined they become seven.
Another explanation says:
the hun resides in the east,
taking the number three from Zhen.
The po resides in the west,
taking the number seven from Dui.
Three hun,
seven po,
combined make ten,
which corresponds to the five phases of heaven
and the five phases of earth.
Two fives combine to make ten,
together forming a human.
The five are the five qi of heaven
and the five flavors of earth.
The Chūnqiū Wěi says:
humans are conceived with ten and thus born,
hence they are born only after ten months.
Furthermore,
some speak of six po;
this comes from the Dàoist Sānhuáng Jīng,
which takes the five organ spirits as the five hun
and the six bowel spirits as the six po.
This also aligns with the meaning of the five phases and six qi.
Hun and po are the foundation of a person;
since they are matched with the bowels and organs,
they are explained here.
Jiǎyǐ says:
hun pertains to essence,
po pertains to spirit.
The five constants are:
benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and faithfulness.
Practiced enduringly over time,
they are eternally indispensable,
hence they are called constants.
They are also called the five virtues,
for by constantly practicing these,
one can achieve virtue,
thus they are called the five virtues.
And these five virtues correspond to the five phases.
Zhèng Xuán,
commenting on the Zhōngyōng chapter of the Lǐjì, says:
the spirit of wood is benevolence,
the spirit of metal is righteousness,
the spirit of fire is propriety,
the spirit of water is faithfulness,
the spirit of earth is wisdom.
The Shī Wěi and others say the same.
Máo Gōng’s commentary tradition,
as well as Jīng Fáng and others,
all take earth as faithfulness
and water as wisdom.
The Hànshū Tiānwénzhì says:
The Year Star, in relation to humans,
corresponds to the constant of benevolence
and the affair of appearance.
If benevolence is deficient and appearance flawed,
contrary to spring commands,
injuring wood qi,
punishment appears in the Year Star.
The Sparkling Deluder, in relation to humans,
corresponds to the constant of propriety
and the affair of sight.
If propriety is deficient and sight flawed,
contrary to summer commands,
injuring fire qi,
punishment appears in the Sparkling Deluder.
The Great White, in relation to humans,
corresponds to the constant of righteousness
and the affair of speech.
If righteousness is deficient and speech flawed,
contrary to autumn commands,
injuring metal qi,
punishment appears in the Great White.
The Chronogram Star, in relation to humans,
corresponds to the constant of wisdom
and the affair of hearing.
If wisdom is deficient and hearing flawed,
contrary to winter commands,
injuring water qi,
punishment appears in the Chronogram Star.
The Quelling Star, in relation to humans,
corresponds to the constant of faithfulness
and the affair of thought.
Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom
take faithfulness as their master.
Appearance, speech, sight, and hearing
take thought as their correct standard.
If all four affairs are flawed,
the Quelling Star will then stir.
According to Máo Gōng, Jīng Fáng, and the Hàn history,
all take earth as faithfulness,
which may be considered appropriate.
The reason for this is:
the meaning of the five constants—
benevolence takes compassion as its substance,
extensive giving as its function.
Propriety takes distinction as its substance,
practicing laws as its function.
Wisdom takes understanding as its substance,
clarity and acuity as its function.
Righteousness takes appropriateness as its substance,
judgment and decision as its function.
Faithfulness takes non-deception as its substance,
adherence to truth as its function.
In relation to the five phases:
wood has covering, sheltering, and flourishing growth—
this is its compassion and extensive giving.
Fire has dispelling darkness and illuminating brightness—
this is its distinction and practicing laws.
Water has containing moisture and flowing circulation—
this is its understanding and clarity.
Metal has hardness, firmness, and sharp edges—
this is its appropriateness and judgment.
Earth has supporting, bearing, and encompassing capacity,
giving birth to all things in their seasons—
this is its adherence to truth and non-deception.
Zhèng Xuán and the Shī Wěi
take earth as wisdom,
because nothing surpasses wisdom in understanding all matters,
and nothing surpasses earth in giving birth to all things;
thus they take it as wisdom.
Water as faithfulness—
because water has tides
that arrive according to their time,
thus they take water as faithfulness.
This reasoning has little evidence and is narrow,
deviating from the meaning.
Regarding the Five Classics:
Benevolence is paired with the Book of Changes,
its position being the East.
Ritual is paired with Fire,
its position being the South.
Righteousness is paired with the Spring and Autumn Annals,
its position being the West.
Wisdom is paired with the Book of Songs,
its position being the North.
Trustworthiness is paired with the Book of Documents,
its position being the Center.
The Book of Changes is paired with Eastern benevolence because
the Book of Changes is a work of creation and establishment,
encompassing all things,
with the meaning of change and transformation.
The East is the beginning of the four seasons,
and the transformative power of benevolence can generate life;
the Changes discards the old and embraces the new.
Moreover, the Emperor emerges from the Zhen trigram,
and first created the Eight Trigrams,
therefore it is paired with benevolence.
Ritual is paired with the South because
ritual can regulate the laws of superiors and inferiors,
distinguish the differences between noble and base,
sovereign and minister, father and son—
none are not restrained by ritual,
just as fire can perfect the five flavors,
illuminating and shining upon all things,
therefore the South is paired with ritual.
The Spring and Autumn Annals are paired with Western righteousness because
the Spring and Autumn Annals are the history of Lǔ,
praising and criticizing successes and failures.
At that time, the Kingly Way had already declined,
the various feudal lords contended by force,
and matters of warfare and campaigns
were all recorded.
Those who acted righteously were praised,
those who lost virtue were criticized,
just as metal uses righteousness to judge,
cutting and regulating all things,
therefore it is paired with righteousness.
The Book of Songs is paired with Northern wisdom because
the Songs express one's intent,
serving as subtle admonitions,
containing subtle and hidden language,
harmonizing and moistening human feelings,
moving ghosts and spirits, and affecting heaven and earth.
Through matters of good and evil,
chanting and singing in music,
they cause listeners to benefit in their conduct,
while the composers incur no blame upon themselves,
just as water flows hiddenly, moistening everything,
therefore it is paired with wisdom.
The Book of Documents is paired with central trustworthiness because
this is a book of high antiquity,
transmitting and relating the words of emperors and kings;
matters of trust and oaths
are all preserved within it.
It can be revered and upheld, therefore,
just as earth possesses trustworthiness,
generating things according to the seasons,
and is revered by the four seasons,
therefore it is paired with trustworthiness.
Jīng (classic) means constant,
also means path/way,
and also means model/law.
It narrates paths and events,
therefore it is called 'path/way'.
Its principles can serve as models,
therefore it is called 'model/law'.
Being constant as instructive canons,
it is thus 'constant'.
However, since the substance of the classics is the constant model,
each respective substance inherently possesses all Five Constants,
though each has its specialized focus.
But each takes one direction as primary,
and without discussing the meaning of the text,
therefore they are not fully explained here.
The practice of the Five Constants
is illuminated through the classics,
hence they are paired for explanation.
The Five Matters:
The "Hóng Fàn" chapter of the Book of Documents says,
"Reverently practice the five matters,"
which pairs human affairs with the Five Phases.
The first is demeanor,
paired with Wood;
the second is speech,
paired with Metal;
the third is sight,
paired with Fire;
the fourth is hearing,
paired with Water;
the fifth is thought,
paired with Earth.
The "Hóng Fàn" chapter of the Book of Documents says: For demeanor, it should be respectful;
for speech, compliant;
for sight, clear;
for hearing, acute;
for thought, profound.
Respectfulness leads to solemnity,
compliance leads to order,
clarity leads to wisdom,
acuteness leads to planning,
profundity leads to sageliness.
"For demeanor, it should be respectful" means
the respectfulness of the Son of Heaven
is called majestic.
If the superior is respectfully solemn,
then the inferiors will be reverent.
Confucius said,
"In his personal conduct, he is respectful;
in serving his superiors, he is reverent."
He also said,
"In bodily form, it is called respectfulness;
applied to others,
and extended to affairs, it is called reverence."
If demeanor is not respectful,
this is called not being solemn;
solemnity is reverence.
Now, among the five matters presented in the "Hóng Fàn",
demeanor is placed first because
in the Changes, demeanor corresponds to Zhèn,
and Zhèn corresponds to Wood;
Wood can be observed.
Therefore, the classics list the three virtues,
with demeanor and bearing being the highest among them.
The Book of Songs says,
"Be reverent and careful in your dignified demeanor,
for it is the model for men."
Having dignity that inspires awe
is called 'dignity' (wēi);
having bearing that can be emulated
is called 'bearing' (yí).
If a ruler possesses dignified bearing,
his ministers will be in awe and love him,
taking him as their model and emulating him,
thus he can long preserve his state.
If ministers possess dignified bearing,
they can long maintain their offices.
A gentleman in position inspires awe,
his giving and forgiving inspire love,
his advances and withdrawals are measurable,
his movements and turns are model-worthy,
his appearance and demeanor are admirable,
his actions are imitable,
his virtuous conduct is exemplary,
his voice and spirit are pleasing,
his movements are cultured,
his speech is well-structured—
governing his inferiors with these,
this is called dignified bearing.
Confucius said,
"Straighten your cap and robes,
dignify your gaze,
so that people look upon you with awe—
is this not dignity without harshness?"
He also said,
"If one does not govern with sternness,
then people will not be reverent."
Therefore, losing the measure of dignified bearing,
becoming negligent, arrogant, and willful,
is called madness.
If mad, then inferiors will not be solemn.
If inferiors are not reverent,
then the superior has no dignity.
If one does not revere his ruler,
and does not follow his governance,
then the yīn energy prevails.
If yīn energy prevails,
then the water phenomenon arrives.
Therefore it is said,
"The corresponding punishment is constant rain."
Rain leads to the arrival of famine and cold.
When famine and cold arrive,
then superiors and inferiors do not trust each other.
Great ministers become treacherous and rebellious,
and the people become bandits and robbers.
If many people suffer punishment,
then clothing anomalies appear.
Clothing anomalies refer to
light, frivolous, dissolute, violent, and disrespectful clothing,
reflecting the transformation of the wind energy.
Regarding the aspect of speech in the Way of the Yì, it is said to correspond to Duì (兌),
Duì signifies the image of the mouth in speech.
When a ruler speaks,
his commands are followed upon issuance.
Therefore, the Yì states:
"With joy to employ the people,
the people forget their toil;
with joy to face difficulties,
the people forget their death."
Thus, an enlightened ruler
lightens taxes and enriches salaries,
in cases of doubtful reward, errs on the side of generosity,
in cases of doubtful punishment, errs on the side of leniency,
thereby aligning with the people's hearts.
Hence, his teachings succeed without severity,
his governance is orderly without harshness.
This wins the people's hearts.
When the people's hearts are won,
the multitude rallies to him.
When the multitude rallies to him,
the people are willing to die for him,
and never forget him.
How much more will they follow his commands!
If a ruler loses the hearts of the multitude,
his governance and commands are not obeyed,
excessive yang dissipates on its own,
and all yīn forces do not adhere.
If those below fear the ruler's severe punishments,
then yang energy prevails.
When yang energy prevails, drought occurs.
Therefore it is said:
"The punishment is constant yang."
Constant yang leads to famine and poverty,
famine and poverty lead to insufficiency.
Insufficiency prevents people from speaking forthrightly,
so it first manifests through songs and ballads.
When energy is perverse, malicious words arise,
locusts and pests are born,
all are matters of the mouth.
Regarding vision, it corresponds to the south,
the image of the eyes.
Vision is called clarity.
Clarity is fundamental to understanding people.
In the Yì, it corresponds to Lí (離).
Lí represents fire and eyes.
If vision is not clear,
weak and uncertain, not knowing whom to trust,
it inevitably fosters prolonged cliques.
Enmity and kinship become indistinguishable.
In such a situation, the worthy are not advanced.
If the worthy are not advanced,
then the unworthy are not removed.
If the unworthy are not removed,
then those who offend superiors are not punished,
the innocent are wrongly penalized,
all offices become corrupt and ruined,
myriad affairs stagnate and are obstructed,
governance and education become lax and slow.
Therefore it is said:
"The punishment is constant warmth."
Warmth leads to winter leakage,
when winter energy leaks, cold does not prevail.
Spring and summer energies become disordered,
and epidemics arise.
If those who offend superiors are not punished,
then grass withstands frost without dying.
If the people's wealth is greedily taken,
then locusts and pests also consume human food.
These are all images corresponding to vision.
Regarding hearing, it resides in the ears.
The ears correspond to Kǎn (坎) in the Yì.
In ancient times, sage kings had banners for presenting good advice,
drums for those wishing to remonstrate,
consulted with grass-cutters and wood-gatherers,
all to broadly extend and widely listen.
If a ruler does not favor counsel,
then those below dare not speak.
If those below dare not speak,
then the ruler hears nothing.
If the ruler hears nothing,
then he does not listen.
Not listening
stems from not deliberating on governance,
hence it is called not listening.
Hearing and knowing nothing,
myriad affairs become obstructed and stifled,
resentment harbored in hearts and mouths,
joy and anger unregulated,
hence it is called urgency.
Cold things are urgent in nature,
winter things all wither urgently.
Withering urgently,
therefore it is said:
"The punishment is constant cold."
Constant cold means the hundred grains do not grow,
if the hundred grains do not grow,
then the people become impoverished.
Therefore, anomalies arise from the ears.
Through mutual activation by category,
there are drum anomalies and sounds of that kind.
Kǎn corresponds to pigs.
If ear energy is damaged, there are pig calamities.
Water's color is black,
there are black disasters.
These all pertain to hearing.
Regarding thought, the heart is the master of the five affairs,
just as the earth body is the master of the five phases.
In the Yì, it corresponds to Kūn (坤).
The energies of the eight cardinal points
also arise from the eight winds.
Wind is the master of the four seasons.
When thought from the heart is attained, it is called capacity.
Capacity means being able to contain and nurture ministers and sons,
hence it is called sageliness.
If thought from the heart is not attained,
all four others are lost,
then one cannot contain and nurture ministers and sons.
Therefore it is said:
"The thought-heart lacks capacity,
this is called non-sageliness."
The fault lies in fog-like confusion and loss of order.
Therefore, wind corresponds to Xùn (巽) in the Yì.
In the third and fourth months, pure yang governs.
Regarding yang, it becomes yīn;
regarding yīn, it becomes yang.
This is the image of high ministers.
If the ruler is fog-like and confused,
then high ministers become autocratic and willful.
When high ministers are autocratic and willful,
yīn energy flourishes.
When yīn energy flourishes, there is response.
Therefore, the punishment is constant wind.
When yīn energy is excessive,
it is overcast without rain,
and in severe cases,
constant darkness and gloom
envelop the heart,
if heart energy is damaged,
then there are gloom anomalies.
The Yì says:
"Kūn corresponds to oxen."
Kūn is earth.
If earth energy is damaged,
then many oxen die.
It also says:
"Earth corresponds to internal affairs,
if internal affairs are disordered,
then there are flower calamities."
These all pertain to matters of thought.
The influences of the five affairs
are exceedingly numerous in their examples.
A brief selection is presented thus.
Composed by Xiāo Jí, Grand Master of Imperial Entertainment with Equal Honors to the Three Excellencies, Duke of Chengyáng Commandery.
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo states:
"Lǜ (律) means to lead."
The Xù Hànshū states:
"Lǜ is method."
The Lǜshū states:
"Lǚ (呂) is sequence."
It sequences and describes the energies of the four seasons,
determining the positions of the twelve months.
Yīn and yang each have six,
together making twelve.
The six yang are the lǜ,
the six yīn are the lǚ.
The six lǜ are:
Huángzhōng, Dàcù, Gūxiǎn, Ruíbīn, Yízé, Wúyì.
The six lǚ are:
Línzhōng, Nánlǚ, Yìngzhōng, Dàlǚ, Jiázhōng, Zhònglǚ.
The Shǐjì states:
"Pitch-pipes and calendrics
are what Heaven uses to circulate the energies of the five phases and eight cardinal points,
ripening and maturing the myriad things."
The Records of Emperors and Kings states:
The Yellow Emperor sent Líng Lún to the west of Dàxià,
on the northern slopes of the Kūnlún Mountains,
to fetch bamboo from the Jiě Valley.
Those with uniform thickness in their hollows
were cut between two nodes,
and blown to make the huángzhōng pitch pipe,
imitating the cry of the phoenix.
There were six male and six female [pipes],
used to establish the pitch standards,
and to divide the stellar lodgings.
Líng Zhōujiū said:
The pitch standards are what establish the musical modes and produce the measures.
Therefore it is said:
They are ordered by three,
balanced by six,
and completed by twelve.
This is the way of Heaven.
This is the origin within the six [yang pitches].
The ancient blind masters,
examining the central tones and measuring them to create regulations,
determined the pitches and tuned the bells.
Hence it was named huángzhōng.
It is used to propagate and nurture the six qi.
The second is called tàicù,
used for metal [instrument] performances,
thereby assisting yang and dispelling stagnation.
The third is called gūxiǎn,
used to purify and cleanse all things,
and to summon spirits and receive guests.
The fourth is called ruíbīn,
used to pacify spirits and men,
for offering toasts and exchanging courtesies.
The fifth is called yízé,
used to chant the nine rules,
so that the people are unified without duplicity.
The sixth is called wúyì,
used to proclaim the virtuous decrees of the wise,
showing the people the models and norms.
As for the six intervals [between them],
they are to uplift what is submerged and suppress what is scattered.
The first interval is dàlǚ,
which assists in propagating things.
The second interval is jiázhōng,
which brings forth the subtleties from the four interstices.
The third interval is zhōnglǚ,
which propagates the central qi.
The fourth interval is línzhōng,
which harmonizes and expands all affairs,
ensuring that none fail in their duties with reverence, purity, and respect.
The fifth interval is nánlǚ,
which assists the flourishing of yang.
The sixth interval is yìngzhōng,
which equalizes and sharpens tools and implements,
ensuring they respond and return [to their function].
When the pitch standards do not change,
there are no deceitful things.
The Comprehensive Meanings of the Three Rituals states:
Lǜ means law.
It means the yang qi bestows life,
each having its own law.
Lǚ means assistance.
It assists in smoothly achieving success.
Another interpretation says:
Lǜ means to lead.
It leads and guides the yang qi,
causing it to circulate and reach everywhere.
Lǚ means companion.
It pairs with yang,
becoming its companion.
It also means to oppose.
It harmonizes the qi of yin and yang,
sometimes opposing each other.
It clarifies that when yang emerges, yin retreats;
when yin rises, yang diminishes.
Hence there is the idea of opposition.
The Continuation of the Book of Han states:
Yang takes the circle as its form,
its nature is movement.
Yin takes the square as its measure,
its nature is stillness.
Movement corresponds to the number three,
stillness corresponds to the number two.
Using yang to generate yin, it is doubled;
using yin to generate yang, it is halved.
Both are based on three and one.
Yang generating yin is called descending generation.
Yin generating yang is called ascending generation.
Both follow the principle of three for heaven and two for earth,
the round canopy and the square base.
This is the way the six even numbers bear the odd.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Numbers begin with one,
but one alone cannot generate.
Therefore it divides into yin and yang.
Yin and yang combine and generate the myriad things.
Therefore one generates two,
two generates three,
three generates the myriad things.
Therefore three months make one season.
This is why sacrifices have three offerings,
funerals have three leaps,
and military affairs have three commands.
All use three as the measure.
Three times three is nine.
Therefore the huángzhōng pitch standard,
being nine inches, tunes the gōng note.
Proceeding by nines,
nine times nine is eighty-one,
thus the number of huángzhōng is established.
The qi of huángzhōng resides in zǐ,
it is established in the eleventh month,
its celestial division is in Xīngjì,
it descends to generate línzhōng.
The number of línzhōng is fifty-four,
its qi resides in wèi,
it is established in the sixth month,
its celestial division is Chúnhuǒ,
it ascends to generate tàicù.
The number of tàicù is seventy-two,
its qi resides in yín,
it is established in the first month,
its celestial division is Zōuzī,
it descends to generate nánlǚ.
The number of nánlǚ is forty-eight,
its qi resides in yǒu,
it is established in the eighth month,
its celestial division is Shòuxīng,
it ascends to generate gūxiǎn.
The number of gūxiǎn is sixty-four,
its qi resides in chén,
it is established in the third month,
its celestial division is Dàliáng,
it descends to generate yìngzhōng.
The number of yìngzhōng is forty-two,
its qi resides in hài,
it is established in the tenth month,
its celestial division is Zhémù,
it ascends to generate ruíbīn.
The number of ruíbīn is fifty-six,
its qi resides in wǔ,
it is established in the fifth month,
its celestial division is Chúnshǒu,
it ascends to generate dàlǚ.
The number of dàlǚ is seventy-six,
its qi resides in chǒu,
it is established in the twelfth month,
its celestial division is Xuánxiāo,
it descends to generate yízé.
The number of yízé is fifty-one,
its qi resides in shēn,
it is established in the seventh month,
its celestial division is Chúnwěi,
it ascends to generate jiázhōng.
The number of jiázhōng is sixty-eight,
its qi resides in mǎo,
it is established in the second month,
its celestial division is Jiànglóu,
it descends to generate wúyì.
The number of wúyì is forty-five,
its qi resides in xū,
it is established in the ninth month,
its celestial division is Dàhuǒ.
It ascends to generate zhōnglǚ.
The number of zhōnglǚ is sixty,
its qi resides in sì,
it is established in the fourth month,
its celestial division is Shíshěn.
The celestial divisions and the monthly establishments interweave as exterior and interior.
That is how they correspond and generate each other.
They are based on the six lines of Qián and Kūn.
Huángzhōng is the initial nine,
it descends to generate línzhōng, the initial six.
Then it ascends to generate tàicù.
The Musical Apocrypha states:
Huángzhōng is the central palace,
its number is eighty-one,
based on the numbers of heaven one, earth two, and man three.
Through increase and decrease,
the pitches form the harmonious qi of the five notes.
Increase governs ascending generation,
decrease governs descending generation.
For ascending generation,
add one-third;
for descending generation,
subtract one-third.
For addition, multiply by four,
and divide by three.
For subtraction, multiply by two,
and divide by three.
The *Sānlǐ Yìzōng* states:
The standard length of the Yellow Bell pipe
is originally nine inches.
The reason for using nine
is that it is the ultimate Yang number.
The origin of numbers
begins with three.
The Way of the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and Man—
combines to form numbers.
Therefore, they are called the Three Powers.
Thus, Heaven, Earth, and Man each have three numbers.
Yang can encompass three,
hence it is called nine.
Yin only encompasses two,
hence it is called six.
Since Yang receives the vital force and encompasses three,
it is therefore multiplied by three.
Three times three equals nine.
Thus, the Yang number nine is the ultimate.
Therefore, the pipe uses nine inches
to measure the Yang energy.
Yang energy emerges in accordance with the season.
This is a naturally divine and proven principle.
Furthermore, it generates upward the Great Frame (9/2),
and generates downward the Southern Pitch (6/2);
it generates upward the Gūxǐ (9/3),
and generates downward the Yìngzhōng (6/3);
it generates upward the Ruíbīn (9/4),
and generates downward the Great Pitch (6/4);
it generates upward the Yízé (9/5),
and generates downward the Jiāzhōng (6/5);
it generates upward the Wúyì (top 9),
and generates downward the Zhōnglǚ (top 6).
Therefore, those in the same position resemble husband and wife,
while those in different positions resemble mother and child.
This is what is meant by "the pitch takes a wife,
and the pitch gives birth to a child."
The *Báihǔ Tōng* says:
What is the Yellow Bell?
Yellow is the harmonious central energy;
Bell means movement.
It means that Yang, beneath the Yellow Springs,
stirs the myriad things.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
Yellow is the color of earth;
Bell is where energy moves.
The Yellow Bell is the ruler,
obtained at the winter solstice.
The *Sānlǐ Yìzōng* states:
Bell means response.
It means that Yang energy stirs hidden beneath the Yellow Springs,
responding to nourish the myriad things,
as sprouts desire to emerge.
Great Pitch:
Great means supreme.
Pitch means to resist.
It means that Yang energy desires to emerge, but Yin resists and hinders it.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
Pitch means to sojourn.
To sojourn and branch out.
The *Sānlǐ Yìzōng* states:
Pitch means to assist.
In the twelfth month, Yang is just beginning to grow,
and Yin energy assists it.
The work of giving birth and nurturing,
its Way is vast and great.
Therefore, another interpretation says:
Pitch means companion.
It acts as a companion to Yang,
jointly giving life to the myriad things.
Great Frame means the myriad things begin to grow large,
gathering and emerging from the earth.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
The myriad things are gathered but have not yet emerged.
The *Sānlǐ Yìzōng* states:
Frame means the principle of gathering.
In the first month,
the myriad things begin to grow large,
gathering and emerging from the earth.
Jiāzhōng means
the myriad things in their seed coats,
emerge by kind.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
Seeds begin to be clasped.
The *Sānlǐ Yìzōng* states:
Jiā means to assist.
In the middle of the second month,
things have not fully emerged.
Yin assists Yang energy,
responding to things as they emerge.
Another interpretation says:
Jiā means to clasp.
It means the myriad things are clasped by their seed coats,
and only at this time are they released,
responding to the bell and emerging.
Gūxiǎn:
Gǔ means ancient.
Xiǎn means fresh.
All things leave the old and embrace the new,
becoming fresh and bright.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Gūxiǎn clears away the old
and brings in the new.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Gū means withered.
Xiǎn means to wash.
In the third month, things grow;
they are newly cleansed, washing away their withered state.
Zhōnglǚ:
All things emerge in the middle.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Zhōng means full.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Lǚ means to resist difficulty.
It says that when yin desires to emerge,
yang qi is within it,
resisting and restraining it.
Another interpretation:
Lǚ refers to the fourth month,
when yang qi flourishes and grows,
and yin's assisting role is subtle.
Hence it is called thus.
Ruíbīn:
Ruí means to descend.
Bīn means to respect.
It says that yang qi descends,
hence it is respected.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Ruíbīn is peaceful and submissive.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Ruí means to hang down.
Bīn means subtle.
In the fifth month, yang qi descends,
and yin qi begins to rise,
mutually respecting each other.
Línzhōng:
Lín means multitude.
All things mature,
and their kinds are numerous.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Línzhōng draws in and halts them.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Lín means lush and abundant.
In the middle of the sixth month,
all things are lush and abundant,
gathered in the wilds.
Hence it is called Lín.
Yízé:
Yí means to injure.
Zé means law.
It says that all things begin to be injured,
subjected to penal law.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Yízé changes its laws.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Yí means level.
Zé means law.
In the seventh month, all things are about to mature,
evenly bearing fruit,
all according to law,
which is auspicious virtue.
Nánlǚ:
Nán means to bear.
It says that yang qi bears life,
nurturing growth.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Nánlǚ
bears and envelops greatly.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Nán means to bear.
In the middle of the eighth month,
all things contain beauty,
having the image of bearing pregnancy,
assisting in the meaning of achieving success.
Wúyì:
Yì means end.
It says that all things follow yang to their end,
and should again follow yin to arise.
There is no final end.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Wúyì means
that humans are never satisfied.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
Yì means to loathe.
It means disgust.
In the ninth month, all things have matured into fruit,
with nothing to loathe.
Yìngzhōng:
It says that all things respond to the season and gather below to store.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Responding to what is gathered.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng states:
In the tenth month,
the year's work is all completed,
the function of yin qi
responds to the work of yang,
gathering and accumulating,
hence it is called Zhōng (gathering).
Also said:
Yìng means the meaning of response and harmony.
It says that at this time, it will again respond to yang qi
and stir below.
The Yuèwěi states:
Huángzhōng is the gōng,
Línzhōng is the zhǐ,
Dàcù is the shāng,
Nánlǚ is the yǔ,
Gūxiǎn is the jué,
Yìngzhōng is the biàn gōng,
Ruíbīn is the biàn zhǐ.
Arranged in order,
the five notes are complete.
Huángzhōng generates Línzhōng below.
Hence Línzhōng is the zhǐ,
next to Huángzhōng.
Línzhōng generates Dàcù above.
Hence Dàcù is the shāng,
next to Línzhōng.
Dàcù generates Nánlǚ below.
Hence Nánlǚ is the yǔ,
next to Dàcù.
Nánlǚ generates Gūxiǎn above.
Hence Gūxiǎn is the jué,
next to Nánlǚ.
Gūxiǎn generates Yìngzhōng below,
hence Yìngzhōng is the biàn gōng,
next to Gūxiǎn.
Yìngzhōng generates Ruíbīn above.
Hence Ruíbīn is the biàn zhǐ.
In all, there are seven tones,
which cyclically serve as the gōng.
The seven tones
are so because the number of mutual generation is seven.
Starting from Huángzhōng generating Línzhōng,
from the twelfth month to the sixth month,
is altogether seven months.
Fú Qiān explains:
The seven pitch-standards are the seven tones.
The Outer Commentary explains:
When King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
the year was in Chúnhuǒ,
the sun was in Tiānsì,
from Chúnhuǒ to Tiānsì,
altogether seven lodgings.
Also, the earthly branch day was in Jiǎzǐ,
from zǐ to wǔ is again seven.
The celestial phenomena and earthly branches,
their numbers are all seven.
The sages used the pitch-pipes to harmonize with these numbers,
summoning with sound.
Hence they used seven tones.
Music uses the seven pitch-standards to match the seven beginnings.
Hence they determine the three origins and the four seasons.
Thus Huángzhōng matches heaven,
Línzhōng matches earth,
Dàcù matches humanity,
Gūxiǎn matches spring,
Ruíbīn matches summer,
Nánlǚ matches autumn,
Yìngzhōng matches winter.
Regarding the three origins:
The Zhōu took the month of Jiànzǐ as the celestial standard.
Hence the Huángzhōng pipe matches it.
The Shāng took the month of Jiànchǒu as the terrestrial standard.
It should be matched by the Dàlǚ pipe.
However, yin numbers are even.
The earth phase of Wèi is not yet king.
It is also the celestial altar.
Therefore, its complementary opposite is taken,
responding to the qi of earth,
and matched by the Línzhōng pipe.
The Xià took the month of Jiànyín as the human standard.
Hence the Dàcù pipe matches it.
Now, yang virtue resides in itself.
Therefore, its position is taken as the standard.
Yin virtue resides in another.
Therefore, its complementary opposite is taken.
The Treatise on Harmonics and Calendrics in the Hànshū states:
The Three Primes refer to
the principles of Heaven's bestowal, Earth's transformation, and human affairs.
In the eleventh month, it is the initial nine of Qián;
the yang qi lies concealed beneath the earth,
beginning to manifest as one.
All things sprout and stir,
concentrated within the Great Yin.
Therefore, the Yellow Bell is the Prime of Heaven.
Its pitch-pipe length is nine inches.
The number nine is that which exhaustively reaches the ultimate in centrality and harmony,
serving as the origin of all things.
The Yì Jīng says:
"That which establishes the Way of Heaven
is called yīn and yáng."
This is it.
In the sixth month, it is the initial six of Kūn;
the yīn qi receives its charge from the Great Yang,
continuing to nurture and transform them softly,
as all things grow and develop.
Luxuriant yet tender,
they are made to become firm and strong.
Therefore, the Forest Bell is the Prime of Earth,
its pitch-pipe length being six inches.
The number six
is that by which yīn receives the bestowal of yáng,
planting it within the six directions,
causing the firm and the soft to have their substance.
"That which establishes the Way of Earth
is called softness and firmness."
This is it.
Qián knows the Great Beginning;
Kūn brings things to completion.
In the first month, it is the nine in the third place of Qián;
all things break through and connect,
bursting forth in Yín.
Humans receive them and bring them to completion,
nurturing them with benevolence,
acting with righteousness,
causing affairs and things each to attain their proper principle.
Yín belongs to wood,
representing benevolence.
Its sound is shāng,
representing righteousness.
Therefore, the Great Bursting Forth is the Prime of Humanity,
its pitch-pipe length being eight inches,
the number eight symbolizing the trigrams.
This is what Fúxī used to accord with Heaven and Earth, communicate with the spirits and luminaries,
and categorize the dispositions of the myriad things.
"That which establishes the Way of Humanity
is called benevolence and righteousness."
This is it.
In Heaven, they form images;
on Earth, they take shape.
The sovereign subsequently arranges and completes the ways of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity.
These are the Three Primes,
the beginning of the pitch-pipes.
The Gǎnjīng Fú states:
The eleventh month establishes Zǐ,
the point where Heaven begins its bestowal,
called the Heavenly System.
The Zhōu dynasty's calendar and ceremonial colors esteemed red,
symbolizing the red color of sprouting things.
The twelfth month establishes Chǒu,
the point where Earth begins its transformation,
called the Earthly System.
The Yīn dynasty's calendar and ceremonial colors esteemed white,
symbolizing the white color of budding things.
The first month establishes Yín,
the point where humanity begins its transformation,
called the Human System.
The Xià dynasty's calendar and ceremonial colors esteemed black,
symbolizing the black color of living things.
These three systems of pitch-pipes and calendars
also follow the succession of the Five Virtues,
taking the Three Sovereigns of antiquity as the standard,
namely, the Heavenly Sovereign, the Earthly Sovereign, and the Human Sovereign.
All took Heaven, Earth, and Humanity as their model,
cycling and beginning anew.
The designation written at the beginning of the year
was accordingly used as their name.
Wishing to embody the Way of the Three Powers,
and to rule over the myriad states.
Therefore, he who receives the Mandate of Heaven and becomes king
must harmonize the six pitch-pipes,
and reform the calendar,
receive the five qi and change the ceremonial colors,
modeling himself on the Way of the Three Systems.
The Zhōu dynasty, with the Heavenly System, esteemed red in ceremonial colors.
The yang way esteems the left,
therefore Heaven rotates to the left.
The Zhōu dynasty ruled by the virtue of Wood,
Fire is its child,
the color of Fire is red,
therefore, rotating leftward, they used its red color.
The Yīn dynasty, with the Earthly System, esteemed white in ceremonial colors.
The yīn way esteems the right,
its rotation turns to the right.
The Yīn dynasty ruled by the virtue of Water,
Metal is its mother,
the color of Metal is white,
therefore, rotating rightward, they used its white color.
The Xià dynasty, with the Human System, esteemed black in ceremonial colors.
Humanity also esteems the left,
the Xià dynasty ruled by the virtue of Metal,
Water is its child,
the color of Water is black,
therefore, rotating leftward, they used its black color.
It also says:
The rise of emperors and kings
often follows auspicious omens.
The Zhōu was moved by the red sparrow,
therefore they esteemed red.
The Yīn received the white wolf,
therefore they esteemed white.
The Xià was bestowed the dark jade tablet,
therefore they esteemed black.
These are all prior manifestations of qi.
The auspicious signs for the king,
the principle of mother and child aiding each other,
as with the Hàn dynasty ruling by the virtue of Fire.
The essence of the planet Saturn
descended as a yellow stone,
granting military authority to Zǐfáng,
aiding the Lord of Pèi in destroying Chǔ.
It is not that the colors of the Five Cycles
support each other for use.
Confucius said:
"The Xià calendar accords with Heaven."
This means it accords with the qi of the four seasons of Heaven's Way,
corresponding to the periods of growth and killing of the eight nodes.
Therefore it is said:
"Use the calendar of the Xià,
ride in the carriage of the Yīn,
wear the ceremonial cap of the Zhōu."
Combining the three dynasties to form the model.
This is probably because it selects what can endure.
The Qín dynasty took the month establishing Hài
as the beginning of the year.
The early Hàn dynasty followed the Qín calendar.
From the Wèi dynasty onward,
they independently used the Xià calendar,
and it has remained unchanged to the present day,
because it accords with Heaven's qi.
Furthermore, in Dùnjiǎ, Tàiyī, Jiǔgōng, and Yuánchén,
there are also Three Primes,
all starting from Jiǎzǐ.
The first is the Heavenly Prime,
completing the six Jiǎ.
The next Jiǎzǐ is the Earthly Prime,
and the next Jiǎzǐ is the Human Prime.
In Dùnjiǎ, after the two solstices of winter and summer,
on the day and night of Jiǎ and Jǐ at midnight,
it is the beginning of the Jiǎzǐ Prime.
Each of the Three Primes is further divided into three.
Therefore, one hundred and eighty days constitute a Prime,
completing the two paths of yīn and yáng,
exhausting the use of one year.
In Tàiyī, the initial sixty-year Jiǎzǐ period is one cycle,
the next Jiǎzǐ is the second cycle,
filling six cycles, three hundred and sixty years, constitutes one revolution.
Jiǔgōng separately takes Jǐhài as the beginning,
divided into Five Primes.
The initial sixty-year Jǐhài is the Heavenly Prime,
the next sixty-year Jǐhài is the Earthly Prime,
the next sixty-year Jǐhài is the Human Prime,
the next sixty-year Jǐhài is the River Prime,
the next sixty-year Jǐhài is the Sea Prime.
Nine years make one revolution,
four times nine is thirty-six,
also completing the great number of the six Jiǎ.
The Three Primes and the calendars
all follow the pitch-pipes,
correspond to the calendar to fix the seasons,
and are all matched with the Five Phases.
Therefore, they are explained together here.
Now, the Seven Governors
are the starting point of the mysterious celestial phenomena,
rectifying the degrees of Heaven.
The king looks up to them,
using them to govern.
Therefore they are called "governors."
"Seven" means the number is seven.
There are generally three explanations.
One says:
The sun, moon, and five planets,
combined, are the Seven Governors.
The second says:
The seven stars of the Northern Dipper are the Seven Governors.
The third says:
The twenty-eight lunar mansions,
distributed in the four directions,
each direction having seven mansions,
together constitute the Seven Governors.
These three kinds of Seven Governors
are all matched with the Five Phases.
They are also the heads of the Three Luminaries.
The sun, moon, and five planets are called the Seven Regulators.
The Shàngshū Kǎo Língyào states regarding the Seven Regulators:
The sun and moon
are the masters of time.
The five planets
are the markers of time.
Therefore it is said,
"Observe the jade sighting-tube and revolving jade sphere,
to harmonize the Seven Regulators."
The Seven Regulators and the Five Regulators refer to the governance of the Five Phases.
The Seven Regulators are precisely the sun, moon, and five planets.
Regarding the sun,
the Hétú Wū Guāng Piān says:
The sun is the beginning of yang essence;
the sun is substance.
The Yuán Mìng Bāo says:
Yang begins with one.
Therefore the sun travels one degree per day.
Yang is completed in three.
Therefore there is the three-legged crow.
The crow is yang essence.
Its cry is "lóu hū."
Common people saw that "lóu hū" resembles a crow.
Therefore they named it thus.
It also says:
Fire essence is yang qi.
Therefore it is hot externally and yin internally,
resembling a crow.
The sun is revered, therefore it is full;
being full, it bestows;
bestowing, it is benevolent.
Being benevolent, it has essence;
essence is on the outside.
Being on the outside, it is large;
the sun's exterior is hot.
The exterior being hot, therefore yang essence is emitted outward.
Heaven has three hundred sixty-five and one-quarter degrees,
distributed across the four directions.
The sun traverses them daily without error or delay.
Causing the four directions to unite as one.
Therefore its character combines four into one.
The Báihǔ Tōng says:
The sun's diameter is one thousand lǐ,
its circumference three thousand lǐ,
and it is seven thousand lǐ below heaven.
The Tàixuán Jīng says:
When the sun moves once to the south, the myriad things die;
when the sun moves once to the north, the myriad things are born.
The Wùlǐ Lùn says:
In summer, yang is abundant and yin declines,
therefore the days are long and the nights short.
In winter, yin is abundant and yang declines,
therefore the days are short and the nights long.
When traveling the yang path, it is long;
it rises and sets north of Mǎo and Yǒu.
When traveling the yin path, it is short;
it rises and sets south of Mǎo and Yǒu.
In spring and autumn, yin and yang are equal.
Therefore it travels the middle path,
and day and night are equal.
The Kǎo Língyào says:
On the first day of spring,
the sun rises at Mǎo and sets at Yǒu.
When the Mǎo star (Pleiades) is at one degree,
it is midnight and dusk.
When the Dǒu star (Dipper) is at twelve degrees,
it is midnight and dawn.
On the first day of midsummer,
the sun rises at Yín and sets at Xū.
When the Xīn star is at five degrees,
it is midnight and dusk.
When the Yíngshì star (Encampment) is at ten degrees,
it is midnight and dawn.
On the first day of autumn,
the sun rises at Mǎo and sets at Yǒu.
When the Xūnǚ star is at four degrees,
it is midnight and dusk.
When the Dōngjǐng star (Well) is at eleven degrees,
it is midnight and dawn.
On the first day of midwinter,
the sun rises at Chén and sets at Shēn.
When the Kuí star is at one degree,
it is midnight and dusk.
When the Dī star is at nine degrees,
it is midnight and dawn.
Mǎo and Yǒu are where yin and yang intersect;
when the sun and moon reach here, it is the middle path.
It is the place where the flourishing and decline of the myriad things emerge and enter,
therefore it is called the Gate of Two and Eight,
corresponding to the second and eighth months.
Therefore the Shī Tuīdù Zāi says:
The juncture of Mǎo and Yǒu is for changing governance.
The Hànshū Tiānwén Zhì says:
The sun is the image of the ruler.
If the ruler's actions are urgent, then the sun's motion is swift;
if the ruler's actions are slow, then the sun's motion is tardy.
If its tardiness or swiftness loses its norm, then an eclipse occurs.
Eclipses occur at the intersection of paths.
An eclipse is the image of yin encroaching upon yang,
of ministers encroaching upon the ruler.
Therefore, when a solar eclipse occurs, cultivate virtue to repel it.
Regarding the moon,
the Chūnqiū Yuán Mìng Bāo says:
The moon is yin essence;
its name means "defect."
That there are toads and hares within it
means yin and yang dwell together, relying on each other.
They are suppressed, bent, unite with yang, and govern together.
Its inner light is bright;
its central qi resembles patterns.
The hare is good at running, symbolizing yang movement.
The word for hare is "xī hū";
"xī hū" is a name for warmth.
The moon is the essence of water.
Therefore it is bright inside and its qi is cold.
That yin is born incomplete
signifies bending before the ruler.
That it becomes full at the full moon
signifies the union of qi and affairs.
That it becomes deficient after being full
signifies bending towards the honored one.
Its qi is lowly;
being lowly, it forms the weft by cultivating the exterior.
Yin receives yang essence;
therefore essence is inside,
which is why metal and water have inner radiance.
Having inner radiance, therefore yin essence sinks and remains unmoving.
The moon is yin essence;
its body inherently has no light.
It borrows the sun's illumination to become bright,
just as a minister inherently has no authority,
but borrows the ruler's power
to establish his authority.
At the beginning of the month, it has not yet faced the sun.
Therefore it has no light and is deficient.
At mid-month, it faces the sun directly.
Therefore its light is full.
After the sixteenth day, it gradually becomes deficient,
also gradually ceasing to face the sun directly.
The Hànshū Tiānwén Zhì says:
The moon travels thirteen and one-quarter degrees per day.
At Lìchūn and Chūnfēn,
it follows the green path from the east.
At Lìqiū and Qiūfēn,
it follows the white path from the west.
At Lìdōng and Dōngzhì,
it follows the black path from the north.
At Lìxià and Xiàzhì,
it follows the red path from the south.
In late summer, it travels the middle path.
Red and green emerge from the yang path;
white and black emerge from the yin path.
If it is seen in the west at the end of the month,
it is called "tiǎo."
If it is seen in the east at the beginning of the month,
it is called "nǜ."
If the ruler is relaxed and slow,
the ministers become arrogant and disrespectful.
Therefore the sun moves slowly,
and the moon moves swiftly.
If the ruler is stern and urgent, then the ministers are fearful.
Therefore the sun moves swiftly,
and the moon moves slowly,
not daring to press close to the ruler's position.
If its motion, whether slow or swift,
loses its proper measure, an eclipse also occurs.
An eclipse occurs when it faces the opposition of the sun,
where there is a dark void.
When the dark void faces the moon,
then a lunar eclipse occurs;
when it faces a star, then the star perishes.
A lunar eclipse is yang encroaching upon yin.
Dǒng Zhòngshū said:
For humans, it is the image of consorts, empresses, great ministers, and feudal lords.
The moon represents punishment.
Therefore, when a lunar eclipse occurs, cultivate punishments to repel it.
Regarding the five planets,
the Shuōwén says:
Stars are the essence of the myriad things.
Some say:
Stars are divisions of the sun.
Therefore the character for star is born beneath the sun.
The Shǐjì says:
Stars are the scattered essence of metal.
When stars fall, they become stones.
This refers to metal.
The Chūnqiū says:
"Stones fell in Sòng";
these were fallen stars.
It also says:
Stars are yin essence.
Metal is also yin.
Distinguishing and speaking of them separately,
each is matched to the Five Phases,
not exclusively governing metal alone.
The Year Star (Suìxīng) is the essence of wood,
its position is in the east, governing spring.
It is the son of the Azure Emperor,
the image of the ruler of men,
the eldest of the five stars,
the official in charge of agriculture,
presiding over blessings and celebrations.
It has six names in total:
first, Shètí;
second, Chónghuá;
third, Yìngxīng;
fourth, Mòxīng;
fifth, Jìxīng;
sixth, Xiūrénxīng.
The states it governs are called Wú and Qí.
Advancing beyond its lodge is called excess;
retreating from its lodge is called contraction.
If its path is deviant, the ruler is deviant;
if its path is correct, the ruler is correct.
If governance is harsh, its movement is swift;
if governance is lax, its movement is slow.
If governance is cruel, it moves in the yin;
if governance is harmonious, it moves in the yang.
Moving in the yang brings drought;
moving in the yin brings floods.
In times of order, it follows its proper course;
in times of chaos, it moves retrograde.
Because it governs the year,
it is named the Year Star.
The Sparkling Deluder (Yínghuò) is the essence of fire,
its position is in the south, governing summer.
It is the son of the Red Emperor,
the image of a feudal lord,
the elder among the five stars.
Above, it receives from the Great Unity;
below, it oversees the ruler of men,
meaning it governs the principles of the Son of Heaven.
It watches for lawlessness,
appearing and disappearing unpredictably,
acting as the heavens' inspector.
Wherever it goes, it presides over military chaos, rebellion, mourning, famine, and disease.
It has two names in total:
first, the Punishment Star;
second, the Upholder of Law.
The states it governs are called Jīng and Yuè.
It is the male counterpart of the Great White.
When it appears in the south, it is the Sparkling Deluder;
when it resides in the west, it is Tiānlǐ;
when in the east, it is Xuánxī.
Because it appears and disappears unpredictably,
it is named the Sparkling Deluder.
The Stabilizer Star (Zhènxīng) is the essence of earth,
its position is in the center, governing the four seasons.
It is the image of the queen.
Presiding over virtue, it is the king among the five stars.
One name is Dìhòu.
It watches over the queen's deviance or correctness;
entering yang signifies external matters;
entering yin signifies internal matters.
When all four other stars err,
the Stabilizer Star then becomes active.
Because it stabilizes its lodge without shifting,
it is named the Stabilizer Star.
The Great White (Tàibái) is the essence of metal,
its position is in the west, governing the beginning of autumn.
It is the son of the White Emperor,
the image of a great general,
overseeing military calamities.
When the sun is in the south and the Great White resides south of it,
or when the sun is in the north and the Great White resides north of it, this is called excess.
When the sun is in the south and the Great White resides north of it,
or when the sun is in the north and the Great White resides south of it, this is called contraction.
If it appears in the east when it should not,
and emerges in the east,
it is named Chónghuá.
If it descends in the east when it should not,
and descends in the east,
it is named Shǎosuì.
If it appears in the west when it should not,
and emerges in the west,
it is named Tàibái.
If it descends in the west when it should not,
and descends in the west,
it is named Báixiào.
It has six names in total:
first, Tiānxiàng;
second, Tiānzhèng;
third, Dàchén;
fourth, Dàhào;
fifth, Míngxīng;
sixth, Dàxiāo.
The Book of Songs says:
In the east, it is called the Opener of Brightness;
in the west, it is called the Long Watcher.
The states it governs are called Qín, Jìn, and Zhèng.
The Great White is the male counterpart of the Year Star.
The Great White presides over military affairs.
Military affairs belong to the west; the color of metal is white.
Therefore, it is called the Great White.
The Chronogram Star (Chénxīng) is the essence of water,
its position is in the north, governing winter.
It is the son of the Black Emperor,
the image of the prime minister, presiding over punishments.
If governance is cruel, it does not enter;
if governance is harmonious, it does not emerge.
It has six names in total.
First, Āntiáo;
second, Xìjí;
third, Xióngxīng;
fourth, Gōuxīng;
fifth, Sìnóng;
sixth, Miǎnxīng.
The states it governs are called Zhào and Dài.
The Chronogram Star presides over virtue.
It is the heavens' upholder of correctness,
appearing and disappearing at regular times.
Therefore, it is called the Chronogram Star.
The Classic of Stars says:
Northwest of the Five Chariots,
the first star is called the Great White;
next, one star to the north is called the Chronogram Star;
next, one star to the northeast is called the Year Star;
next, one star to the southeast is called the Stabilizer Star;
next, one star to the southwest is called the Sparkling Deluder.
This corresponds to the distribution of qi among the five stars.
It also says:
The Year Star transforms into comets, banner clouds, spear clouds, and celestial dogs;
the Sparkling Deluder transforms into comets, the banner of Chīyóu, and Gézé;
the Stabilizer Star transforms into Yùhàn, Tiānfèi, Xúnshǐ, and rainbows;
the Great White transforms into comets and sweeping stars;
the Chronogram Star transforms into wild arrows, celestial spears, and celestial clubs.
These are all the qi of the five stars,
chaotically manifesting as baleful stars.
The ruler observes them
to know gains and losses.
The Kǎo Líng Yào says:
The Year Star is the compass;
the Sparkling Deluder is the square;
the Stabilizer Star is the marking line;
the Great White is the balance beam;
the Chronogram Star is the weight.
The weight, balance beam, compass, square, and marking line
all have their origins,
cycling and beginning anew.
Therefore, if governance fails in spring,
the Year Star becomes full and topples,
not residing in its normal place.
If governance fails in summer,
the Sparkling Deluder moves retrograde.
If governance fails in late summer,
the Stabilizer Star loses its proper course.
If governance fails in autumn,
the Great White errs in its path,
appearing and disappearing improperly.
If governance fails in winter,
the Chronogram Star does not appear in its expected region.
If all five aspects of governance fail,
the five stars do not shine brightly.
If spring governance does not fail,
the five grains proliferate.
If summer governance does not fail,
sweet rain falls timely.
If late summer governance does not fail,
there are no calamities in season.
If autumn governance does not fail,
the people flourish.
If winter governance does not fail,
there is little illness and mourning.
If all five aspects of governance do not fail,
the sun and moon are bright and luminous.
Thus, the sun, moon, and five stars
together constitute the Way of the Seven Governors.
They are also called the Seven Luminaries.
This is because they are luminous bodies that move and shine.
The Big Dipper is one of the Seven Administrators.
The Big Dipper is the Celestial Pivot.
Heaven has seven guidelines,
and the Dipper has seven stars.
The first to the fourth stars form the Bowl,
and the fifth to the seventh stars form the Handle,
making seven in total.
The *Shàngshū Wěi* states:
"The Jade Sighting-Tube and the four stars of the Dipper's Bowl,
and the Jade Balance, which holds the three stars crosswise,
together make seven.
They harmonize the four seasons and the five authorities."
The five authorities refer to the Five Phases.
In humans, the five authorities correspond to the five destinies,
and the seven stars correspond to the seven faculties.
The Big Dipper resides at the center of heaven,
above Kūnlún.
The direction to which it points as it revolves
follows the twenty-four solar terms,
corrects the twelve Earthly Branches,
and establishes the twelve months.
Furthermore, the divisions of provinces and states, as well as the fate of years,
are all governed by it.
Therefore, it is one of the Seven Administrators.
The *Yú Lù* states:
"The seven stars of the Big Dipper,
based on the Jade Sighting-Tube and the Jade Balance,
harmonize the Seven Administrators."
The Administrators are what the Son of Heaven uses to govern the world.
Thus, the king
receives the mandate of heaven to implement laws.
The *Héchéng Tú* states:
"The Big Dipper has seven stars,
and the Son of Heaven has seven administrations.
The Dipper resides in the yin and distributes the yang,
hence it is called the Northern Dipper."
Each of its seven stars has four names.
The *Héchéng Tú* states:
"The first star of the Dipper is named Shū,
the second Xuán,
the third Jī,
the fourth Quán,
the fifth Héng,
the sixth Kāiyáng,
and the seventh Biāoguāng."
The *Huángdì Dǒu Tú* states:
"The first is named Tānláng,
belonging to those born in the zǐ hour.
The second is named Jùmén,
belonging to those born in the chǒu and hài hours.
The third is named Lùcún,
belonging to those born in the yín and xū hours.
The fourth is named Wénqū,
belonging to those born in the mǎo and yǒu hours.
The fifth is named Liánzhēn,
belonging to those born in the chén and shēn hours.
The sixth is named Wǔqū,
belonging to those born in the sì and wèi hours.
The seventh is named Pòjūn,
belonging to those born in the wǔ hour."
The *Kǒngzǐ Yuánchén Jīng* states:
"The first is named Yángmíng Star,
the second Yīnjīng Star,
the third Zhēnrén Star,
the fourth Xuánmíng Star,
the fifth Dānyuán Star,
the sixth Běijí Star,
and the seventh Tiānkāi Star."
The *Dùnjiǎ Jīng* states:
"The first is named Kuízhēn Star,
the second Kuíyuán Star,
the third Quánjiǔjí Star,
the fourth Kuíxì Star,
the fifth Bìgāng Star,
the sixth Jìjì Star,
and the seventh Piāoxuányáng Star."
The first corresponds to Water,
the second to Water and Earth,
the third to Wood and Earth,
the fourth to Metal and Wood,
the fifth to Metal and Earth,
the sixth to Fire and Earth,
and the seventh to Fire.
The reason why zǐ and wǔ each belong exclusively to one star,
while the others are shared by two hours,
is that zǐ and wǔ are the warp of heaven and earth.
The first and seventh stars of the Dipper, the Bowl and the Handle,
are also the warp of the Dipper.
They establish the direction it points to.
As for the others, which are not the ones pointed to,
they are therefore shared by two hours.
Thus, the sixty Jiazi cycles begin with the first star,
starting with Jiǎzǐ to match them,
circling back and forth,
until the numbers are exhausted.
The Big Dipper leads the twenty-eight lunar mansions.
Each star governs one of the four seasons.
The Bowl begins with Shì,
and the Handle begins with Jiǎo,
with the others assigned in order.
If a person's annual fate
reaches Shì and the five planets
arrive at this mansion,
the fortune or misfortune follows the star.
The *Héchéng Tú* states:
"The Shū star corresponds to Yōngzhōu,
the Xuán star to Jìzhōu,
the Jī star to Qīngyǎnzhōu.
The Quán star corresponds to Xúyángzhōu,
the Héng star to Jīngzhōu,
the Kāiyáng star to Liángzhōu,
and the Biāoguāng star to Yùzhōu.
This is the principle of the three realms.
All are governed by the Dipper."
The twenty-eight lunar mansions are among the Seven Administrators
because they determine the divisions of states and territories,
establish offices, and assign positions.
The *Yùndǒu Shū* states:
"Heaven has the positions of generals and ministers,
assisting the constellations as guards.
All are based on the Jade Sighting-Tube and the Jade Balance
to harmonize the Seven Administrators.
They distribute virtue through the four seasons
and rectify the three paths of vital energy."
The *Shàngshū Kǎolíngyào* states:
"The twenty-eight lunar mansions
span three hundred sixty-five and one-quarter degrees of the celestial sphere.
Thus, they harmonize the seasons and months,
correct the days, and regulate the stars."
The twenty-eight lunar mansions are matched with the Five Phases
in two ways:
one is the general matching,
and the other is the specific matching.
The general matching is as follows:
The seven mansions of the Azure Dragon in the east—
Jiǎo, Kàng, Dǐ, Fáng, Xīn, Wěi, and Jī—correspond to Wood.
They comprise thirty-two stars
and seventy-five degrees.
The seven mansions of the Vermilion Bird in the south—
Dōngjǐng, Yǔguǐ, Liǔ, Qīxīng, Zhāng, Yì, and Zhěn—correspond to Fire.
They comprise sixty-five stars
and one hundred twelve degrees.
The seven mansions of the White Tiger in the west—
Kuí, Lóu, Wèi, Mǎo, Bì, Zī, and Shēn—correspond to Metal.
They comprise fifty-one stars
and eighty degrees.
The seven mansions of the Black Tortoise in the north—
Dǒu, Qiānniú, Xūnǚ, Xū, Wēi, Yíngshì, and Dōngbì—correspond to Water.
They comprise thirty-five stars
and ninety-eight degrees.
Those belonging to Earth are:
in the east, Jiǎo and Kàng;
in the south, Jǐng and Guǐ;
in the west, Kuí and Lóu;
in the north, Dǒu and Niú.
All reside in the four seasons and correspond to Earth.
Zēngzǐ said:
"At the spring equinox, the Bird Star sets at dusk.
The one governing spring
knows that millet can be planted.
At the summer solstice, the Heart Star sets at dusk.
The one governing summer
knows that millet and beans can be planted.
At the autumn equinox, the Xū Star sets at dusk.
The one governing autumn
knows that wheat can be planted.
At the winter solstice, the Mǎo Star sets at dusk.
The one governing winter
knows that mountain people can forge tools and weapons.
Families can harvest reeds, store supplies, and hunt.
The king observes from among the four stars
and understands the urgency of the people's needs.
In urgent times, he does not impose labor or conscription.
Thus, it is said: 'Respectfully grant the people their seasons.'"
This is the general matching.
The separate allocation of the Five Elements is as follows:
The two stars of Jiǎo form the Celestial Gate, the path of the Three Luminaries.
Twelve degrees,
at the time corresponding to Chén,
the Zhèng division, Wood element.
The four stars of Kàng form the Celestial Court, the bureau of the Imperial Secretary.
Nine degrees,
at the time corresponding to Chén,
the Zhèng division, Fire in spring and summer,
Water in autumn and winter.
The four stars of Dī form the lodging palace, where the resting chamber is located.
Fifteen degrees,
at the time corresponding to Mǎo,
the Sòng division, Metal in spring and summer,
Water in autumn and winter.
The six stars of Fáng form the Hall of Light, the path of governance and instruction.
Five degrees, at the time corresponding to Mǎo,
the Sòng division, Earth element.
The three stars of Xīn form the position of the Celestial King.
Five degrees,
at the time corresponding to Mǎo,
the Sòng division, Wood in spring and summer,
Fire in autumn and winter.
The nine stars of Wěi form the palace of the rear court, the residence of consorts and concubines.
Eighteen degrees,
at the time corresponding to Yín,
the Yān division, Water element.
The four stars of Jī form the dwelling of the queen, the chamber for receiving the sovereign.
Eleven degrees,
at the time corresponding to Yín,
the Yān division, Wood element.
Metal in spring and summer,
Earth in autumn and winter.
The six stars of Dǒu govern noble ranks and emoluments,
commending the worthy and advancing scholars.
Twenty-six degrees,
at the time corresponding to Chǒu,
the Wú division, Wood element.
The six stars of Qiānniú govern bridges,
the beginning of the Seven Governors.
Eight degrees,
at the time corresponding to Chǒu,
the Wú division, Wood element.
The four stars of Xūnǚ govern textiles,
the inner treasury of Heaven.
Twelve degrees,
at the time corresponding to Zǐ,
the Yuè division, Water in spring and summer,
Fire in autumn and winter.
The two stars of Xū form the Hall of Suppression, governing sacrificial affairs.
Eleven degrees,
at the time corresponding to Zǐ,
the Qí division, Water in spring and summer,
Metal in autumn and winter.
The three stars of Wēi form tombs,
to recognize ancestors.
Seventeen degrees,
at the time corresponding to Zǐ,
the Qí division, Water in spring and summer,
Fire in autumn and winter.
The two stars of Yíngshì govern military provisions,
to supply soldiers.
Sixteen degrees,
at the time corresponding to Hài,
the Wèi division, Wood in spring and summer,
Earth in autumn and winter.
The two stars of Dōngbì form the repository of writings, charts, and books.
Nine degrees,
at the time corresponding to Hài,
the Wèi division, Metal in spring and summer,
Water in autumn and winter.
The sixteen stars of Kuí form the arsenal of the five weapons,
to suppress violence and disorder.
Sixteen degrees,
at the time corresponding to Xū,
the Lǔ division, Metal in spring and summer,
Fire in autumn and winter.
The three stars of Lóu form the park pastures,
governing offerings for sacrifices.
Twelve degrees,
at the time corresponding to Xū,
the Lǔ division, Water in spring and summer,
Fire in autumn and winter.
The three stars of Wèi form the granaries,
where the five grains are gathered.
Fourteen degrees,
at the time corresponding to Yǒu,
the Zhào division, Wood in spring and summer,
Water in autumn and winter.
The seven stars of Mǎo govern judicial affairs,
overseeing trials and judgments.
Eleven degrees,
at the time corresponding to Yǒu,
the Zhào division, Fire in spring and summer,
Metal in autumn and winter.
The eight stars of Bì form the border troops, preparing against barbarians.
Ten degrees,
at the time corresponding to Yǒu,
the Zhào division, Metal in spring and summer,
Water in autumn and winter.
The three stars of Zīxī form the storehouse,
gathering and checking autumn produce.
Two degrees,
at the time corresponding to Shēn,
the Jìn division, Fire in spring and summer,
Earth in autumn and winter.
The ten stars of Shēnfá form the Celestial General,
reaping and harvesting.
Nine degrees,
at the time corresponding to Shēn,
the Jìn division, Fire in spring and summer,
Earth in autumn and winter.
The eight stars of Dōngjǐng govern the water balance,
to regulate peace and order.
Thirty-three degrees,
at the time corresponding to Wèi,
the Qín division, Fire in spring and summer,
Water in autumn and winter.
The five stars of Yúguǐ form the vision of clarity,
governing the detection of treachery and plots.
Four degrees,
at the time corresponding to Wèi,
the Qín division, Water in spring and summer,
Fire in autumn and winter.
The eight stars of Liǔ form the superior food,
governing the harmonization of flavors.
Fifteen degrees,
at the time corresponding to Wǔ,
the Zhōu division, Water in spring and summer,
Fire in autumn.
The seven stars of Xīng form clothing,
governing the covering of the body.
Seven degrees,
at the time corresponding to Wǔ,
the Zhōu division, Fire in spring and summer,
Water in autumn and winter.
The six stars of Zhāng govern guests,
bestowing gifts and feasting pleasures.
Eighteen degrees,
at the time corresponding to Wǔ,
the Zhōu division, Water element.
The twenty-two stars of Yì form the celestial song,
governing amusement and entertainment.
Eighteen degrees,
at the time corresponding to Sì,
the Chǔ division, Wood in spring and summer,
Metal in autumn and winter.
The four stars of Zhěn form death and mourning, to know disasters and inauspiciousness.
Seventeen degrees,
at the time corresponding to Sì,
the Chǔ division, Wood in spring and summer,
Earth in autumn and winter.
The "Treatise on Astronomy" in the Hànshū states:
Jiǎo, Kàng, Dī correspond to Hán, Zhèng, and Yǎnzhōu.
Fáng, Xīn correspond to Sòng and Yùzhōu.
Wěi, Jī correspond to Yān and Yōuzhōu.
Jǐng, Guǐ correspond to Qín and Yōngzhōu.
Liǔ, Qīxīng, Zhāng correspond to Sānhé.
Yì, Zhěn correspond to Chǔ and Jīngzhōu.
Kuí, Lóu, Wèi correspond to Lǔ and Xúzhōu.
Mǎo, Bì correspond to Zhào and Jìzhōu.
Zī, Shēn correspond to Wèi and Liángzhōu.
Dǒu corresponds to Jiānghú.
Qiānniú, Xūnǚ correspond to Wú and Yángzhōu.
Xū, Wēi correspond to Qí and Qīngzhōu.
Shì, Bì correspond to Wèi and Bìngzhōu.
These all correspond to the divisions they govern,
rectifying the good and evil of their provinces and states.
Thus, it pertains to governance.
The Shí Clan's Celestial Officials Explanation states:
The two stars of Jiǎo are the upper horns of the Azure Dragon's head.
Between the two horns lies the path of heaven,
where the sun, moon, and five planets travel,
hence the name Jiǎo (horn).
Kàng represents the imperial court,
responding to and upholding the king,
day and night deliberating and consulting within the four seas,
hence the name Kàng.
Dī is the chamber where the main resting place thaws,
hence the name Dī.
Fáng is where the Son of Heaven resides in the four seasons,
hence the name Fáng (chamber).
The star in front of Xīn is the crown prince,
the middle one is the Son of Heaven,
the rear one is the common son,
just as the heart is central as the master of the body,
hence the name Xīn (heart).
Wěi is the tail of the eastern Azure Dragon constellation,
hence the name Wěi (tail),
representing its shape.
Jī is near Dǒu,
resembling the winnowing of the five grains,
hence the name Jī (winnowing basket).
Dǒu is a measuring vessel,
for apportioning ranks and emoluments,
its shape resembles a dipper,
hence the name Dǒu (dipper).
Niú also resembles ox horns,
the beginning of the seven regulators,
hence the name Niú (ox).
Nǚ resembles the image of proper cutting and tailoring,
like maidservants and concubines,
hence the name Nǚ (woman).
Xū means depletion,
its emptiness resembles a temple hall,
hence the name Xū (emptiness).
Wēi resembles a house,
also like a tomb,
hence the name Wēi (danger).
Yíngshì has six stars,
serving as a detached palace,
resembling a palace chamber,
hence the name Shì (chamber).
Bì stands upright like a wall,
Confucius stored books in a wall,
emulating this meaning,
hence the name Bì (wall).
Kuí is the arsenal master of weapons,
its form resembles a tightly enclosed arsenal,
thus Kuí means perverse,
weapons are raised due to perversity and conflict,
hence the name Kuí.
Lóu is like a tower pavilion,
also resembling a bell tower,
thus it nurtures sacrificial animals,
hence the name.
Wèi among the viscera is the storehouse of the five grains,
governing granaries,
hence the name.
Mǎo appears haggard and clustered like prisoners in a jail,
thus it governs legal matters.
Mǎo is a star,
clustering brings worry,
hence named Mǎo.
Bì resembles border tribes with hairy heads,
like the Son of Heaven's alert completion,
the hairy heads chant it,
completion achieved.
Chanting to alert the multitude's hearts,
hence named thus.
Zī means gathering.
It is the nose of the White Tiger,
gathered between the tiger's mouth and whiskers,
hence the name.
Shēn means together.
Mixing metal and earth energies,
jointly executing killings and punishments,
hence named Shēn.
Jǐng means essence.
Holding water steadily.
Extremely subtle and refined,
this star models laws and measures,
like water's levelness,
hence named Jǐng (well).
Guǐ means return.
Yang returns to yin,
therefore one star within is dim and not bright,
the image of a ghost,
hence the name.
Liǔ means to detain.
The Spring and Autumn Annals says:
some feast at Rèn.
Liǔ is also named Rèn.
Sacrificing to spirits and deities,
harmonizing the five flavors,
detains the spiritual essence.
Hence named thus.
Qīxīng counts seven,
like a bird's feathers covering above,
hence the name.
Zhāng means to open and expand,
being the crop of the Vermilion Bird,
having capacity to contain,
thus it governs guests.
Yì is like six quills,
resembling a bird's two wings flying,
hence named Yì (wing).
Zhěn resembles a small four-sided carriage.
The rear crosspiece is called zhěn.
Used for inauspicious affairs.
Hence the name.
Their appearances, disappearances, deviations, correctness, eclipses, transits, and occultations,
scatter as calamitous anomalies,
comets, bursts, flying stars.
Such kinds,
are all used for divination and prognostications, explained separately.
Thus not detailed here.
The three categories and seven regulators,
already matched with the five phases,
briefly stated thus.
The eight trigrams:
the Zhōu Yì says:
In ancient times, when Fúxī ruled the world,
he looked up to observe images in heaven,
looked down to observe patterns on earth,
observed the markings of birds and beasts and the suitability of the land,
taking from near his own body,
taking from afar various things.
Thereupon he first created the eight trigrams,
to comprehend the virtue of spiritual illumination,
to categorize the circumstances of the myriad things.
Combining the three talents and doubling them.
Thus six lines form a hexagram.
Because the eight directions connect the eight winds,
they form the qi of the eight seasonal nodes.
Therefore, there are eight trigrams.
Those that correspond to the Five Phases are:
Qián and Duì as metal,
Kǎn as water,
Zhèn and Xùn as wood,
Lí as fire,
and Kūn and Gèn as earth.
Each is explained according to its direction.
The Yì Tōng Guà Yàn states:
Gèn in the northeast governs the Beginning of Spring,
Zhèn in the east governs the Spring Equinox,
