Xùn in the southeast governs the Beginning of Summer,
Lí in the south governs the Summer Solstice,
Kūn in the southwest governs the Beginning of Autumn,
Duì in the west governs the Autumn Equinox,
Qián in the northwest governs the Beginning of Winter,
and Kǎn in the north governs the Winter Solstice.
Kǎn occupies the northern direction because
on the day of the Winter Solstice,
yang qi stirs beneath the Yellow Springs.
Although the zǐ position is that of great yīn,
yang qi stirs beneath it.
Therefore, this trigram is yīn on the outside and yang on the inside,
symbolizing water, which is bright within and harbors yang at its core.
Thus, it resides in the zǐ position,
corresponding to water.
Gèn is in the northeast because
its trigram has one yang line above,
symbolizing the time of the Beginning of Spring,
when yang qi has already emerged
and is upon the earth.
Below are two yīn lines,
symbolizing that yīn qi is still thick
and yang qi remains slight.
Since Gèn represents a mountain,
with its heavy yīn below accumulating deep earth,
the trigram is also in the chǒu position.
Chǒu is opposite wèi,
so it corresponds to earth.
Zhèn occupies the eastern direction because
Zhèn is the eldest son,
capable of taking charge and responsibility,
thus residing in a bright and prominent place.
The east corresponds to spring.
All things are able to sprout and emerge,
clear, pure, and conspicuous.
Zhèn represents thunder;
when thunder stirs, all things emerge.
At the time of the Spring Equinox,
heavenly qi descends,
earthly qi rises,
heaven and earth harmonize,
and all things begin to stir.
Thus, Zhèn resides in mǎo.
Mǎo is the position of lesser yang wood,
so it corresponds to wood.
Xùn occupies the southeast because
its trigram has two yang lines above,
symbolizing the time of the Beginning of Summer,
when yang qi is already strong above
and yīn qi is weak below.
Wood, as a substance,
enters the earth the least
and emerges from the earth the most.
The Xùn trigram has two yang lines above,
symbolizing wood emerging abundantly from the earth.
One yīn line resides below,
symbolizing wood entering the earth sparingly.
The substance of wood is yang,
and it should also be bright and evident.
Thus, it is in the southeast,
corresponding to wood.
Lí occupies the southern direction because
at the time of the Summer Solstice,
yīn stirs beneath the Yellow Springs.
Wǔ is the position of flourishing yang,
yet yīn qi stirs.
Therefore, its trigram is yang on the outside and yīn on the inside,
symbolizing fire, which is bright on the outside and dark within,
harboring yīn qi.
Thus, it is in the south,
corresponding to fire.
Kūn occupies the southwest because
the Kūn trigram is the image of pure yīn;
nothing surpasses the earth in nourishing all things.
The yīn substance is humble and compliant,
daring not to take the lead.
Yīn stirs at wǔ,
and becomes evident only by wèi.
Thus, Kūn follows the position of wǔ.
The earth accumulates yīn;
since Kūn is pure yīn, it symbolizes earth.
According to ritual, the central earth is at wèi;
earth is soil.
Thus, it is in the southwest,
corresponding to earth.
Duì is in the west because
the Duì trigram has one yīn line above,
symbolizing the time of the Autumn Equinox,
when yang qi has already deepened.
Metal is lesser yīn,
so one yīn line resides above.
Yǒu is the position of metal.
Thus, it is in the west,
corresponding to metal.
Qián occupies the northwest because
the Qián trigram is the image of pure yang;
nothing surpasses heaven in giving birth to all things.
Qián is the foremost in generating things.
Yang qi arises at zǐ;
Qián is the root of yang qi.
Thus, it precedes the position of zǐ.
Because it is pure yang, firm and strong,
it is in the northwest,
corresponding to metal.
The Yì Zhuàn states:
Zhèn governs the Spring Equinox and Grain Rain.
If Grain Rain obtains Heaven's Duì,
then all things fully grow.
Duì is the trigram of the west.
At this time, the sun is in Mǎo,
Mǎo being a western constellation.
Because the sun is in the west,
it is called Heaven's Duì.
If appearance is compliant and wood is obtained,
then Heaven's Duì brings harmony.
If appearance is errant and wood is contrary,
then Heaven's Duì brings harm,
and constant rain serves as punishment.
Duì governs the Autumn Equinox and Frost's Descent.
If Frost's Descent obtains the stirring qi of Heaven's Zhèn,
then frost falls across the land,
and all things perish.
Zhèn is the eastern trigram.
At this time, the sun is in Fáng,
Fáng being an eastern constellation.
Because the sun is in the east,
it is called Heaven's Zhèn.
If speech is compliant and metal is obtained,
then Heaven's Zhèn brings harmony.
If speech is errant and metal is contrary,
then Heaven's Zhèn brings harm, and drought serves as punishment.
The reason appearance brings rain and speech brings drought is that
Zhèn is yang and Duì is yīn;
yang brings drought, yīn brings rain.
The reason wood brings rain and metal brings drought is that
if human affairs err in appearance,
then discontent below leads to yīn flourishing,
hence rain.
If speech errs, then the masses are lost;
solitary yang stands alone,
and the multitude of yīn does not adhere,
hence drought.
In spring and autumn,
Zhèn and Duì face each other,
heaven and earth's qi harmonize,
so extreme cold and heat do not occur.
Kǎn governs the Winter Solstice and Great Cold.
If Great Cold obtains the qi of Heaven's Kǎn,
then great cold prevails across the land.
At this time, the sun is in Xū,
Xū being a northern constellation.
Thus, it is called Heaven's Kǎn.
If hearing is compliant and water is obtained,
then Heaven's Kǎn brings harmony.
If hearing is errant and water is contrary,
then Heaven's Kǎn brings punishment.
Hence constant cold.
Lí governs the Summer Solstice and Great Heat.
Great Heat fosters growth;
if it further obtains the qi of Heaven's Lí,
then great heat prevails across the land,
and all affairs fully emerge.
At this time, the sun is in the Seven Stars,
the Seven Stars being the seven southern constellations.
Thus, it is called Heaven's Lí.
If sight is compliant and fire is obtained,
then Heaven's Lí brings harmony.
If sight is errant and fire is contrary,
then Heaven's Lí brings punishment,
hence constant warmth.
In winter and summer,
heaven and earth's qi combine;
Kǎn and Lí each occupy their respective directions,
so extreme cold and heat occur.
Now, dividing the Eight Trigrams,
to match the directions:
Kǎn, Lí, Zhèn, Duì
each correspond to the appropriate directional hour;
the four corner trigrams
have Chǒu and Yín belonging to Gèn,
Chén and Sì belonging to Xùn,
Wèi and Shēn belonging to Kūn,
Xū and Hài belonging to Qián.
The Eight Trigrams thus connect with the Eight Winds.
The eight directions regulate the qi of the eight seasonal nodes.
Therefore, Kǎn generates the Vast Desert Wind,
arriving after forty-five days.
Gèn generates the Regulating Wind,
arriving after forty-five days.
Zhèn generates the Bright Multitude Wind,
arriving after forty-five days.
Xùn generates the Clear Bright Wind,
arriving after forty-five days.
Lí generates the Scorching Wind,
arriving after forty-five days.
Kūn generates the Cool Wind,
arriving after forty-five days.
Duì generates the Changhe Wind,
arriving after forty-five days.
Qián generates the Incomplete Wind,
and after forty-five days, it returns to Kǎn.
Yang qi generates from five to nine,
five times nine is forty-five.
Thus, moving leftward for forty-five days
brings one transformation.
The Vast Desert Wind:
"Vast" means extensive,
"Desert" refers to sandy deserts.
The cold qi spreads far and wide,
coming from the deserts.
It is also said that
at this time, yang qi is below,
and yin is vast and extensive.
The Regulating Wind:
"Regulating" means to reach through.
At this time, it reaches and gives life to all things.
The Bright Multitude Wind:
"Multitude" means many.
At this time, yang bestows the virtue of kindness,
and all things emerge brightly.
The Clear Bright Wind:
The sky is clear, pure, and cool.
At this time, the clear wind blows upon all things,
making them flourish, bright, and pure to behold.
The Scorching Wind:
"Scorching" means high.
All things reach their peak height at this time.
It is also said that
"scorching" means completion.
The yang path reaches its end here.
The Cool Wind:
The autumn wind is cool.
At this time, yin qi is desolate and cool,
harvesting and completing all things.
The Changhe Wind:
"Chang" means flourishing.
At this time, all things are abundant and are gathered in.
The Incomplete Wind:
"Complete" means all-encompassing.
All things are fully formed.
"Incomplete" means blocked and not penetrating.
It is said that at this time, pure yin lacks yang,
and everything is blocked and impenetrable.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
The northeast is called the Azure Gate,
generating the Regulating Wind.
The east is called the Opening Brightness Gate,
generating the Bright Multitude Wind.
The southeast is called the Yang Gate,
generating the Clear Bright Wind.
The south is called the Heat Gate,
generating the Scorching Wind.
The southwest is called the White Gate,
generating the Cool Wind.
The west is called the Changhe Gate,
generating the Changhe Wind.
The northwest is called the Dark Capital Gate,
generating the Incomplete Wind.
The north is called the Cold Gate,
generating the Vast Desert Wind.
The Azure Gate:
In the northeast, wood is about to take charge,
the beginning of spring,
hence called the Azure Gate.
The Opening Brightness Gate:
"Brightness" refers to yang.
It is where the sun rises,
hence called the Opening Brightness Gate.
The Yang Gate:
The lunar month is established in Sì,
pure yang takes charge,
hence called the Yang Gate.
The Scorching Gate:
It is the time of flourishing and decline,
hence called the Heat Gate.
The White Gate:
The lunar month is established in Shēn,
the beginning of metal qi,
hence called the White Gate.
The Changhe Gate:
The eighth month is established in Yǒu,
when all things are about to be harvested.
"Chang" means great, "he" means closing,
the time of harvesting and closing,
hence called the Changhe Gate.
The Dark Capital Gate:
"Dark" means obscure and dim.
Xuánmíng is about to begin taking charge,
yin gathers, hence it is dark,
so it is called the Dark Capital Gate.
The Cold Gate:
It is where cold accumulates,
hence called the Cold Gate.
These are the directions of the eight poles.
They are where the Eight Winds arise.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
The east has the Surging Wind,
the southeast has the Stirring Wind,
the south has the Great Wind,
the southwest has the Chilly Wind,
the west has the Whirling Wind,
the northwest has the Harsh Wind,
the north has the Cold Wind,
the northeast has the Blazing Wind.
This meaning is the same as before.
The Military Treatise of Tàigōng states:
Kǎn is called the Great Hard Wind;
Qián is called the Breaking Wind;
Duì is called the Small Hard Wind;
Gèn is called the Baleful Wind;
Kūn is called the Scheming Wind;
Xùn is called the Small Weak Wind;
Zhèn is called the Infant Wind;
Lí is called the Great Weak Wind.
The Great Hard Wind:
the energy of the Great Yin delights in killing,
therefore it is hard.
The Breaking Wind:
metal is strong and can break things.
The Small Hard Wind:
is also due to the killing nature of metal.
The Baleful Wind:
Gèn lies in the Ghost Gate,
the place of baleful harm.
The Scheming Wind:
Kūn represents earth,
the root of the Great Yin,
thus full of yin schemes.
The Small Weak Wind:
Xùn represents the eldest daughter,
therefore called weak.
The Infant Wind:
Zhèn represents the eldest son,
beloved,
therefore called infant.
The Great Weak Wind:
Lí represents the middle daughter,
even weaker than the eldest daughter.
Great Hard and Small Hard winds favor the guest;
Great Weak and Small Weak winds favor the host.
Baleful indicates events of baleful harm;
Scheming indicates people with rebellious schemes.
Breaking indicates the general's death;
Infant Wind indicates the host is strong.
These are all used by military strategists to observe the waxing and waning of guest and host,
awaiting the direction from which the wind comes.
Yángquán states:
Spring energy is soft,
its wind warm and harmonious,
a joyful wind.
Summer energy is abundant,
its wind bright and steadfast,
a happy wind.
Autumn energy is vigorous,
its wind swift and clear,
an angry wind.
Winter energy is cold,
its wind congealing and severe,
a sorrowful wind.
Also, the winds of the four corners
follow the generating energy,
differing according to the land and direction,
each following what it senses.
However, wind is Heaven's command,
an image of governance.
If the ruler has virtuous decrees,
then the wind does not shake the branches,
but is clear, harmonious, and well-regulated.
If governance and decrees are faulty,
then the energy is angry and violent,
flying sand and breaking trees.
This is the principle of Heaven and Earth's retribution.
These are all energies of the Five Phases,
therefore they are explained together.
In the Zuǒ Zhuàn, Zǐchǎn states:
"Follow the brightness of Heaven."
Heaven has the three lights,
therefore it is called bright.
"Conform to the nature of Earth."
Nature is generation.
It generates the myriad things,
therefore use them according to what is generated.
Generate its six energies,
use its five phases.
The five phases
correspond to the five natures.
The six energies
connect to the six emotions.
Yì Fèng states:
The five phases in humans are nature;
the six pitches in humans are emotions.
Nature consists of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and faithfulness.
Emotions consist of joy, anger, sorrow, happiness, liking, and disliking.
The five natures reside within, controlling yang,
metaphorically storing the five viscera.
The six emotions reside without, controlling yin,
metaphorically storing the six limbs.
Therefore, if emotions overcome nature, there is disorder;
if nature overcomes emotions, there is order.
Nature emerges from within,
emotions come from without.
The interaction of nature and emotion
leaves no space for a hair's breadth.
The Shuōwén states:
Emotion is the yin energy of humans,
possessing desires and cravings.
Nature is the yang energy of humans,
that which is good.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì states:
Nature is the substance of humans,
what humans receive at birth.
Emotion is the number of yin,
internally transmitted and flowing,
connecting to the five viscera.
Therefore, nature is the root,
emotion is the branch.
Nature governs stillness,
serenely maintaining constancy.
Emotion governs movement,
changing upon encountering circumstances.
Movement and stillness interact,
therefore the space is subtle and dense.
The Heshanggōng Zhāngjù states:
The ghost of the five natures
is called hún, which is male.
The ghost of the six emotions
is called pò, which is female.
This clarifies that nature is yang and emotion is yin.
The six emotions are connected to the six qi.
Now, first following Fù's commentary on the Zuǒ Zhuàn, it says:
The six qi are
yīn, yáng, wind, rain, darkness, and brightness.
Yīn corresponds to earth,
yáng and wind correspond to wood,
rain corresponds to metal,
darkness corresponds to water,
and brightness corresponds to fire.
Only heaven's yáng does not change.
Yīn corresponds to earth because
earth embodies the meaning of yīn.
Thus, yīn congeals to form earth.
Wind corresponds to wood because
wind is movement.
Wood also moves,
breaking through the earth to emerge.
The constellation Jī is an eastern asterism
that governs wind.
Also, Xùn corresponds to wood and wind.
Rain corresponds to metal because
rain is water.
The nature of water is to dissolve,
and the nature of metal can also dissolve.
The constellation Bì is a western asterism
that governs rain.
Thus, the Shī says:
"When the moon passes through Bì,
the rain falls in torrents."
Therefore, rain corresponds to metal.
Darkness corresponds to water because
darkness is obscurity.
When there is obscurity, water is produced.
Dark black is the color of water.
Brightness corresponds to fire because
brightness illuminates things.
Thus, it is fire.
All follow their categories accordingly.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the Lǐjì says:
Wood corresponds to rain,
metal corresponds to yáng,
fire corresponds to warmth,
earth corresponds to wind,
and water corresponds to cold.
Zhèn governs the spring equinox.
During the spring equinox and grain rain,
if one attains heaven's Duì,
then all things fully grow.
Duì is the trigram of the west.
At this time, the sun is in Mǎo.
Mǎo is a western asterism.
Because the sun is in the west,
it is called heaven's Duì.
If appearance follows the virtue of wood,
then heaven's Duì brings harmony,
so wood corresponds to rain.
The Shī says:
"The gentle valley wind,
brings both shade and rain."
Metal corresponds to yáng because
in autumn, the sun travels in the east,
in the constellation Fáng.
It attains the qi of heaven's Zhèn.
If speech follows the virtue of metal,
then heaven's Zhèn brings harmony.
Zhèn corresponds to yáng.
In autumn, things mature,
so they are warmed,
which is its harmony.
If metal qi is opposed, there is drought as punishment,
so metal corresponds to yáng.
Earth corresponds to wind because
the Zhuàn says:
"If thoughts in the heart are faulty,
the punishment is constant wind."
Wind is the qi of earth.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"The great clod exhales qi,
its name is wind."
Earth corresponds to the ruler.
The ruler establishes teachings and commands,
so it corresponds to wind.
Earth governs the four seasons.
Thus, if commands are faulty, wind becomes a disaster.
Zhèng takes wood as rain,
while Fù takes wood as wind.
Fù takes metal as rain,
while Zhèng takes metal as yáng.
Zhèng takes earth as wind,
while Fù takes earth as yīn.
The two explanations are contradictory,
each having its own meaning.
Now, judging by the five phases,
Fù's is closer.
The reason for this is:
Water is born from metal,
and the substance of metal is not yáng.
Wood is lesser yáng,
so it should not correspond to rain.
Earth is the ground,
and the ground is originally yīn.
Wind is naturally the qi of yīn and yáng,
not solely born from earth.
Fù takes wood as wind
based on Xùn wood.
Thus, it is appropriate.
The six qi connect to the six emotions as follows:
Fondness corresponds to yáng,
aversion corresponds to yīn,
anger corresponds to wind,
joy corresponds to rain,
sorrow corresponds to darkness,
and happiness corresponds to brightness.
Fondness corresponds to yáng because
yáng qi favors life,
hence it is fondness.
Aversion corresponds to yīn because
yīn qi favors killing,
hence it is aversion.
Anger corresponds to wind because
Yáng Quán said:
"Wind is the qi passing through yīn and yáng,
aroused and stirred up,
similar to a person's internal qi,
which is aroused by joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness."
Zēngzǐ said:
"When yīn and yáng are angry, they become wind."
Joy corresponds to rain because
Zēngzǐ said:
"When yīn and yáng harmonize, they become rain."
Harmony and moisture bring joy.
Sorrow corresponds to darkness because
darkness is obscurity.
Worry leads to blockage,
hence obscurity.
Thus, it is darkness.
Happiness corresponds to brightness because
happiness causes emotions to relax and disperse,
hence brightness.
The Hànshū Lǐyuè Zhì says:
"Humans contain the qi of heaven, earth, yīn, and yáng,
and have the emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness."
The Lùnhéng says:
"Among the five viscera, the heart is the ruler.
The heart generates wisdom,
and the other four viscera follow it.
The liver governs joy,
the lungs govern anger,
the kidneys govern sorrow,
and the spleen governs happiness.
Thus, the sages regulate them,
fearing they may harm nature."
Yì Fèng said:
"Fondness is received by the bladder.
Water favors forward movement,
hence it is called fondness.
Anger is received by the gallbladder.
Lesser yáng begins to flourish,
and all things sprout forward.
Aversion is received by the small intestine.
Summer nurtures all things, but aversion is false.
Hence it is called aversion.
Joy is received by the large intestine.
Metal is a precious thing,
so all rejoice.
Happiness is received by the stomach.
Earth nurtures all things,
and all above and below are happy.
Sorrow is received by the triple burner.
It is the residence of yīn and yáng.
Yáng rises and yīn ends,
and its palace is exhausted.
Hence it is called the triple burner,
and thus sorrowful."
The Lùnhéng discusses the viscera according to the four seasons,
while Yì Fèng discusses the bowels through wind connecting the six emotions.
The spleen and kidneys are two kinds;
the viscera and bowels are the same.
The liver and lungs are two viscera,
but the bowels differ:
The viscera take the lungs as having a punitive nature,
hence anger.
The bowels take the pairing with the lungs' metal as precious in function,
hence joy.
The liver, with spring qi, gives life,
hence joy.
The gallbladder, pairing with fire, can burn,
hence anger.
Both principles are valid.
It also says:
The qi of joy is warmth, corresponding to spring;
the qi of anger is clear, corresponding to autumn;
the qi of happiness is yáng, corresponding to summer;
the qi of sorrow is yīn, corresponding to winter.
This aligns with the meaning of the Lùnhéng.
Yì Fèng said:
The East is of the nature of benevolence and the emotion of anger;
anger is governed by the hidden thief.
The South is of the nature of propriety and the emotion of aversion;
aversion is governed by integrity and loyalty.
The Lower direction is of the nature of trustworthiness and the emotion of sorrow;
sorrow is governed by fairness and justice.
The West is of the nature of righteousness and the emotion of joy;
joy is governed by generosity and magnanimity.
The North is of the nature of wisdom and the emotion of desire;
desire is governed by greed and rapacity.
The Upper direction is of the nature of aversion and the emotion of pleasure;
pleasure is governed by treachery and wickedness.
Greed and rapacity govern the seeking and demanding of wealth and goods.
Since it is called greed and rapacity,
it naturally involves seeking and requiring.
The hidden thief governs robbery and theft.
This is also without doubt.
Integrity and loyalty govern receiving guests and promotions.
Yín is the beginning of yang,
Wǔ is the peak of yang,
hence it is called receiving guests.
Since there is the nature of integrity and loyalty,
it naturally involves being summoned and appointed to high positions.
Generosity and magnanimity govern feasting and auspicious celebrations.
Generosity and magnanimity involve much accommodation,
hence there are auspicious celebrations.
Auspicious celebrations necessarily involve setting out wine and food.
Treachery and wickedness govern illness, debauchery, and deceit.
Debauchery and deceit arise from wickedness.
Wickedness necessarily gives rise to illness.
Fairness and justice govern holding grudges, disputes, and remonstrance.
Being upright enables contention,
being impartial enables holding grudges and enmities.
The emotion of desire:
water is born in Shēn and peaks in Zǐ.
The nature of water is to flow upon touching the ground,
to moisten upon touching objects,
thus it has many desires,
hence it is called desire.
Having many desires,
then greed becomes insatiable.
Hence it is called greed and rapacity.
Governed by Shēn and Zǐ.
The emotion of anger:
wood is born in Hài and peaks in Mǎo.
Its nature receives the qi of water to be born,
piercing through the earth to emerge.
Hence it is called anger.
Mǎo wood is born from Zǐ.
Water and Mǎo mutually harm each other,
Hài also harms itself.
Thus, yin qi harms each other,
hence it is called the hidden thief.
Governed by Hài and Mǎo.
Greed and rapacity must obtain the hidden thief to then act;
the hidden thief must obtain greed and rapacity to then be used;
these two yin operate together.
Therefore, the king
avoids the days of Zǐ and Mǎo.
These are days of mutual harm.
The emotion of aversion:
fire is born in Yín and peaks in Wǔ.
The nature of fire is blazing and fierce,
accepting nothing,
hence it is called aversion.
Its qi is clear, bright, and refined,
ordering itself with propriety,
hence it is called integrity and loyalty.
Governed by Yín and Wǔ.
The emotion of joy:
metal is born in Sì and peaks in Yǒu.
Metal is a precious substance,
those who see it are joyful,
also joyful to use sharp blades upon all things,
hence joy.
Where sharp blades are applied,
there is nothing not broad and wide.
As a vessel, it can accommodate much.
Hence it is called generosity and magnanimity.
Governed by Sì and Yǒu.
These two yang operate together.
Therefore, the king finds auspiciousness on the days of Wǔ and Yǒu.
The emotion of pleasure:
refers to the North and East,
where yang qi sprouts and is born.
Hence it is called the Upper,
also governing the center.
Chén is where water reaches its end.
Wood falls and returns to its root,
water flows and returns to its end.
Hence wood’s harm is in Wèi,
water’s harm is in Chén,
peak and decline each attain their place,
hence pleasure.
Water reaching its end means there is no crevice it does not enter.
Wood rising upward to its end,
then moving sideways becomes slanted,
hence it is called treachery and wickedness.
Governed by Chén and Wèi.
The emotion of sorrow:
refers to the South and West,
where yin qi sprouts and is born,
hence it is called the Lower,
Xū is where fire reaches its end.
Chǒu is where metal reaches its end.
Metal is hard, fire is strong,
each returns to its own home.
Hence fire’s harm is in Wǔ,
metal’s harm is in Yǒu,
at the peak of metal and fire,
they are harmed by themselves.
Reaching the end with nowhere to return,
hence it is called sorrow.
The nature of fire is without selfishness,
the nature of metal is firm and decisive,
hence it is called fairness and justice.
Governed by Xū and Chǒu.
Therefore it is said:
The five natures reside in the root,
the six emotions are in the branches.
Emotions arise from natures,
natures are expressed through emotions.
Natures and emotions are interdependent.
Hence this is explained in detail.
Governing and administration:
governing means to order.
Order established gives it its name.
Administration means to rectify.
Not being wicked is its designation.
The common people cannot order themselves,
so a ruler is established to order them.
The myriad people cannot rectify themselves,
so leaders are established to rectify them.
Rectification makes them not wicked,
orderly commands make them not chaotic.
Not chaotic, hence peaceful;
not wicked, hence good.
Good, then robbers and thieves do not arise;
peaceful, then each safeguards their own livelihood.
Thus, they can overcome cruelty and eliminate killing.
On the roads, they move like geese in formation,
lizards and snakes can be trodden upon,
unicorns and dragons can be harnessed.
Such is called orderly governance.
Confucius said:
“To govern by virtue,
is like the North Star dwelling in its place,
and all the stars revolving around it.”
The Dà Dài Lǐ says:
“The ruler is the foundation of order;
without a ruler, how can there be order?”
Being able to emulate the Five Phases
is called conforming to the Way.
Thus, leniency and severity are compared to water and fire,
benevolence and righteousness are drawn from metal and wood.
Following the four seasons to teach the people,
utilizing the five materials for application.
Employing people and employing strength,
the principle returns to a single measure.
The "Governing in Accordance with the Five Phases" chapter of the *Chūnqiū Fánlù* states:
When Wood holds sway,
its qi is warm and turbid,
and it is green for seventy-two days.
When Fire holds sway,
its qi is warm and yang,
and it is red for seventy-two days.
When Earth holds sway,
its qi is warm and turbid,
and it is yellow for seventy-two days.
When Metal holds sway,
its qi is firm and congealing,
and it is white for seventy-two days.
When Water holds sway,
its qi is clear and cold,
and it is black for seventy-two days.
When Wood again holds sway,
then practice gentle kindness,
and advance scholars of the classics and arts.
Upon the arrival of Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring),
release those lightly imprisoned,
remove delays and detentions,
remove shackles and fetters,
open what is closed and shut,
clear obstructions and blockages,
care for the young and orphaned,
pity the widowed and solitary.
All these are in accordance with the bestowals of spring.
Do not cut down trees;
extend kindness to plants and trees,
then the vermilion grass appears.
This is what the poet sang of,
kindness extending to the walking reeds.
Not cutting down trees
means one must not violate the qi of heaven's yang growth.
If the ruler gallops without restraint,
indulges in wine and follows his desires,
imposes heavy corvée labor,
robs the people of their seasons,
levies heavy taxes,
then the people suffer from epidemic diseases and rashes,
suffer from foot ailments,
and harm the spring qi.
Therefore, these are all Wood illnesses.
If Wood is injured and defeated,
then dragons deeply hide,
and Wood birds fear and do not appear.
Whales emerge and bring calamity.
Scale-and-shell creatures possess Metal qi,
which is why they injure Wood.
When Fire holds sway,
then rectify borders,
and cultivate fields.
Upon the arrival of Lìxià (Beginning of Summer),
promote the worthy and good,
enfeoff the virtuous,
reward the meritorious,
and send envoys to the four directions.
This is in accordance with Fire's transformative power,
nurturing and growing the myriad things.
Do not set fires indiscriminately;
then Fire complies with human use,
sweet dew descends,
the fènghuáng comes,
the yellow swan appears.
The fènghuáng is of the same category as the Vermilion Bird,
joyful, therefore it emerges and appears.
Sweet dew and the yellow swan
both are sons celebrating their mother.
If the ruler employs slanderers and flatterers,
alienates flesh and blood,
estranges loyal ministers,
abandons laws and decrees,
lets women govern,
then the people suffer from blood swellings,
the state becomes unclear,
Fire becomes a disaster,
winter geese do not come,
birds become monstrous,
Fire is not good.
Therefore, birds undergo strange transformations, worry, and fear,
hence they do not come.
When Earth holds sway,
care for the elders,
pity the widowed and solitary,
bestow rewards for filial piety and fraternal duty,
and spread kindness and favor.
This is in accordance with Earth's virtue of broadness, harmony, and nurturing.
Do not initiate earthworks;
let the regulations for palaces and buildings have distinctions,
and the kindness among relatives have order,
then the five grains will ripen,
auspicious grain will appear,
and sages and worthies will come.
Earth qi is harmonious,
therefore the auspicious grain ripens in harmony.
Virtue is vast and great,
therefore sages and worthies delight in it and come.
If the ruler indulges in licentious pleasure without restraint,
insults his elderly relatives,
oppresses the common people,
then the people suffer from illnesses of the abdomen and heart.
The heart and abdomen govern Earth;
the qi is not harmonious, hence illness.
Worthies hide and conceal themselves,
the hundred grains do not ascend,
and naked insects become a disaster.
Earth's nature is injured,
therefore farming and harvests do not succeed,
worthies detest it,
which is why they are not seen.
Naked insects belong to Earth qi.
Injured, therefore they undergo transformation.
When Metal holds sway,
repair the inner and outer city walls,
mend walls and enclosures,
carefully examine prohibitions and restrictions,
prepare armor and weapons,
alert the hundred officials,
and punish the lawless.
All these are in accordance with Metal,
with its qi of awesomeness, sternness, and killing.
Do not burn metal or stone;
then the white tiger appears.
The tiger is a Metal beast,
joyful, therefore it emerges.
If the ruler is greedy for bribes,
fond of using military force,
then the people suffer from illnesses of coughing, muscle cramps, and nasal congestion.
The nose governs the lungs;
the lungs are ill,
therefore one coughs and the nose is congested.
These are all illnesses caused by Metal.
Furred creatures, metal, and stone become monstrous.
Metal qi is injured,
therefore they undergo strange transformations.
When Water holds sway,
close the village gates,
apprehend those deserving punishment,
and prepare passes and bridges.
All these are in accordance with Water,
the meaning of closing and storing.
Do not breach ponds or dams,
for fear that Water qi will leak and overflow.
If so, then sweet springs emerge,
kindness extends to birds and insects,
then the numinous turtle appears.
The *Shū* says,
"Favor extends to the insects."
Shelled creatures belong to Water,
joyful, therefore they appear.
If the ruler neglects sacrifices,
is negligent towards the ancestral temple,
enforces laws contrary to principle,
goes against heaven's qi,
then the people suffer from illnesses of flowing swellings, water distension, atrophy, and paralysis,
and the orifices do not open.
These all signify the meaning of Water qi being obstructed and congealed.
The sages placed Water in the position of Tàiyīn (Great Yin).
Yin is dark and empty,
comparable to the ancestral temple.
When a person dies, the essence-qi scatters and disperses;
the ancestral temple is established to gather it.
The hall and chambers are empty and silent,
dark and without people.
This is likened to Water.
Neglecting sacrifices
means the way of filial piety is abandoned.
Therefore, the qi of Tàiyīn,
affected, causes people to fall ill,
resulting in these diseases.
Water becomes a disaster and harm,
the numinous turtle deeply hides,
ghosts wail, and armored insects become monstrous.
Armored insects belong to Water;
the qi is injured,
therefore they turn to hiding and are not seen.
The ancestral temple is not sacrificed to,
the soul-qi is injured and resentful.
Therefore, ghosts wail.
The Apocrypha of the Xiaojing states:
The qi of wood generates wind,
the qi of fire generates locusts,
the qi of earth generates insects,
the qi of metal generates frost,
the qi of water generates hail.
If governance fails regarding wood,
then wind comes in response.
If governance fails regarding fire,
then locusts come in response.
If governance fails regarding earth,
then insects come in response.
If governance fails regarding metal,
then frost comes in response.
If governance fails regarding water,
then hail comes in response.
Cruel actions lead to wind,
encroachment leads to locusts,
greed and brutality lead to insects,
harshness and venom lead to frost,
tyranny and cruelty lead to hail.
All these follow their respective categories in response.
Huánzǐ's New Treatise says:
Humans embody the form of heaven and earth,
harbor pure and unadulterated essence,
and are the most intelligent among living beings.
Therefore, appearance corresponds to wood,
speech corresponds to metal,
sight corresponds to fire,
hearing corresponds to water,
and thought corresponds to earth.
The functions of the Five Phases,
in motion and stillness, interact with the spirits.
If appearance is respectful, there is solemnity;
when solemn, timely rain follows.
If speech is compliant, there is order;
when orderly, timely sunshine follows.
If sight is clear, there is wisdom;
when wise, timely warmth follows.
If hearing is acute, there is planning;
when planning, timely cold follows.
If the mind is stern, there is sageliness;
when sagely, timely wind follows.
Metal, wood, water, and fire are all borne by earth.
Rain, sunshine, warmth, and cold
all originate from wind.
Appearance, speech, sight, and hearing
all arise from the mind.
Shīzǐ says:
The mind is the ruler of the body.
The Son of Heaven receives the mandate for the world from his mind;
if the mind is improper, calamity befalls the world.
Feudal lords receive the mandate for their states from their minds;
if the mind is improper, the state perishes.
Commoners receive the mandate for their persons from their minds;
if the mind is improper, their persons are destroyed.
Thus, the human mind
is the essence of heaven and earth,
the foundation of all living beings.
Therefore, order or chaos in governance
depends on the ruler's mind.
Thus, when sages receive the mandate and become kings,
they all invariably follow heaven and earth,
model themselves on the Five Phases,
cultivate the five affairs,
and thereby govern the cosmos,
nurturing the common people.
Their institutions, laws, and regulations
all take the Five Phases as their foundation.
Carriages, attire, dignity, and ceremonies,
court rituals and movements,
farming, sericulture, sowing, and planting,
bestowing benefits and granting rewards correspond to wood.
Distinctions of noble and humble, superior and inferior,
institutions, rituals, and forms,
conferring titles and rewarding achievements,
occupying high positions and gazing afar correspond to fire.
Palaces, halls, terraces, and pavilions,
husband and wife, relatives, and kin,
spreading virtue and nurturing,
salaries, ranks, pardons, and forgiveness correspond to earth.
Weapons, armor, and tools,
hunting and military preparations,
punishments, penalties, prisons, and prohibitions correspond to metal.
Ancestral temple sacrifices,
storing and sealing away treasures,
mourning rituals, regulations, and remembrance,
divination and resolving doubts correspond to water.
Through the Five Phases, the hundred officials are established;
through the hundred officials, all affairs are managed.
When all affairs are managed, the four seas are at peace—
this is the origin of governance.
Their dwellings, clothing, and conveyances,
the utensils and implements they use,
all take the Five Phases as their foundation,
thereby connecting with the Way of governance.
The Book of Rites states:
In the months of spring,
the Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of the Qīngyáng Hall,
rides in a carriage with phoenix bells,
drives azure dragons,
displays blue banners,
wears blue robes,
and carries azure jade.
In the months of summer,
he resides in the left chamber of the Bright Hall,
rides in a vermilion carriage,
drives red steeds,
displays red banners,
wears vermilion robes,
and carries red jade.
For central earth, he resides in the Great Chamber of the Grand Temple,
rides in the grand carriage,
drives yellow steeds,
displays yellow banners,
wears yellow robes,
and carries yellow jade.
In the months of autumn,
he resides in the left chamber of the Zǒngzhāng Hall,
rides in a military carriage,
drives white steeds,
displays white flags,
wears white robes,
and carries white jade.
In the months of winter,
he resides in the left chamber of the Xuántáng Hall,
rides in a dark carriage,
drives iron-black steeds,
displays dark banners,
wears dark robes,
and carries dark jade.
The Kǎo Língyào states:
In spring, issue commands abroad,
practice benevolent governance,
follow the constant ways of heaven,
and wear blue at that time.
In summer, one may melt and refine copper,
preparing against fire,
revering the brightness of heaven,
and wear red at that time.
For central earth,
promote men of the Way,
consult with them on state affairs,
may execute criminals,
but must not undertake earthworks,
violating the constants of earth,
and wear yellow at that time.
In autumn, do not melt or refine metal or copper,
violating the firmness of yin,
at that time take up arms,
and it is appropriate to kill fierce beasts,
wearing white at that time.
In winter, do not cause things to be un-stored,
do not harm waterways,
preserve harmony with the qi,
and wear black at that time.
The Family Sayings states:
In the first month of early spring,
the Eastern Palace wears green-colored garments,
plays the qín and sè,
its weapon is the spear,
and its tree is the willow.
In the second month of mid-spring,
the Eastern Palace wears garments, plays music, and uses weapons as before,
and its tree is the apricot.
In the third month of late spring,
the Eastern Palace wears garments, plays music, and uses weapons as before,
and its tree is the plum.
In the fourth month of early summer,
the Southern Palace wears red-colored garments,
blows the shēng and yú,
its tree is the peach,
and its weapon is the halberd.
In the fifth month of mid-summer,
the Southern Palace wears garments, plays music, and uses weapons as before,
and its tree is the elm.
In the sixth month of late summer,
the Central Palace wears yellow-colored garments,
beats the great drum,
its tree is the catalpa,
and its weapon is the bow.
In the seventh month of early autumn,
the Western Palace wears white-colored garments,
strikes the great bell,
its tree is the chinaberry,
and its weapon is the sword.
In the eighth month of mid-autumn,
it wears garments, plays music, and uses weapons as before,
and its tree is the cudrania.
In the ninth month of late autumn,
it wears garments, plays music, and uses weapons as before,
and its tree is the pagoda tree.
In the tenth month of early winter,
the Northern Palace wears black-colored garments,
strikes the qìng,
its tree is the sandalwood,
and its weapon is the shield.
In the eleventh month of mid-winter,
the Northern Palace wears garments, plays music, and uses weapons as before,
and its tree is the oak.
Discussing the seasonal ordinances,
to await what is appropriate for storing and preserving.
The Zhou Officials states:
In spring, form the spear formation,
with bows as the vanguard;
in summer, form the square formation,
with halberds as the vanguard;
in the sixth month, form the circular formation,
with spears as the vanguard;
in autumn, form the yin formation,
with swords as the vanguard;
in winter, form the ambush formation,
with shields as the vanguard.
This military preparedness also follows the five qi.
The Recorded Charts states:
When a ruler rides on wood and becomes king,
his people are of green color,
with long necks and beautiful hair,
his subjects are tall with broad shoulders,
and they esteem benevolence.
Tallness,
all resemble wood.
Benevolence is the nature of wood.
When virtuous, then seasonal grasses flourish luxuriantly,
fine grains grow together,
birds do not suffer harm in the womb,
because the wood qi is abundant.
When failing, then the constellations vanish,
colors become disordered,
grains do not ripen,
and many people are crushed to death.
Wood grows upward and outward,
encountering earth causes injury,
then it turns green but cannot rise,
hence they are crushed to death.
Riding on fire and becoming king,
his people are of red color,
with large eyes,
for Lí represents the eyes,
hence they see clearly with large vision.
His people have pointed heads and long waists,
are swift and agile, and esteem filial piety,
long waists take after Duì,
swiftness and agility are the nature of fire.
Lí represents the sun,
the sun has a crow,
and the crow represents filial piety.
When virtuous, then worthy men are employed,
governance is praised as peaceful,
and dappled horses and patterned foxes arrive.
Horses are fire animals,
hence they come when virtuous.
Foxes also come forward.
When failing, then there is summer frost.
The sun is the essence of fire,
failing thus causes changes like eclipses and raining earth,
suddenly obscuring the image of light.
Inheriting earth and becoming king,
his head is prominent,
a large head signifies earth.
His people have broad shoulders and large feet.
They love to laugh, play, and dance.
Broad and large resemble earth,
harmony thus leads to leisure and joy.
When virtuous, then sweet dew descends,
sweet springs respond together to his virtue.
When failing, then insects and locusts arise,
heaven rains and there are constant winds and chaotic mists.
All are injuries to earth qi,
hence manifesting anomalies.
Inheriting metal and becoming king,
his people are of white color,
with uneven shoulders, ears, and square faces with hair.
His subjects have white necks and are tall and large,
and esteem righteousness.
All are metal qi.
When virtuous, then great cowries and bright pearls appear,
foreign countries from afar offer pearls and cowries.
The function of metal qi is firm,
able to control distant people,
hence they come to offer tribute.
When failing, then fire flies,
heaven rumbles and earth splits,
rivers overflow and mountains collapse,
evil men advance,
insects and beasts cause disasters.
Fire can overcome metal,
when metal has failures,
thus fire attacks it and it flies.
Inheriting water and becoming king,
his people are of black color,
with large ears,
for Kǎn represents the ears and governs the kidneys,
water qi thus makes them large.
His subjects have keen hearing,
Kǎn is water.
Openings and passages connect, hence keen hearing.
When virtuous, then auspicious clouds arrive,
turtles and dragons are adorned with patterns,
all are water qi manifesting as auspicious signs.
When failing, then the toad leaves the moon,
many people drown and die,
constant rain causes harm.
All are sorrows of water.
This together clarifies the way of governing,
not exceeding the five phases.
Hence it is prepared for explanation.
Written by Xiāo Jí, Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments with Equal Honors to the Three Excellencies, Duke of Chengyáng Commandery
As for the various spirits,
their spiritual intelligence has no fixed direction,
hidden and manifest, unfathomable.
Confucius said:
The essence qi of yang is spirit.
He also said:
That which is unfathomable by yin and yang is called spirit.
One explanation says:
Spirit means to extend.
All things have substance,
obstructed and bent, unable to extend.
Spirit is the clear and empty qi,
without any obstruction or stagnation,
hence it is called extension.
Speaking of spirits,
their names are myriad and varied,
the way of the three materials,
the hundred numina are not one.
All follow the five phases,
difficult to exhaustively cover.
Now, let us discuss what is matched with the five phases.
To distinguish between auspicious and inauspicious:
The Dìxì Pǔ states:
At the beginning of Heaven and Earth's emergence,
there was born the Heavenly Sovereign.
He ruled by virtue of Wood.
The Sānwǔ Lìjì says:
The Heavenly Sovereign had thirteen heads.
The Dìxì Pǔ states:
The Earthly Sovereign ruled by virtue of Fire.
The Sānwǔ Lì says:
There was a divine being,
with eleven heads,
called the Earthly Sovereign.
The Chūnqiū Mìnglì Xù says:
The Human Sovereign had nine heads.
Sòng Jūn's commentary states:
There were nine brothers.
The Dòngjì says:
The Human Sovereign divided and governed the nine provinces.
Ancient language was simple and unadorned,
hence they spoke in terms of head counts.
Táo Huáyáng says:
These Three Sovereigns governed from the Purple Tenuity Palace,
their essence being the Heavenly Sovereign, the Great Emperor.
The Shìjì says:
The Heavenly Sovereign, the Great Emperor, is Yàopòbǎo;
the Earthly Sovereign is Tiānyī;
the Human Sovereign is Tàiyī.
Gān Gōng's Xīngjīng says:
The Heavenly Sovereign, the Great Emperor,
originally held the Chart of Ten Thousand Deities.
There is one star within the Hooked Array,
named Yàopòbǎo.
It is the revered ancestor of the Five Emperors.
Tiānyī and Tàiyī preside over attending to the deities.
"Attending" means serving.
There are two stars,
outside the gate of the Purple Tenuity Palace,
both are attendant stars to the Heavenly Sovereign, the Great Emperor.
Tiānyī presides over warfare,
and knows auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
On days of Jiǎ, Wù, Gēng, and Rén,
it governs the Jade Hall Palace;
on days of Yǐ, Jǐ, and Xīn,
it governs the Bright Hall Palace;
on days of Bǐng, Dīng, and Guǐ,
it governs the Crimson Palace.
These are the three palaces of the great deities.
Tàiyī presides over wind, rain, flood, drought, war, famine, pestilence, and disasters,
and further dispatches sixteen deities to roam the Nine Palaces.
Tiānyī is that which nurtures and fosters the myriad things;
Tàiyī is that which inspects calamities and misfortunes.
These are the ministers of the Celestial Emperor.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the Qiánzàodù states:
Tàiyī is
the name of the deity of the Northern Dipper.
When residing in its place, it is called the Great Emperor;
when moving among the Eight Trigrams and the days and hours,
it is called Tàiyī,
or sometimes Tiānyī.
In its comings and goings,
it rests outside the Purple Palace.
Its star is thus named accordingly.
The movements of Tiānyī
are like the Son of Heaven's tours of inspection to the sacred mountains,
and human rulers likewise follow and conduct inspections;
each time it concludes, it returns.
Tàiyī moves through the palaces of the Eight Trigrams,
and every season,
it enters the center.
The great divisions of celestial numbers emerge with yang
and enter with yin.
Yang arises from Zǐ,
yin arises from Wǔ.
Therefore, when Tàiyī descends to roam the Nine Palaces,
it begins from Kǎn.
The Jiǔgōng Jīng says:
The movements of Tiānyī
begin from the Lí Palace;
the movements of Tàiyī
begin from the Kǎn Palace.
Tiānyī presides over abundance and harvest;
Tàiyī presides over flood, drought, war, and famine.
Together with twelve deities,
they roam the Nine Palaces.
The twelve positions proceed from the lesser to the greater.
The Liùrén Shìjīng says:
Among the twelve divine generals,
Tiānyī is the chief.
On days of Jiǎ, Wù, and Gēng,
at dawn it governs Dàjí,
at dusk it governs Xiǎojí.
On days of Yǐ and Jǐ,
at dawn it governs Shénhòu,
at dusk it governs Chuánsòng.
On days of Bǐng and Dīng,
at dawn it governs Wēimíng,
at dusk it governs Cóngkuí.
On days of Xīn,
at dawn it governs Shèngxiān,
at dusk it governs Gōngcáo;
on days of Rén and Guǐ,
at dawn it governs Tàiyī,
at dusk it governs Tàichōng.
All these are outside the gate of the Purple Tenuity Palace.
Tiānyī and Tàiyī
are not within the Purple Tenuity.
The name of the Northern Dipper is the Great Emperor.
Zhèng Xuán was mistaken.
As for the sixteen deities of Tàiyī:
Dìzhǔ is in Zǐ;
here yang qi stirs in the Yellow Springs,
and the myriad things are nurtured and produced from the earth.
Zǐ is the beginning of yang qi,
hence called Dìzhǔ (Earth Lord).
Yángdé is in Chǒu;
yang can give birth to the myriad things.
By Chǒu, it begins to produce,
hence called Yángdé (Yang Virtue).
Hédé is in the Northeast corner.
At this time, yin and yang qi harmonize,
giving birth to the myriad things,
hence called Hédé (Harmonious Virtue).
Lǚshēn is in Yín.
Lǚ means great.
Shēn means to extend, to lengthen.
The myriad things gradually extend and become great.
Hence called Lǚshēn.
Gāocóng is in Mǎo;
the myriad things cluster and grow tall,
hence called Gāocóng (High Cluster).
Tàiyáng is in Chén;
after the stirring of Zhèn,
yang qi becomes greatly abundant,
hence called Tàiyáng (Great Yang).
Dàhào is in the Southeast corner;
at this time yang is already manifest,
shining brightly and illuminating,
hence called Dàhào (Great Brightness).
Dàshén is in Sì;
the myriad things are already ripe,
their qi rises vigorously,
hence originally called Dàshén (Great Spirit).
Dàwēi is in Wǔ;
yang declines and yin is born.
Form and qi begin to stir,
hence called Dàwēi (Great Awe).
Tiāndào is in Wèi;
the hundred things are all formed,
none are not provided for use,
hence called Tiāndào (Heavenly Way).
Dàwǔ is in the Southwest corner;
yin qi is in operation,
the myriad things are all injured,
hence called Dàwǔ (Great Martial).
Wǔdé is in Shēn;
shepherd's purse and wheat are just sprouting,
yin harbors yang nature,
hence called Wǔdé (Martial Virtue).
Dàzú is in Yǒu;
yin qi greatly destroys,
all kinds are exhausted,
hence called Dàzú (Great Clan).
Yīnzhǔ is in Xū;
yang qi descends and hides,
yin qi remains freely above,
hence called Yīnzhǔ (Yin Lord).
Yīndé is in the Northwest corner;
Qián represents Heaven.
Yin qi reaches its extreme here,
only then can it generate yang,
hence called Yīndé (Yin Virtue).
Dàyì is in Hài;
the myriad things here conceive and bear.
Yin qi contains yang,
hence called Dàyì (Great Righteousness).
Furthermore, the Nine Palaces and Twelve Deities:
Tiānyī is in the Li Palace,
Tàiyī is in the Kǎn Palace,
Tiānfú is in the Central Palace,
Shètí is in the Kūn Palace,
Xuānyuán is in the Zhèn Palace,
Zhāoyáo is in the Xùn Palace,
Qīnglóng is in the Qián Palace,
Xiánchí is in the Duì Palace,
Tàiyīn is in the Gèn Palace.
Tàiyī in Sì is as explained earlier.
The remaining seven deities,
are all names of stellar palaces.
Together with Tiānyī and Tàiyī,
they move through the Nine Palaces,
shifting once each year,
returning to their original positions after nine years.
Tiānyī governs abundance and harvest,
Tàiyī governs water and cold,
Tiānfú governs famine,
Shètí governs sickness and suffering,
Xuānyuán governs thunder and rain,
Zhāoyáo governs wind and clouds,
Qīnglóng governs frost and hail,
Xiánchí governs soldiers and bandits,
Tàiyīn governs secret plots.
There is also another Qīnglóng,
which moves through the Twelve Earthly Branches.
This is the name for Tàisuì.
In ancient times, the year was called Qīnglóng.
This deity governs blessings and celebrations,
Tàiyīn moves once every three years,
moving rightwards through the Twelve Earthly Branches,
this is the yīn deity of Tàisuì.
It symbolizes the empress and consorts,
governing water, rain, and private affairs.
The harmful energy moves rightwards through the four Mèng months,
shifting once each year,
causing harm wherever it arrives,
hence it is called harmful energy.
Together they form the Twelve Deities,
which are used in the Nine Palaces.
Furthermore, the Xuánnǚ Shì Jīng states:
The twelve deities employed in Liùrén are:
Shénhòu governs the Zǐ water deity,
Dàjí governs the Chǒu earth deity,
Gōngcáo governs the Yín wood deity,
Tàichōng governs the Mǎo wood deity,
Tiāngāng governs the Chén earth deity,
Tàiyī governs the Sì fire deity,
Shèngxiān governs the Wǔ fire deity,
Xiǎojí governs the Wèi earth deity,
Chuánsòng governs the Shēn metal deity,
Cóngkuí governs the Yǒu metal deity,
Hékuí governs the Xū earth deity,
Zhēngmíng governs the Hài water deity.
Regarding the Zǐ deity Shénhòu:
Zǐ corresponds to Huángzhōng,
the way of the ruler.
Therefore it is called Hòu (Empress),
the beginning of yang.
Yang stirs within but has not yet taken form,
therefore it is called Shén (Deity).
Regarding Chǒu Dàjí:
All things reach Chǒu,
and all sprout, attaining yang life,
therefore it is Dàjí (Great Auspiciousness).
Regarding Yín Gōngcáo:
All things reach Yín,
their achievements are already visible.
Cáo means multitude.
The achievements of the multitude of things become visible at Yín.
Regarding Mǎo Tàichōng:
All things reach Mǎo,
they all greatly surge, their hearts and skins burst forth with calyxes.
Regarding Chén Tiāngāng:
It aligns with the handle of the Dipper stars,
its deity is strong and firm.
Regarding Sì Tàiyī:
Pure Qián is in charge,
the virtue of heaven resides there,
therefore Tàiyī is Shénhòu.
Regarding Wǔ Shèngxiān:
Yang energy is greatly powerful,
yin energy stirs at times.
Only yang is first, thus victorious.
Regarding Wèi Xiǎojí:
All things are fully ripe and completed,
therefore it is Xiǎojí (Minor Auspiciousness).
Regarding Shēn Chuánsòng:
It transmits the completed things,
sending them to be stored for winter.
Regarding Yǒu Cóngkuí:
It follows the second star of the Dipper's handle.
Regarding Xū Hékuí:
Hé means head.
It aligns with the head of the Dipper's handle.
Regarding Hài Zhēngmíng:
The water body is internally bright,
not visible externally.
Subtly, its yang energy reaches Zǐ and then becomes bright.
Shénhòu governs women,
Dàjí governs farming,
Gōngcáo governs relocation of states,
Tàichōng governs facing officials,
Tiāngāng governs killing and conquest,
Tàiyī governs gold and treasures,
Shèngxiān governs sacrifices to deities,
Xiǎojí governs marriages and gatherings,
Chuánsòng governs capture and arrest,
Cóngkuí governs death and mourning,
Hékuí governs illness and disease,
Zhēngmíng governs summons and appointments.
Furthermore, the Twelve Generals are:
Tiānyī, earth general;
First front: Téngshé, fire general;
Second front: Zhūquè, fire general;
Third front: Liùhé, wood general;
Fourth front: Gōuzhèn, earth general;
Fifth front: Qīnglóng, wood general;
First rear: Tiānhòu, water general;
Second rear: Tàiyīn, metal general;
Third rear: Xuánwǔ, water general;
Fourth rear: Tàicháng, earth general;
Fifth rear: Báihǔ, metal general;
Sixth rear: Tiānkōng, earth general.
Tiānyī is as explained earlier.
Téngshé governs fright and alarm,
Zhūquè governs documents,
Liùhé governs congratulations,
Gōuzhèn governs obstruction and restraint,
Qīnglóng governs blessings and assistance,
Tiānhòu is the same as Shénhòu,
the consort of Tiānyī.
Tàiyīn governs private affairs,
Xuánwǔ governs death and illness,
Tàicháng governs bestowal and rewards,
Báihǔ governs conflict and litigation,
Tiānkōng governs emptiness and depletion.
The nine spirits of Dùnjiǎ:
Tiānféng is in Kǎn,
also named Zǐjīng,
a wood spirit.
In the Dipper, it resides at the Pòjūn star.
Tiānnèi is in Kūn,
also named Zǐchéng,
a water spirit.
In the Dipper, it resides at the Pòjūn star.
Tiānchōng is in Zhèn,
also named Zǐqiào,
a metal spirit.
In the Dipper, it resides at the Pòjūn star.
Tiānfǔ is in Xùn,
also named Zǐwén,
an earth spirit.
In the Dipper, it resides at the Wǔqū star.
Tiānqín is in Kūn,
also named Zǐgōng,
a fire spirit.
In the Dipper, it resides at the Liánzhēn star.
Tiānxīn is in Qián,
also named Zǐxiāng,
a wood spirit.
In the Dipper, it resides at the Wénqū star.
Tiānzhù is in Duì,
also named Zǐwéi,
a water spirit.
In the Dipper, it resides at the Lùcún star.
Tiānrèn is in Gèn,
also named Zǐjīn,
a metal spirit.
In the Dipper, it resides at the Jùmén star.
Tiānyīng is in Lí,
also named Zǐshā,
an earth spirit.
In the Dipper, it resides at the Tānláng star.
From Tiānféng downward,
all are names of stars.
Zǐjīng:
because zǐ and wǔ form the warp of heaven and earth.
Its position being in Kǎn,
it is therefore named Jīng.
Tiānnèi Zǐchéng:
Kūn is earth.
It can complete the myriad things.
Tiānchōng Zǐqiào:
Qiào means stirring appearance;
it is the image of stirring in Zhèn.
Tiānfǔ Zǐwén:
Xùn is for commands,
having literary patterns.
Tiānqín Zǐgōng:
It occupies the position of the fifth earth,
lodged in Kūn.
Earth is the father of the myriad things,
hence it is called Gōng.
Tiānxīn Zǐxiāng:
Xiāng means good.
Qián is heaven,
which benevolently bestows, therefore it is good.
Tiānzhù Zǐwéi:
Duì governs metal.
Metal involves killing and warfare,
which goes against the way of heaven, hence the name.
Tiānrèn Zǐjīn:
Gèn is at chǒu.
Chǒu is the root of metal.
Tiānyīng Zǐshā:
Lí is fire.
Fire has the meaning of burning.
The Dùnjiǎ Jīng says:
Tiānféng is suitable for securing borders and maintaining stability.
Tiānnèi is suitable for honoring the Way and forming friendships.
Tiānchōng is suitable for sending out armies and avenging enemies.
Tiānfǔ is suitable for cultivating rites and establishing teachings.
Tiānqín is suitable for requesting blessings and eliminating evils.
Tiānxīn is suitable for avoiding illness and seeking medicine.
Tiānzhù is suitable for hiding, garrisoning, and defending firmly.
Tiānrèn is suitable for celebrations, visits, and facilitating wealth.
Tiānyīng is suitable for distant travel and making music.
The names of the nine spirits:
above they are all called "tiān,"
below they are all called "zǐ" because
these spirits belong to the Northern Dipper,
and are all subordinate to heaven.
"Zǐ" is an honorific,
because these spirits are revered and esteemed.
Kǒngzǐ Yuánchén says:
The first spirit of the Northern Dipper,
styled Xīshénzǐ;
the second spirit,
styled Zhēnwénzǐ;
the third spirit,
styled Lùcúnzǐ;
the fourth spirit,
styled Shìhuìzǐ;
the fifth spirit,
styled Wèibùlínzǐ;
the sixth spirit,
styled Wēihuìzǐ;
the seventh spirit,
styled Dàjǐngzǐ.
These also all use "zǐ."
Chūnqiū Zuǒzhùqī says:
The first star spirit is named Zhíyīn,
surname Jǐngliáng;
the second star spirit is named Dòuliàng,
surname Yīyǔdāng;
the third star spirit is named Jùlǐ,
surname Yīngdāolǐngxǔ;
the fifth star spirit is named Fángwǔ,
surname Jīyǐndǔ;
the sixth star spirit is named Kāibǎo,
surname Chī,
also named Cāng'érbù;
the seventh star spirit is named Zhāo,
surname Féituōluòféng.
The names of the seven stars
are all associated with people's year and destiny,
constantly thought of and recited
to seek blessings.
Huángdì Bā Shén Tú says:
The Qián spirit is Xuānyuán,
heaven's assistant envoy,
lodged at the Chén star.
The Duì spirit is Shíxíng,
envoy of the Northern Dipper,
lodged at the Niú star,
presiding over chariots and tools.
The Kūn spirit is Zhāoyáo,
heaven's senior duke envoy,
lodged at the Jiǎo star,
presiding over killing and harm.
The Lí spirit is Hàoshí,
heaven's roaming inciter envoy,
lodged at the Yì star.
The Xùn spirit is Tiānhòu,
heaven's law enforcement envoy,
lodged at the Zī star.
The Zhèn spirit is Léigōng,
the Great Yin's observer envoy,
lodged at the Qīxīng.
The Gèn spirit is Qūlóng,
the Tiānhòu Dōngmíng's envoy,
lodged at the Kuí star.
The Kǎn spirit is Xiánchí,
heaven's rain master envoy,
lodged at the Jǐng star, presiding over rain.
These are the eight envoy spirits.
When women give birth and nurse,
they should avoid facing them directly.
These are also spirits of the Nine Palaces.
Since spirits are pure and ethereal,
they wander without fixed abodes.
Therefore, within the palaces,
their appearances sometimes differ.
Since the eight trigrams are matched with the five phases,
the methods of divination and observation for these various spirits are appended here.
Each has separate annotations;
there is no need here
to elaborate on the trivial meanings of the names.
Therefore, a brief discussion suffices.
As for the sun, moon, stars, and constellations,
wind, rain, thunder, and lightning,
mountains, rivers, peaks, and waterways,
wells, stoves, crossbeams, and gates,
and even the various spirits of the human body—they are not uniform.
They are revered and sacrificed to by emperors and kings,
and prayed to by the common people.
Examples such as these
are extremely numerous in name and number.
Regarding the five phases,
they hold no distinct significance.
Therefore, they are not fully discussed.
Moreover, the various spirits used in divination and milfoil stalks,
the killing calendars and various spirits,
are precisely within the intervals of the years and months,
between the sequences of the seasons and months.
Nor is there need for detailed discussion.
Why labor over forced interpretations?
The aforementioned various spirits
are the guiding principles for divination and observation,
the essential principles of the three realms.
Therefore, they are described in sequence.
Since ancient times,
the discussions about the Five Emperors
have generally been of three types.
The Hé Tú states:
The Blue Emperor of the East,
Líng Wēi Yǎng,
is the Wood Emperor.
The Red Emperor of the South,
Chì Biāo Nù,
is the Fire Emperor.
The Yellow Emperor of the Center,
Hán Shū Niǔ,
is the Earth Emperor.
The White Emperor of the West,
Bái Zhāo Jù,
is the Metal Emperor.
The Black Emperor of the North,
Xié Guāng Jì,
is the Water Emperor.
Táo Huáyáng states:
There were five brothers: Huáng Bó, Huáng Zhòng, Huáng Shū, Huáng Jì, and Huáng Shào.
These are Líng Wēi Yǎng and the others,
all five being heavenly deities.
They descend to govern the world,
overseeing spirits and ghosts,
succeeding one another in order,
and ruling from the Tàiwēi Palace.
Their essences form the seats of the Five Emperors.
The five stars follow the reigning king and receive their vital force.
These are the ones worshipped in the Bright Hall.
Therefore it is said:
"Sacrificing to King Wén in the Bright Hall,
to match him with the Supreme God."
The Book of Rites says:
In the month of spring,
its emperor is Dà Hào;
in the month of summer,
its emperor is Yán Dì;
in the central earth,
its emperor is Huáng Dì;
in the month of autumn,
its emperor is Shào Hào;
in the month of winter,
its emperor is Zhuān Xū.
Dà Hào, Fúxī of the East, presides over spring,
the sovereign of the blue essence.
Yán Dì, Shénnóng of the South, presides over summer,
the sovereign of the red essence.
Huáng Dì, Xuānyuán of the Center, presides over the four seasons,
the sovereign of the yellow essence.
Bái Dì, Jīntiān of the West, presides over autumn,
the sovereign of the white essence.
Hēi Dì, Zhuān Xū of the North, presides over winter,
the sovereign of the black essence.
The Book of Changes says:
"The emperor emerges from Zhèn."
This marks the beginning of human emperors,
starting with Fúxī.
In the order of the Five Phases,
Wood comes first;
in the alternation of the four seasons,
spring is the beginning.
Therefore, Fúxī is the first of the Five Emperors.
Furthermore, various histories refer to Shào Hào, Zhuān Xū, Gāo Xīn, Táng, and Yú
as the Five Emperors.
This refers to the period before Shùn,
where the Five Phases succeeded one another in the emperorship.
The Book of Changes, however, takes Fúxī from above
down to Yú Shùn,
not mentioning the three emperors in between,
because they followed and cultivated without creating anew.
How can this be explained?
Therefore, they are not discussed.
The Great Hào Emperor Fúxī
had the surname Fēng.
His mother, Huá Xū,
trod in a giant's footprint
and gave birth to him in Chéngjì,
with a serpent's body and a human head.
He ruled the world by the virtue of Wood,
being the first of the hundred kings.
The Book of Changes says:
"The emperor emerges from Zhèn."
Zhèn is Wood,
the East presiding over spring,
symbolizing the brightness of the sun;
hence he was called Dà Hào.
Based on the patterns of a turtle's shell,
he drew the Eight Trigrams,
and made nets for hunting and fishing.
In ancient times,
humans and animals preyed on each other,
causing much harm.
The emperor observed a spider's web
and taught the people to capture sacrificial animals,
to supply the kitchen;
hence he was called Páo Xī,
also known as Xī Huáng.
Later generations mispronounced it,
calling him Fú Xī,
or sometimes Mì Xī.
He also had the title Xióng Huáng Shì.
The Xiàojīng Gōu Mìng Jué states:
Fúxī had a horn-like forehead, pearl-like eyebrows, and wore a victory headdress.
The Lǐ Hán Wén Jiā states:
Fúxī's virtue harmonized above and below;
heaven responded with the patterns of birds and beasts,
earth responded with the turtle's script.
Fúxī took these images and created the Eight Trigrams.
Yán Dì, Shénnóng,
had the surname Jiāng.
His mother, Rén Sì,
named Nǚ Dēng,
was moved by a divine dragon and gave birth to the emperor in Chángyáng,
with a human body and an ox's head.
Succeeding Wood with Fire,
he held the southern position, presiding over summer.
Hence he was called Yán Dì.
He created the plow and spade,
first teaching the people to farm,
distinguishing plants,
and having people eat grains,
to replace the lives of sacrificial animals.
Hence he was called Shénnóng,
also known as Kuí Wéi Shì.
He was the Agricultural Emperor.
The Lǐ Hán Wén Jiā states:
Shénnóng created the way of farming,
devising the plow and spade.
Heaven responded with auspicious grains,
earth brought forth sweet springs.
Huáng Dì, Xuānyuán,
had the surname Jī.
His mother, Fù Bǎo,
saw a great lightning flash encircling the pivot star of the Northern Dipper,
illuminating the countryside,
and was moved to give birth to the emperor in Shòuqiū.
Succeeding Fire with Earth,
he held the central position.
Hence he was called Huáng Dì.
He regulated the five vital forces, established the five stars,
first made garments with upper and lower parts,
created boats and carts,
and built houses.
In ancient times, people lived in nests and caves.
Huáng Dì changed this,
using pillars above and eaves below,
to shelter from wind and rain;
hence he was called Xuānyuán.
It is also said
he lived on Xuānyuán Hill,
and thus took this as his name.
He was also called Dì Hóng Shì,
or Guī Cáng Shì,
or Yǒu Xióng Shì.
The Chūnqiū Wén Yào Gōu states:
Huáng Dì had a dragon-like countenance, possessing a heavenly brow,
modeled after the central constellations,
taking the image of Wénchāng.
The Lǐ Hán Wén Jiā states:
Huáng Dì cultivated military arms,
and through virtuous conduct,
the yellow dragon arrived,
and the phoenix came to perform.
Shào Hào, Jīntiān,
had the surname Jī.
His given name was Zhì,
courtesy name Qīng Yáng.
His mother, Nǚ Jié,
saw a great star like a rainbow descending to Huá Zhǔ,
dreamt of union, was moved, and gave birth to the emperor.
Succeeding Earth with Metal,
he was called Jīntiān.
He is the Bái Dì Zhū Xuān mentioned in the charts and prophecies.
He held the western position, presiding over autumn.
Metal has brightness,
occupying the lesser yin position.
Hence he was called Shào Hào.
The Wén Yào Gōu states:
Emperor Kù bore a shield,
this is called clarity and brightness.
He initiated the nodes and shifted the measures.
He modeled himself after Zhāoyáo.
Zhuān Xū, Gāoyáng,
had the surname Jī.
His mother, Jǐng Pú,
saw the shimmering light star piercing the moon like a rainbow,
was moved, and gave birth to the emperor at Ruò Shuǐ.
Succeeding Metal with Water,
he held the northern position, presiding over winter.
Hence he was called Zhuān Xū.
The Wén Yào Gōu states:
Zhuān Xū combined the stem,
modeling above on the moon and constellation Shēn,
gathered authority to complete order,
to regulate yin and yang.
These Five Emperors are the ones matched with the five directions in the rites.
Emperor Kù, of the Gāoxīn clan, bore the surname Jī.
He was born with divine and extraordinary qualities,
and he himself said his name was Qūn.
With wood succeeding water,
he named officials according to the Five Phases,
hence he was called Gāoxīn.
The "Records of Emperors and Kings" states:
Gāoxīn had overlapping teeth,
possessed sagely virtue,
and could harmonize with the three luminaries.
Emperor Yáo, of the Táotáng clan, bore the surname Qí.
His mother, Qìngdū,
went out to the Luò River islet and encountered a red dragon,
conceived through spiritual influence for fourteen months,
and gave birth to the Emperor at Dānlíng,
naming him Fàngxūn.
With fire succeeding wood,
his elder brother, Emperor Zhì,
enfeoffed him at Táng.
Therefore, he was called the Táotáng clan.
The "Wényào Gōu" states:
Yáo had eyebrows of eight colors,
which is called "penetrating brightness."
He observed and modeled himself on the sun and moon,
established regulations and examined achievements.
The "Lǐ Hánwénjiā" states:
Yáo's influence broadly extended to the four borders,
reaching even to tortoises and dragons.
Emperor Shùn, of the Yǒuyú clan,
bore the surname Yáo.
His mother, Wòdēng, saw a great rainbow,
and through spiritual influence conceived and gave birth to the Emperor at Yáoxū.
His name was Chónghuá,
and his courtesy name was Dūjūn.
His eyes had double pupils,
hence he was named Chónghuá.
With earth succeeding fire,
Yáo enfeoffed him at Yú,
hence he was called the Yǒuyú clan,
and established five-colored garments.
The "Wényào Gōu" states:
Shùn had double pupils.
This is called "zīliàng,"
responding above to Shètí,
to govern the three lights.
The "Lǐ Wénjiā" states:
Shùn diminished himself
to bring peace to the hundred clans,
causing birds and beasts to gather harmoniously,
and phoenixes to come and perform.
These three emperors, together with Shǎohào and Zhuānxū,
constitute the Five Emperors.
The "Records of the Grand Historian" takes Fúxī, Nǚwā, and Shénnóng as the Three Sovereigns,
and those from Huángdì onward as the Five Emperors.
The "Records of Emperors and Kings"
takes Xīhuáng, Shénnóng, and Huángdì as the Three Sovereigns,
and those from Shǎohào onward as the Five Emperors.
Now, examining the "Book of Rites,"
the suburban sacrifices match the Five Virtues,
from Fúxī to Zhuānxū as the Five Emperors.
This is their correct position.
The reason for this is
the "Book of Changes" states that the Emperor emerges from Zhèn.
This is the beginning of the Five Virtues.
Proceeding in order,
reaching Zhuānxū,
the count of the Five Virtues ends.
If Shǎohào were taken as the beginning,
then metal is not the first of the Five Virtues.
If Huángdì were taken as the beginning,
earth occupies the center,
and is fundamentally not the initiating phase.
Therefore, taking wood as the first,
Fúxī is the beginning of the Five Virtues.
The "Book of Changes" statement is correct.
From Emperor Kù onward,
all follow in succession according to order.
The Supreme Deities are five.
Matters such as the surnames of Língwēiyǎng and others,
due to the great antiquity of Fúxī's era,
and the loss and omission of classical texts,
cannot be fully explained.
However, the succession of the Five Virtues
means receiving the Mandate of Heaven,
which must be preceded by auspicious signs,
to manifest flourishing convergence.
If it is a ruler responding to the Mandate,
they all receive the essence of the Five Emperors of Tàiwēi,
to be born into the world,
and there must be prior omens,
showing their budding signs.
When wood reigns, it is the son of the Green Emperor;
when fire reigns, it is the son of the Red Emperor;
when earth reigns, it is the son of the Yellow Emperor;
when metal reigns, it is the son of the White Emperor;
when water reigns, it is the son of the Black Emperor.
Therefore, the "Lùtú" states:
The Eastern Green Emperor,
his body is the Azure Dragon.
Such a person has a long head,
a large face with prominent horn bones,
and full, broad eyebrows and back.
He succeeds metal and passes to fire.
The Southern Red Emperor,
his body is the Vermilion Bird.
Such a person has a pointed head,
a round face, square jaw, wide-open eyes,
narrow above and broad below,
with beard and sideburns lying on the chest.
He succeeds water and passes to earth.
The Central Yellow Emperor,
his body is Xuānyuán.
Such a person has a square face with a broad forehead,
a pointed chin and relaxed lips,
and a full, thick back.
He succeeds wood and passes to metal.
The Western White Emperor,
his body is the White Tiger.
Such a person has a square forehead.
A straight face with a pointed mouth,
a large nose and small horn.
He succeeds fire and passes to water.
The Northern Black Emperor,
his body is the Dark Warrior.
Such a person has a narrow face and pointed head,
deep-set eyes and thick ears,
a hanging belly and reversed feathers.
He succeeds earth and passes to wood.
These all represent the qi of the Five Phases,
following their order of succession,
to be passed on in turn.
The "Gǎnjīng Fú" states:
The Green Emperor, from afar appears broad,
up close appears vast.
The Red Emperor, from afar appears like fire,
blazing brightly,
up close appears pointed above.
The Yellow Emperor, from afar appears small,
up close appears large,
broad, thick, and square.
The White Emperor, from afar appears bright,
up close appears lush.
The Black Emperor, from afar appears huge,
up close appears tender.
The "Yuánmìng Bāo" states:
When the Green Essence is in charge,
it corresponds to the year star.
When the Red Essence is in charge,
it corresponds to the spark star.
When the Yellow Essence is in charge,
it corresponds to the stabilizing star.
When the White Essence is in charge,
it corresponds to the great white star.
When the Black Essence is in charge,
it corresponds to the celestial star.
These all show how the Five Virtues correspond to the Five Phases,
with mother and son passing on in succession.
If it is not in the correct order,
there will necessarily be conquest and attack,
and it will not reach its end.
The Qín dynasty, with its metal virtue, attacked Zhōu,
and perished in two generations.
The Hàn dynasty, with its fire phase, succeeded Zhōu,
attacking Qín's false metal.
Therefore, its reign was long-lasting.
If it is in accordance with this order,
then there will be auspicious signs.
The "Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo" states:
Yáo was of the fire essence,
therefore Qìngdū, through spiritual influence from a red dragon, gave birth to him.
The Hàn, because Confucius obtained the unicorn,
received a chart and text stating:
The Jī lineage of Zhōu will perish,
the fire brilliance of Liú will arise,
the Emperor with the character for "gold" in "卯金."
Therefore, Gāozǔ beheaded the white snake,
and a divine mother wept, saying:
"The son of the Red Emperor has killed my son, the White Emperor."
Guāngwǔ, through spiritual influence from the Red Talisman, restored the dynasty.
These are all omens of the fire virtue.
The spiritual influences for the other four phases
are all examples like this.
The auspicious signs of past emperors and kings are not singular.
They cannot all be recounted.
Now, briefly discussing the Five Emperors,
their correlation with the Five Phases is as above.
Since the time of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
the establishment of official positions has not been fixed.
All were based on auspicious signs,
with different names and titles.
Some used birds or dragons,
others used clouds or fire.
Without exception, they observed the heavens above and the earth below,
setting up positions according to circumstances.
Although the eras were not the same,
the Five Phases remained consistent.
By the time of Zhuānxū,
official positions were established based on human affairs.
The Southern Regulator Zhòng was in charge of the heavens and connected to the spirits,
while the Northern Regulator Lí was in charge of the earth and connected to the people.
Thus, spirits and people were not separated.
Gāoxīnshì established official titles based on the Five Phases.
Gōumáng was appointed as the Wood Regulator,
Zhùróng as the Fire Regulator,
Rùshōu as the Metal Regulator,
Xuánmíng as the Water Regulator,
and Hòutǔ as the Earth Regulator,
each taking charge of their respective duties.
Shàohàoshì had four sons:
Zhòng, Gāi, Xiū, and Xī.
Zhòng became Gōumáng,
the spirit of the Wood Office.
Gāi became Rùshōu,
the spirit of the Metal Office.
Xiū and Xī together became Xuánmíng,
the spirit of the Water Office.
The son of Zhuānxūshì, named Lí,
became Zhùróng,
the spirit of the Fire Office.
The son of Gònggōngshì, named Gōulóng,
became Hòutǔ,
the spirit of the Earth Office.
These five spirits were born as high nobles
and became revered spirits after death.
They are also called the Five Sacrifices,
already matched with the Five Phases.
The Book of Zhou states:
King Wǔ of Zhōu was constructing Luòyì but had not yet completed it.
The spirits of the Four Seas all gathered and said,
"The King of Zhōu is divine and sagely,
he should know our names.
If he does not know, floods and droughts will ruin him."
The following year, it snowed for over ten ten-day periods,
accumulating over ten feet deep.
Five great officials rode in carriages,
followed by two horsemen, and stopped at the king's gate.
Tàigōng said,
"The carriages and horses leave no tracks—
this indicates they are transformed humans."
He then sent someone to offer them porridge, saying,
"We do not know the ranks of the guests."
The horseman replied,
"First serve the Ruler of the South Sea,
then the Ruler of the East Sea,
then the Ruler of the North Sea,
then the Ruler of the West Sea,
then Hébó,
then Fēngbó,
then Yǔshī."
King Wǔ asked Tàigōng,
"What are all their names?"
Tàigōng replied,
"The spirit of the South Sea is named Zhùróng,
the spirit of the East Sea is named Gōumáng,
the spirit of the North Sea is named Xuánmíng,
the spirit of the West Sea is named Rùshōu."
The Book of Rites, Monthly Ordinances states:
In the months of spring,
its spirit is Gōumáng;
in the months of summer,
its spirit is Zhùróng;
in the central earth,
its spirit is Hòutǔ;
in the months of autumn,
its spirit is Rùshōu;
in the months of winter,
its spirit is Xuánmíng.
This is correct.
These five directional spirits
are matched with the Five Phases.
Moreover, the Yellow Emperor established the positions of the Three Dukes,
to correspond to the Three Platforms stars.
Fēnghòu corresponded to the Upper Platform,
Tiānlǎo corresponded to the Middle Platform,
Wǔshèng corresponded to the Lower Platform,
and he established left and right overseers.
This also refers to the Five Phases.
The Four Directors separately governed the four directions,
which is the method of the four seasons.
Yáo used the four sons of Yìhé,
