Wèi corresponds to the sheep, hawk, and wild goose.
The Shì Jīng states:
Wèi is Xiǎojí.
It governs marriage ceremonies and betrothals.
Marriage ceremonies use sheep and wild geese.
Zhèng Xuán's Hūnlǐ Yè Wén states:
The wild goose observes yin and yang,
awaiting the proper time to act.
The Yì takes Kūn as the sheep.
Kūn is in Wèi.
The Book of Rites, Monthly Ordinances states:
in the late summer month,
young hawks begin to learn.
This is paired according to the seasonal phenomena.
The *Běnshēng Jīng* states: The old wood is
because *wèi* is the tomb of wood.
Wood reaches its old age in the sixth month.
*Shēn* is associated with monkeys and apes because
autumn is the season of killing energy.
All things grow old,
and the appearance of monkeys and apes
resembles that of old men.
In the seventh month, mountain fruits all ripen.
Monkeys and apes become kings during their time of storing food.
The *Shì Jīng* states:
When the metal energy is strong,
it can age all things.
This is the appearance of monkeys and apes.
The *Jiāyǔ* states:
Five times nine is forty-five,
five corresponds to sound,
and sound governs the ape.
Apes are born in the fifth month.
*Wǔ* contains the bathing metal,
but the killing energy is not yet strong.
When it reaches *shēn*, metal becomes king,
and the killing energy begins to strengthen.
It also says:
While in fire, there is no sound;
only upon leaving the fire does its sound form.
Therefore, both are associated with *shēn*.
The *Běnshēng Jīng* says that dawn is associated with jade because
jade has a warm, moist, and clanging sound.
Hence, it is associated with dawn.
Dusk is associated with dead stone because
stone is of the jade category
and also has sound.
It is said that its energy declines,
so at dusk it is called dead.
Both jade and stone are the essence of metal,
so they are both assigned to the metal position.
The ape is also of the same category.
Therefore, it is assigned accordingly.
*Yǒu* is associated with chickens, pheasants, and crows because
*yǒu* corresponds to metal,
which represents martial prowess.
The chicken possesses five virtues,
with martial virtue being foremost.
It will fight upon seeing an enemy.
This is its inherent nature.
The *Shuōtí Cí* states:
The chicken accumulates yang,
symbolizing the south.
Fire, yang, and refined things ascend.
Therefore, when yang emerges, the chicken crows,
resonating through similarity.
The *Kǎoyì Yóu* states:
The chicken is a fire animal.
*Chǒu* is near *yín*.
*Yín* has yang and generates fire.
It rejoices, hence it crows.
Martial affairs must have commands,
so it is placed in the west.
*Xùn* corresponds to the chicken,
also representing commands.
*Chén* and *sì* both combine with *yǒu*,
hence it is in *yǒu*.
The pheasant is a fire bird.
It embodies martial majesty.
The *Fāngjì Zhuàn* states:
When Venus shines brightly,
the chicken crows;
when Mars flows with radiance,
the pheasant is startled.
The *Yì Tōng Guà Yàn* states:
The pheasant is yang.
When the male calls, the female responds.
This signifies yang leading and yin harmonizing.
It calls at the appropriate time,
also representing the idea of commands.
The crow is a yin bird,
yet resides in the sun.
The *Yuánmìng Bāo* states:
The crow in the sun
symbolizes yang embracing yin.
Because it resides in the sun and receives yang energy,
it is benevolent and can feed its parents in return.
Its association with *yǒu* is because
in spring, the sun approaches *duì*,
and *yǒu* is the gate of two eights,
the place where the sun sets,
signifying its end.
Therefore, all are assigned to *yǒu*.
It also says dusk is associated with dead right because
it signifies the decline of metal energy.
The *Qín Biàn* says dusk is associated with dead earth because
earth reaches the end of metal,
and its energy declines and decays.
The *Běnshēng Jīng* states dusk is associated with the falcon because
the falcon also strikes swiftly and has martial utility.
Lacking the five virtues, it is associated with dusk.
*Xū* is associated with dogs, wolves, and jackals because
*xū* represents dusk.
*Qián* is the heavenly gate.
Since *xū* belongs to *qián*,
it is the time of darkness,
requiring vigilance and defense.
Jīng Shì's *Biéduì* states:
The dog is the master of movement,
guarding against treachery.
The *Yì Jīng* says:
*Gèn* corresponds to the dog.
*Gèn* represents gates and barriers.
The dog is for guarding and defense.
The *Jiāyǔ* states:
Seven times nine is sixty-three,
three governs the Dipper,
and the Dipper governs the dog.
Dogs are born in the third month.
*Chén* opposes *xū*,
and *yín* combines with *xū*,
hence it is in *xū*.
The *Lǐjì Yuèlìng* states:
In the ninth month,
jackals sacrifice animals.
Therefore, they are assigned accordingly.
Wolves are similar in form.
The *Shuōwén* states:
Jackals belong to the wolf family.
Therefore, both reside in *xū*.
One says dusk is associated with dead metal because
metal declines and decays by *xū*.
The *Qín Biàn* says dusk is associated with dead fire because
*xū* is the tomb of fire.
*Hài* is associated with pigs, boars, and badgers because
the *Shì Jīng* states:
*Hài* is mixed water,
symbolizing filth, turbidity, and latrines,
where pigs dwell.
Pigs are black in color,
resembling the color of water.
Their cloven hooves
symbolize yin.
They invariably rise at the fifth watch,
never missing their routine,
just as water has tides that do not miss their time.
The Family Sayings states:
Six times nine is fifty-four,
four governs the seasons,
the seasons govern the pig.
The pig is born in the fourth month.
It clashes with Sì, thus it is in Hài.
The pig is the smaller kind of swine.
The yá is also taken for its kind,
and it likes to roam at night.
This is due to its yin nature.
Therefore, both are in Hài.
One says that at dawn it is the living wood—
wood is born in Hài.
At dusk it is the slug—
■ (quǎn + yú) should be yóu.
I fear the character is mistaken.
Another says at dawn it is the suckling pig—
the suckling pig is the same as the pig.
One says at dusk it is the rotten wood—
wood, when first born, is soft;
when submerged in water,
it thus rots and decays.
Question:
The categories of birds and insects are numerous.
Why then are the qilin and phoenix not chosen as zodiac animals,
but instead earthworms, snakes, rats, and small insects are taken?
Answer:
The selection of the twelve zodiac animals
is based on their awareness of seasonal changes and qi,
whether in color or form,
all corresponding to yin and yang.
The qilin and phoenix are already paired with the Five Numinous Creatures.
It is not that they are left unused without reason.
Another question:
Since the qilin and phoenix are already paired with the Five Numinous Creatures,
and are no longer chosen,
the dragon and tiger are also paired,
why are they reused?
Answer:
When the dragon stirs, clouds arise;
when the tiger roars, winds rise.
This is a response to the qi of yin and yang.
Therefore, they must be chosen.
Though the qilin and phoenix are numinous,
they do not stir or act,
thus they are not reused.
These twelve zodiac animals
are all the qi of the Dipper stars.
Scattered, they become human fate,
connected to the Northern Dipper,
hence they are used as zodiac animals.
The Chunqiu Yundou Shu states:
The Pivot Star scatters to become the dragon and horse;
the Whirl Star scatters to become the tiger;
the Mechanism Star scatters to become the dog;
the Balance Star scatters to become the snake;
the Jade Balance scatters to become the chicken, rabbit, and rat;
the Harmony Star scatters to become the sheep and ox;
the Shaking Light scatters to become the monkey and ape.
These all correspond to celestial stars above,
and belong to human fate below.
The thirty-six animals,
each occupying a direction,
serve as the leaders of birds and insects,
commanding three hundred sixty,
multiplied by ten,
reaching three thousand six hundred.
All are matched with the Five Phases,
interconnected and leading one another.
Since they are not used for divination,
they are not explained in detail.
